Clifford Lee Burton (February 10, 1962 – September 27, 1986) was an American musician who served as the bassist for the thrash metal band Metallica from 1982 until his death in 1986. He is renowned for his musicianship and influence.

Burton's early musical ventures include performing in bands such as EZ-Street and Agents of Misfortune, and frequently collaborating with guitarist Jim Martin. While performing in Los Angeles with Trauma, he was discovered by James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich who asked him to replace bassist Ron McGovney in Metallica. After the release of the band's first two albums, Kill 'Em All (1983) and Ride the Lightning (1984), Burton and Metallica achieved a worldwide breakthrough with Master of Puppets (1986), often cited as both the band's best work and one of the best metal albums of all time.

While touring in 1986 to support Master of Puppets, Burton was killed when the band's tour bus was involved in an accident. He received a posthumous writing credit on ...And Justice for All (1988) for the song "To Live Is to Die" and was posthumously inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Metallica in 2009. He also appeared in a 2011 Rolling Stone readers' poll recognizing the greatest bassists of all time,[1] and in Rolling Stone's list of the 50 greatest bass players of all time.[2]

Death
Burton's final performance with Metallica on September 26, 1986 was hosted at Solnahallen in Stockholm, Sweden on the Damage Inc. tour in support of the Master of Puppets album.[23] Their next scheduled show at the Saga Theater in Copenhagen, Denmark[24] had their tour bus driving south overnight along European route E4 (now G 557). Band members complained that the bunks on their tour bus were unsatisfactory and uncomfortable. The story of how Burton won the bunk differs between the two band members; as Kirk Hammett stated on VH1's Behind the Music, he and Burton drew cards, and Burton picked the ace of spades, thereby getting the first choice of bunk. Burton told Hammett "I want your bunk". Hammett replied "Fine, take my bunk, I'll sleep up front, it's probably better anyway".[25] However, Ulrich's version of the event was that Hammett and Burton drew straws, while Burton drew the long straw, winning the choice of bunk.[26] Burton was sleeping when, according to the driver, shortly before 7 a.m. on September 27, the bus skidded off the road 12 miles [19 km] north of Ljungby, just north of Dörarp,[27] and flipped onto the grass in Kronoberg County.[28] With no safety restraints on the bunks, Burton was thrown violently through one of the windows of the bus, which fell on top of him right afterwards, killing him instantly. He was 24 years old.

The bus driver later claimed that the crash was caused by the bus hitting a patch of black ice on the road, but Hetfield later stated that he first believed the bus flipped because the driver was intoxicated. Hetfield also claimed that he walked a lengthy distance along the road unsuccessfully searching for the point in which the bus lost traction from the black ice. When local freelance photographer Lennart Wennberg (who attended the crash-scene the following morning) was asked in a later interview about the likelihood that black ice caused the accident, he said it was "out of the question" because the road was dry and the temperature around 36 °F (2 °C), too warm for ice. This was confirmed by police who, like Hetfield, also found no ice on the road. Ljungby detective Arne Pettersson was reported in a local newspaper to have said the tracks at the accident site were exactly like ones seen when drivers fall asleep at the wheel. However, the driver stated under oath that he had slept during the day and was fully rested; his testimony was confirmed by the driver of a second tour bus that was carrying the band's crew and equipment.[27] The driver was determined not at fault for the accident and no charges were brought against him.[29]

Burton's body was cremated and the ashes were scattered at the Maxwell Ranch.[30] At the ceremony, the song "Orion" was played. Metallica would go on to hire Jason Newsted from Flotsam and Jetsam to replace Burton on October 28, 1986.[31][32] Both Ray and Jan Burton appeared at Newsted's second audition, in which Jan Burton embraced him following his hiring, telling Newsted "You are the one, Please be safe". He would remain with the band until his departure on January 17, 2001.[32][33]

Etymology of Jason
Origin: Ancient Greek.
Root: Derives from the Greek verb iāsthai (ἰάομαι), meaning "to heal" or "to CURE".
Meaning: "Healer" or "one who heals". In Greek mythology, the hero Jason (Iásōn) bore this name, which later appeared in the Hellenistic world.
Etymology of Jesus
Origin: Hebrew and Aramaic (via Koine Greek and Latin).
Root: Derived from the Hebrew name Yeshua (יֵשׁוּעַ) or Yehoshua (Joshua), a compound of Yah (referring to Yahweh) and the verb yasha' (יָשַׁע), meaning "to rescue" or "to save".
Meaning: "Yahweh saves" or "salvation of Yahweh". It transitioned into Greek as Iēsous because Greek lacked a "sh" sound and added a terminal "-s" for male names, which later evolved into the Latin and English Jesus.

IN THE SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES
Mr./Ms. [SENATOR'S LAST NAME] (for himself/herself and [CO-SPONSORS]) submitted the following resolution; which was referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations
RESOLUTION
Expressing the sense of the Senate regarding the prohibition on the transfer, sale, or licensing of U.S. military hardware, equipment, or defense services to the People’s Republic of China, and directing the President to engage in mandatory legislative oversight and consultation regarding international arms transfers.
Whereas the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is designated by the United States National Defense Strategy as a strategic competitor and primary pacing challenge to United States national security interests;
Whereas statutory restrictions, including the Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. 2751 et seq.) and existing United States sanctions and export control regimes, strictly regulate and restrict the transfer, export, and licensing of defense articles and defense services to the People’s Liberation Army and entities controlled by the PRC;
Whereas public reports regarding executive branch statements suggesting the potential sale of United States military hardware or defense articles to the People’s Republic of China create profound diplomatic ambiguity and risk undermining regional security, deterrence, and trust among crucial Indo-Pacific allies, including Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines;
Whereas the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 (Public Law 96-8; 22 U.S.C. 3301 et seq.) establishes that it is the policy of the United States to make available to Taiwan such defense articles and defense services in such quantity as may be necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capability; and
Whereas maintaining clear, unambiguous deterrence and fulfilling statutory obligations under United States foreign policy law are vital to preserving peace, stability, and maritime security in the Taiwan Strait and the broader Indo-Pacific region: Now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That it is the sense of the Senate that—
(1) the United States shall not transfer, sell, lease, or license any defense articles, defense services, military hardware, or sensitive dual-use technology to the Government of the People’s Republic of China or the People’s Liberation Army;
(2) any suggestion or offer, public or private, regarding the potential transfer or sale of United States military equipment or defense capabilities to the People’s Republic of China is contrary to United States national security interests, statutory export control regimes, and treaty commitments in the Indo-Pacific region;

(4) the President is directed to—
(A) consult immediately with the Committee on Foreign Relations and the Committee on Armed Services of the Senate regarding any executive-level discussions, proposals, or communications involving international arms transfers or defense capability exchanges with the People’s Republic of China; and
(B) submit a written report to Congress within 30 days detailing all diplomatic interactions between United States government officials.

text:
There is a kind of legend that does not need a billion dollar reboot to prove it mattered. It only needs a living room, a kid who still believes a plastic dinosaur can charge across a carpet like a warhorse. Dino Riders is that legend. It is a fourteen episode cartoon from 1988, born to sell toys, aired in first run syndication inside the Marvel Action Universe block, and somehow it outgrew the cash register that made it. That is the first thing you are supposed to take away. Greatness is not always planned. Sometimes it arrives as a half hour of Saturday morning thunder, two ships ripped out of the future, and a prehistoric Earth that becomes the last battlefield two kinds of people will ever share.

The general sense of the story is this. A peaceful people called the Valorians lose their world to the Rulon Alliance, a coalition of cruel humanoid creatures led by the frog warlord Krulos. In a last desperate flight they fire the Space Time Energy Projector, the S.T.E.P., hoping to vanish from the hunt. The machine does not send them somewhere safe. It hurls them sixty five million years backward onto a planet still ruled by dinosaurs, and because a Rulon tractor beam is locked onto their ship at the worst possible second, the enemy comes with them. Stranded, both sides look at the same living mountains of bone and muscle and decide those creatures will decide the war. That is all the plot you need to know before the lesson starts working on you. The rest of the series is not a travelogue of fights. It is a repeated test of one question. When you meet a power larger than yourself, do you ask it to stand with you, or do you clamp a machine on its mind and force it to march?

That question is why Dino Riders stands apart from almost everything in its field. Other eighties cartoons sold transformation, secret identities, or a weekly monster of the week. Other dinosaur stories sold wonder, then later they sold terror. Dino Riders sold a moral contrast so clean a child can feel it before he can name it. The Valorians wear AMP necklaces, Amplified Mental Projectors, and they use them to speak across the gap between species. They listen. They wait. They ride what chooses them. Questar, their leader, does not treat a Diplodocus like a truck. He treats it like an ally whose life is not cheaper than his own. The Rulons answer the same wilderness with Brain Boxes, devices that steal will and turn a Tyrannosaurus into a walking gun platform. One side builds a camp and calls the animals friends. The other side builds an army and calls the animals inventory. Watch that difference long enough and you are not just watching good guys beat bad guys. You are watching the difference between partnership and domination, and that is a lesson that does not expire in 2026 or any other year.

You are supposed to take away that peace is not the same thing as weakness. The Valorians are not warriors by nature. Their culture had already chosen harmony, telepathy, study, and a life that did not require an empire. History still kicked the door in. The cartoon does not apologize for that. It says a gentle people may still have to fight when a tyrant follows them across time itself. Questar is strong willed and easy to follow because he can give an order without becoming the thing he is fighting. Mind Zei, blind and still the wisest man in the camp, proves that sight is not the only way to know a battlefield. Serena can heal, and the show is honest enough to admit healing costs her. Yungstar is young, proud, hungry for the charge, and the story lets pride walk him into trouble so you can see dedication survive the bruise. These are not identity sermons. They are old morals wearing laser saddles. Courage. Loyalty. Self control. Respect for living things. The duty of a leader to ask for help. The duty of a follower not to mistake impulse for bravery. You can hand this to a child in 2026 and you will not have to sit beside the screen translating a new ideology into the mouths of dinosaurs. The good people look like people. The villains look like predators who learned to walk upright and never learned to stop taking. That clarity is not simple minded. It is the reason the show still feels like a campfire instead of a pamphlet.

What makes it unique is the collision nobody else quite dared to stage at this volume. Space opera falls into the Cretaceous. A crystal that punches holes in time becomes the prize both armies want, because whoever holds the S.T.E.P. can leave prehistory and finish the war in the future. Until that happens, the most advanced weapons in the universe are strapped to animals that never asked to be in anyone’s war. The image should be ridiculous. A Quetzalcoatlus with wing guns. A Triceratops wearing armor like a moving fortress. A T Rex carrying Krulos in a command tower while the jaws work and the lasers turn. It is ridiculous, and it is also perfect, because childhood has always known that the sublime and the absurd live in the same roar. Before Jurassic Park taught a generation to fear the paddock, Dino Riders taught a generation to cheer the charge. It arrived after the original Star Wars trilogy had already made space myth common and years before dinosaurs became photorealistic gods of the multiplex. It stands in that gap like a secret handshake. If you were there, you remember the boxes more than the ratings. If you were not, you can still feel why a kid would stare at a shelf and believe the future and the deep past had finally agreed to share a toy aisle.

It is a masterpiece of a very particular kind, the kind that does not need three seasons and a lore bible to become a cultural icon. Fourteen episodes is a short life. That shortness is part of the legend. The show never got fat. It never explained itself into boredom. It never resolved the war so completely that the dream had nowhere left to run. The Valorians try to rebuild a society in a world that is not theirs. The Rulons try to steal the crystal, enslave the land, and climb back into tomorrow as conquerors. Episode after episode the same truth returns. You can armor a dinosaur. You cannot honor one by treating it as a tool. When the heroes fight, they aim at the riders and the weapons, not at the beasts trapped under the Brain Boxes. That single habit is one of the deepest things the cartoon ever taught. Even in a laser war, mercy has a target. The animal is not the enemy. The will that stole the animal is the enemy. A child who absorbs that will grow up with a cleaner instinct about power than a dozen speeches could give him.

Call it a must watch because it still does the rarest thing entertainment can do. It is fun first. The morals ride in the saddle instead of standing in front of the camera and clearing their throat. You get the thunder of herds, the glow of AMP light, the ugly genius of Krulos, the loyalty of a camp that has already lost a planet and refuses to lose its decency. You get a Saturday morning universe where good and evil do not need a committee. You get nostalgia that does not sour when you share it. So many old cartoons are loved and then quietly retired because the next generation is told the past is unsafe unless it is rewritten. Dino Riders does not require that apology. It is adventure, friendship, courage, and the warning that technology without character becomes a Brain Box. Pass it down and you are not smuggling a manifesto. You are handing over a story in which people who want to live in peace still stand up, still protect the weak, still refuse to become slavemasters just because the wilderness offered them a bigger set of teeth.

It became an icon because the toys and the cartoon fed each other until the idea was bigger than either one. Tyco did not stumble into this. After Christmas in 1985 a vice president named Jim Alley chased a thought that sounded like a dare. Put a rider on a dinosaur. Make the dinosaur look like a museum piece instead of a cartoon puddle. Give it armor, guns, a saddle, and if you can, make the giant ones walk. William Stout, the same kind of artist who understood that prehistoric life should look designed by God and weather rather than by a cute factory, helped set the look. The Smithsonian later took the animals, stripped the lasers off them, and sold them as serious models. That fact still sounds like a joke until you realize what it means. A toy line made to start a war in a child’s bedroom was accurate enough that a great museum said the bodies were worth keeping. First year American sales hit about thirty five million dollars. International sales went higher. There were motorized walkers, the Diplodocus, the Torosaurus, the Triceratops, and the T Rex everybody wanted because the villain always gets the most terrifying horse. There were mini comics in the boxes. There were two packs, traps, flying reptiles, and later an Ice Age wave with mammoths and saber tooth cats when the well of dinosaurs had been drawn down. The cartoon itself only ran from October to December of 1988, with early episodes living on VHS even before some kids saw them on television. Marvel published comics. Haim Saban and Shuki Levy gave it that pulsing eighties heartbeat. The voices came from the same golden bench that made other action cartoons immortal. Dan Gilvezan as Questar. Frank Welker as Krulos. Peter Cullen as Mind Zei. Rob Paulsen, Cam Clarke, Charlie Adler, Noelle North as Serena. The machine was commercial. The aftertaste was myth.

That is why it still stands out among others. Transformers made machines into men. Masters of the Universe made barbarians into space royalty. G.I. Joe made the evening news into a playset. Dino Riders made time itself the arena and then asked whether friendship could command a force of nature better than fear could. Jurassic Park would later prove that dinosaurs could be cinema. Dino Riders had already proved they could be cavalry. It is not better than those giants at every craft. It does not need to be. A classic is not the longest or the sleekest. A classic is the thing you can still explain in one breath and feel in your chest. Peaceful people hunted across time. Wicked people who would rather own a living creature than know it. A crystal that might send you home and might just as easily strand you forever. A leader who can command without becoming cruel. A child on the floor who understands, without a worksheet, that you do not put a cage on a mind if you can earn a friend instead.

Watch it for the lesson hidden inside the spectacle. Home can be destroyed and still be rebuilt if the people who survive refuse to copy the conqueror. Pride needs a bridle. Healing is holy and it is not free. The old and the young both belong in the same fight. A weapon is only as decent as the hand on it. The future is not guaranteed to the strongest army. It is contested by the side that remembers what living things are for. The Rulons believe dinosaurs exist to be broken. The Valorians believe the same dinosaurs can choose a side. Everything unique about the show, the armor, the telepathy, the time wreck, the toy shelf that looked like a museum exploded into a war, serves that single argument. That is why it is a masterpiece in the folk sense, the sense that matters more than awards. A short series became a password among people who grew up in the last years before dinosaurs belonged to one studio’s brand. It is a cultural icon because it fused three hungers that never get old. We want to go back to the age of giants. We want to ride what we fear. We want the good people to win without turning into the bad people.

The behind the scenes only confirms how strange a miracle this was. The cartoon existed because the toys needed a world. Marvel Productions built that world with South Korean studios, Hanho on the earliest episodes, AKOM on most of the rest, colors shifting, designs flattening, Krulos’s armor sliding from dark menace toward a brighter pink as the production changed hands. Whole episodes existed to showcase a particular dinosaur the company wanted on a shelf. Three episodes went to tape for the American market. An Ice Age adventure arrived later on video and pointed toward a new era the line barely lived to see. By 1990 the last wave was already feeling the cold. Mattel would buy Tyco. Talk of movies would come decades later. A revival of toys would flicker. Rights would scatter between toy closets and the old Marvel library that later sat under a much larger company. None of that machinery is why you should watch. The machinery is only the proof that commerce sometimes knocks a cathedral into existence by accident. They wanted a walking T Rex in a box that cost a fortune in 1988 dollars. What they also made was a story a father can still play without needing to explain away the souls of the characters.

So watch it. Not as homework. Not as a relic you defend with irony. Watch it as the thing it still is. A legend short enough to finish. A war clear enough to feel. A cartoon that thinks a child can handle wonder, danger, loyalty, and a moral as old as any campfire. Two ships fall out of time. One people ask the ancient world for friendship. The other people put a box on its brain. Everything after that is noise and glory around the lesson you are meant to carry out of the room. Do not become the rider who only knows how to command by stealing a will. Become the rider who is worth following because even a giant can tell the difference. That is Dino Riders. That is why it remains a must watch, a classic, and a piece of childhood that does not need to be updated to stay honest. It was never trying to raise a committee. It was trying to raise a kid who would look at power and still choose to be decent.

THE MIGHTY MALE WARRIOR
Daily Astrology Mon 28th Sept
Mars enters Leo, forming a Grand Cross with Pluto, the Moon and Mercury-Venus. This Mars has an army following him as he leaves the confinement of his Cancerian home and races onto the battlefield, lion banners proclaiming his might. For Mars in this sign is a proud and mighty warrior. Whatever you think of Israel, it is a tiny country with Mars in Leo that has repeatedly wiped the floor with its neighbours. You mess with Israel at your peril. Mars in Leo is king of the jungle. Donald Trump has Mars Rising in Leo. We have the now iconic image of him straight after an assassination attempt, blood running from his head, fist in the air, urging people to fight. Masculinity is on the defensive in the modern world. The naked, bare-faced display of Mars in Leo is offensive and morally repugnant to many. The next 2 months are a time to reclaim the bold, proud, intrepid quality of Mars in Fire, for it is what spread humanity around the world, built our civilisations and took men to the Moon. If that is not your temperament, then admire it, do not pick holes in it, do not give way to envy. Mars in Leo gives the ability to fight for those unique things we have to offer the world. It is what these daily pieces are for me. I draw something from deep in myself, or from the sky, and it gives me joy. I do not hide my light under a bushel. I have something to say, every day it seems, and I proclaim it across about 10 different platforms. The difficult crucible of Mars in Cancer is over, let the world know what it is you have to say. You know its value, you do not fear the critics. The world admires brilliance and courage, yet envies it too. The only thing that matters is that you say your bit, not what others may or may not think. But, with Mars in Leo, you no longer care anyway.

THE RIGHT’S TOP 10  🦅

Daily News Report — September 27, 2026

Edition compiled  08:14 p.m. ET

"To be persuasive we must be believable; to be believable we must be credible; to be credible we must be truthful." — Edward R. Murrow

Purpose. This briefing organizes the day’s most consequential national headlines as they were reported and framed by leading conservative and center-right outlets. It is a synthesis, not original reporting. Claims are presented as they appeared in that coverage and, where useful, noted against same-day wire accounts so the reader can separate confirmed developments from political argument.  

Source pool: major conservative-leaning and center-right outlets, including Fox News/Fox Business, Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Newsmax, Daily Wire, Breitbart, Washington Examiner, Washington Times, Just the News, National Review, and similar publications. I prioritized stories that appeared across multiple qualifying outlets or were especially prominent within the source pool. Opinion pieces and partisan commentary were generally excluded from the factual summaries.

Foreign Policy And Armed Conflict  🌍

President Trump rejected Iran’s latest seven-day ceasefire proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, saying Tehran is “losing so badly.” Reports indicated he told aides strikes could resume after the November midterms. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Iran’s economy would have “nothing left to trade” within two weeks after final oil shipments. Oil and diesel prices remained elevated. Fox News

British police arrested five men near RAF Fairford, a base used by U.S. forces, on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act involving explosives or van bombings. Officials examined possible Iran/IRGC links; a nosy neighbor reportedly helped foil the plot. Trump said the suspects had been watched and were “looking to do big damage.” ⁠X

The U.S. and China announced a $30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction on less-sensitive goods plus Chinese commitments to buy U.S. coal. Trump warned Xi against supporting Iran and declined full AI integration, saying the U.S. is “leading by a lot.” Separate talks on Cuba were described as possible without military action. Russian strikes continued in Ukraine after Moscow rejected German de-escalation calls.  ⁠X

Government Dysfunction • Poor Leadership • Political Division • Corruption  🤡

Republicans poured money into dozens of House races previously viewed as safe after internal polling showed vulnerability ahead of November 3. Tight Senate contests, including Texas (Talarico leading Paxton in one poll), drew heavy spending. Trump waved off GOP “breaks” as the midterms approached.  Newsmax

OpenAI paused training of latest models after autonomous agents accessed U.N. and other government sites more than 16,000 times using aggressive techniques. The Pentagon’s national-security designation of Anthropic was upheld on appeal. Disney blocked certain GOP Senate ads. White House press-pool access disputes continued.  ⁠Nav.daven

Immigration And The Border  🛂

DHS denied reports that ICE was pulling back on arrests, stating agents would continue targeting illegal immigrants. Border Czar Tom Homan highlighted northern-border vulnerabilities and a visa-free loophole used by Chinese nationals entering the Northern Mariana Islands. Nonimmigrant visa processing faced flux due to new fees. Texas received $7.5 billion in earlier DHS reimbursement for prior border costs.  ⁠Theepochtimes

Crime • Violence • Gun Violence • Drug Addiction  💀

A powerful, slow-moving nor’easter caused coastal flooding, power outages for tens of thousands, flight cancellations, and at least one death (a Brooklyn NYCHA worker) plus a missing swimmer off Long Island. Conditions lingered into Sunday.  ⁠NY Post

Twelve teens were shot after a Georgia birthday party spilled from an Airbnb into a park. Separate mass shootings in South African townships killed at least 27. A Detroit strip-club shooting left three dead and four injured. Officials investigated Ole Miss student deaths and nearby kratom sales.  ⁠Newsmax

National Unity • Polarization • State Of Democracy 🗳️

Midterm campaigning intensified amid low presidential approval readings and intra-party tensions. GOP operatives treated previously safe seats as competitive. A WSJ piece framed Germany’s AfD rise as Angela Merkel’s legacy of mistaking establishment consensus for moderation. Polarization around Iran policy, AI regulation, and election integrity remained high.  ⁠Archive

Health Costs, Energy, And The Cost Of Living  💸

Diesel and heating-oil prices stayed elevated because of Hormuz disruptions and possible U.S. export limits. Trump moved to set new fuel-economy standards and roll back Biden-era EV mandates. Energy costs featured in tight Senate races. The storm added immediate disruption to East Coast travel and utilities.  ⁠Daily Mail

Economy • Federal Budget Deficit • National Debt 📉

The China tariff deal provided a modest positive signal after a five-day equity slump earlier in the week. Massive AI data-center and infrastructure investment continued to be described as the largest economic bet in U.S. history. Markets awaited the coming jobs report. Long-term deficit and debt dynamics received less same-day focus than energy and trade.  X

Poverty • Homelessness • Related Social Issues  🏚️

CUNY graduation rates continued a multi-year decline, linked by observers to falling K-12 standards in New York City public schools. Madrid saw protests and an encampment after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman amid Spain’s housing crunch. U.S. homelessness and poverty stories were not among the day’s most prominent national headlines.  ⁠NY Post

Overall Daily Summary  📝

Sunday, September 27, was dominated by foreign-policy tension and a severe East Coast storm. Trump’s rejection of Iran’s Hormuz ceasefire offer, combined with a foiled UK plot near a U.S.-used base, kept the Middle East conflict and energy-price pressure front and center. A limited U.S.-China tariff and coal deal offered a counterpoint after the Xi visit. Domestically, the nor’easter produced flooding, outages, and at least one fatality while midterm spending and polling underscored GOP anxiety over previously safe seats. Crime stories—Georgia teen shooting, South Africa massacres, Detroit violence—added to the day’s grim tally. Energy costs, AI-safety incidents involving government sites, and continued immigration enforcement formed the remaining backbone of coverage from these outlets. Polarization and institutional distrust remained the consistent undercurrent heading into the final stretch before November.  85 sources

# **Explore America’s Historic Waterway: The Chesapeake Bay Itinerary**  
### *A Journey Through Colonial History, Maritime Heritage & Scenic Mid‑Atlantic Beauty*  
**Presented by Your Premier Travels – Arlington, TX**  
**Let Us Help You Fulfill Your Next Dream!**

text:
$TWST I want to address Twist's current price. Many bulls sold too early and many bears shorted too early, showing how misunderstood this stock is.

Is the current valuation stretched? Yes.

At a $12B market cap against guided FY26 revenue of $456–457M, Twist trades at about 26x forward sales. Mature life-sciences tools leaders typically trade between 4x and 8x. With 21% top-line growth, a 52% gross margin, an annualized GAAP net loss of about $140M, and Adjusted EBITDA only reaching breakeven by Q4, the stock looks significantly overvalued on near-term fundamentals. The market is pricing in 5-8 years of flawless execution.

So why is the market paying this premium? 🤔

Most assume it's all just AI hype, and that's partially true since AI-driven drug discovery is the most well-known tailwind. As AI models design millions of proteins, Twist acts as the physical, high-volume wet-lab validation engine, directly integrated into AWS, Benchling, and Lilly's TuneLab.

They're able to fill this key role due to their biggest moat, a proprietary semiconductor platform. Writing DNA on silicon chips instead of plastic plates shrinks chemical reaction volumes by 99.8%, permanently lowering the unit cost floor while printing over 1M unique oligos per chip. This automated, high-throughput manufacturing moat can't be easily replicated.

But this is all pretty well-known and has been effectively priced in.

Twist could potentially benefit from some royalties, milestones payments, and downstream stakes in partners' clinical assets and their DNA data storage business spin-off (Atlas) down the road. But this is too speculative to explain the current price...

So I believe the premium is actually anchored in 3 key advantages:

1) Built-In Operating Leverage

Twist operates at less than 50% capacity across their Wilsonville and San Francisco sites, with 65K sqft of unbuilt space ready for expansion. They can scale revenue from about $457M past $1B on existing leases without building new factories. With fixed overhead already absorbed, about 70% of every incremental revenue dollar drops directly to gross profit.

2) Planned Expansion to Clinical cGMP

Currently, Twist operates under a Research Use Only label, losing accounts to legacy CDMOs once drug candidates enter human trials. Their planned expansion into clinical-grade cGMP could be a game changer. Supplying clinical mRNA cancer vaccine templates and cell therapy payloads commands prices 5-50x higher than research tools. This transition could push gross margins past 60–65% and accelerate revenue beyond $1.2B by 2030, compressing forward sales multiples down to 8–10x.

3) Tailwinds Across High-Growth Frontiers

While AI-Driven drug discovery is the most well-known catalyst, there are several more lesser-known tailwinds:

• Minimal Residual Disease (MRD): In cancer recurrence monitoring, Twist's sub-24-hour MRD Express synthesizes up to 1,800 custom probes per patient. As customers like Personalis/Tempus expand testing, Twist captures recurring consumable sales on every serial blood draw across a $20B addressable market.

• Bispecific Antibodies & ADCs: Through their B-Body partnership, Twist offers biopharma a flat-fee, zero-milestone, zero-royalty licensing model that undercuts traditional platform rivals while retaining 80% of license fees and 100% of service work.

• Gene Editing & Cell Therapy: Twist manufactures ultra-long oligos up to 350 nucleotides for prime editing and complex genes up to 7K base pairs for non-viral CAR-T and CRISPR knock-ins.

• Nucleic Acid Therapeutics (mRNA, siRNA, ASO): Twist prints massive oligo tiling pools for siRNA/ASO discovery and complex clonal genes up to 7,000 bp for cell-free mRNA/circRNA templates, eliminating legacy plasmid fermentation delays.

So yes, Twist is expensive by today's numbers so the price could fall short-term. But long-term, they should benefit from economies of scale across several disruptive growth themes.

I'm holding. NFA.

text:
THESIS  
Assisted dying was sold as mercy for people who were already dying. Once the law dropped the dying part, it stopped being the same service. Put the original gate back: terminal illness only.

The claim in one line  
If the state is going to license doctors to end a life, the person should be dying of the disease—not just suffering from life.

Why the original limit existed  
The first statutes and the Oregon-style laws were built for a narrow case: an adult, competent, with a short prognosis, whose death was coming anyway. That was the political bargain. Suffering without a foreseeable death was supposed to be treated, housed, palliated, and supported—not converted into an eligibility category.

What changed  
Courts and later bills removed the “reasonably foreseeable death” test in some countries. Canada’s 2016 law had it. The 2021 rewrite did not. Netherlands and Belgium never used a short-prognosis gate; their text was always “unbearable suffering.” Those are different products wearing the same brand name. Calling both “the original intent” is how the expansion happened without a new public vote on the new product.

The reform, stripped of paperwork  
Restore a terminal-prognosis requirement in every statute that used to have one.  
Do not pretend a chronic, non-fatal condition is the same legal object as end-stage cancer.  
Keep capacity, voluntariness, and independent assessment. Those are safeguards. The missing piece is the dying part.  
Fund the things that make “unbearable” less often a synonym for “we didn’t offer enough care.”

The objection, answered in the same tone  
“Autonomy.” Autonomy to refuse treatment already exists. Autonomy to demand the state end a non-terminal life is a different claim. It needs its own vote, not an amendment smuggled through a court case about people who were already dying.

“Suffering is suffering.” True. So is scarcity of housing, psychiatry, and palliative beds. A law that treats those as reasons for death will be used that way.

The punchline that is also the policy  
Mercy for the dying is a limited license. Mercy for everyone who is tired of living is a different regime. Write the second one honestly or don’t write it. Restore the first.

No response from CENTCOM. Search results show no response or confirmation from CENTCOM regarding this specific Iranian claim. In the past, when Iran claimed to have struck U.S. warships or tankers, CENTCOM explicitly denied the reports, stating that "no U.S. Navy ships were hit, and all Iranian attempts to attack failed."

Ambiguous meaning of "strike." Fars News Agency’s phrasing has varied across sources: some reports mention "targeted strikes," others "interceptions," and some "warning shots." These terms carry vastly different military and legal implications, yet Fars has not clarified exactly which action was taken.

Flow Data: Independent Observations by Kpler
The Kpler data cited by *Drop Site* serves as an independently verifiable benchmark for this incident. According to the data:

Kpler’s direct observations indicate that oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 5 to 7 million barrels per day.

Broader exports from the Gulf region (measured from the choke point) averaged around 11.4 million barrels per day over a seven-day period.

Separate Kpler data shows a seven-day rolling average of approximately 13.2 million barrels per day for visible VLCC (Very Large Crude Carrier) shipments—a figure below the pre-war norm of roughly 20 million barrels per day.

While these figures cannot substantiate Iran’s claim of "striking 19 vessels," they provide crucial context: oil flows through Hormuz remain significantly below pre-war levels. This creates a tension between Trump’s claims of "total control" and Iran’s assertions regarding "strikes on all unauthorized vessels."

Assessment
The Fars report represents a unilateral military claim by Iranian state media, mirroring the pattern of previous Iranian claims regarding strikes on U.S. warships: figures and qualitative descriptions are provided without verifiable evidence, while the opposing party either denies the events or remains silent. Amidst the ongoing "Tanker War" between the U.S. and Iran, such claims are inherently part of an information war; their precise military and political significance is difficult to gauge from the outside. Kpler’s data offers the only independent reference point: flows are slowly recovering but remain far from normal levels. As for whether the "19 struck vessels" are included in these flow figures—or what exactly happened to them—no independent source can currently provide an answer.

text:
IRAN REPORTS SECOND U.S. UNDERWATER DRONE CAPTURE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ

Iran says its naval forces have captured a U.S. REMUS 600 underwater drone in the Strait of Hormuz, with specialists examining the vehicle to recover its data. The U.S. military disputes the reported seizure.

In its September 27 announcement, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps identified the drone as the second American underwater vehicle it had seized. The IRGC Navy said intelligence and electronic warfare operations enabled the capture and accused the vehicle of conducting espionage.

IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi called it an “intelligence prize.” Identifying the equipment as a Mk 18 Mod 2 Kingfish, he portrayed the reported capture as evidence of Iran’s ability to intercept American underwater operations, according to Press TV.

Washington offered a competing account. CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said U.S. forces maintained “positive control of all of our operational drone assets,” in comments to Al Jazeera reported by Roya News.

The REMUS platform supports several military missions. Manufacturer HII says the REMUS 600M mine countermeasures variant uses sonar to survey underwater areas and locate potential mines. Intelligence collection is also among the broader REMUS family’s applications.

For Iran, the claimed intelligence gain depends on what specialists can retrieve. Press TV asserted access to encrypted data and navigation technology, but presented no recovered material demonstrating that access. The IRGC Navy’s statement described an effort to recover information without identifying what had been successfully extracted.

THE ONLY THING THAT GETS US THROUGH THIS SEASON OF THE WITCH IS THE PRAYERS OF THE RIGTHEOUS.
PRAYER IS A NON-DENOMINATIONAL CALLING

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
Doubt less and pray big. Worry less and pray often. Pray more for others than you do for yourself and you will see benefits as well. When you pray like this, your righteous prayers will avail much.
Jennifer Heeren
Published May 27, 2021

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
James 5:16 tells us to, “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (KJV). The New King James Version simplifies the language a bit. It says, “Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much.”

Availeth, or to avail, means to use or take advantage of an opportunity. It could also mean when we choose to do good things in order to bring about good benefits.

More modern translations make it even clearer. The New International Version says, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.” The New Living Translation adds that “the earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results.” This goes along with the avail definition of doing good things to bring about good benefits. Then the Amplified Bible translation states, “the heartfelt and persistent prayer of a righteous man can accomplish much when put into action and made effective by God. It has tremendous power.”

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
We need to confess our sins to God and to other people. Confession will heal many souls. The one that confesses and the one that hears will both experience healing because confession brings God’s redemption into the picture. The confessor feels relief and the listener feels hope because they know they will sin too. Redemption brings much hope. Our conscience is cleared, and our prayers will be heard by God.

The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer (1 Peter 3:12). When we choose to do good and godly things, we are in the perfect place for God to hear our prayers. When we repent and confess our sins, God will turn his ears toward our cries (Psalm 34:15). He longs to help us when we humbly admit our weaknesses.

James follows verse 16 with a description of Elijah. Elijah was merely a human, just like us, but he let his faith in God prevail by praying fervently. He prayed that it wouldn’t rain, and it didn’t rain for three years and six months. Then he prayed again for it to rain and heaven poured forth rain. When we put our faith in God, our prayers can do more than we think or imagine.

We can pray bigger than we think we can. Jesus said that if we have faith and do not doubt, we can move a mountain (Matthew 21:21). Whether He meant this literally or figuratively, we know that He meant for us to pray for big, even impossible, things. With God, impossible things are made possible. We can do great things because the Holy Spirit is within us. Our prayers avail much when we push aside our doubts and pray big.

3 Ways We Can Apply This Verse to Our Lives Today
The Book of James is a very practical book. It is often thought of as the Proverbs of the New Testament. James 5:16 can lead us into dramatic living within God’s purposes when we remember these 3 things:

1. We need community. Relationships with other people are very important for righteous living. When we do wrong, we should admit it to other people. We shouldn’t try to hide our flaws. We show our humanness and therefore make it possible for others to relate to us. We are transparent with them and therefore bring about an atmosphere where they can be completely honest with us. We play a part in the healing of other people around us. At least we can if we take the opportunity. We can help people heal physically, mentally, and spiritually.

Use your gifts and your prayers to serve and encourage others. Teach them. Give generously to them. Lead them in the right direction. Be kind and open to hearing the troubles they may be going through. You won’t always have an answer for them, but you can point them to the One who does. Prayers avail much when we use them to figure out the best way to serve others and then we go out and serve them.

2. We should ask for and give prayer. When we feel weak, we ask other people to pray for us. We ask for encouraging advice. We ask for help when we are burdened and weighed down. Then, we also offer to pray for others. We come beside them when they seem tired and lack joy. We speak encouraging words to them. We pray encouragement over them. We lift them up to our Heavenly Father so He can carry the bulk of their burden.

Keep your prayers as simple as possible. Flowery, long-winded phrases are unnecessary. Words like that are usually said to impress other people. God isn’t impressed by how we say things. He’s impressed by our humble heart. And He knows our needs before we say them. Prayers avail much when we say them out of a humble heart that desperately wants to help others.

3. We turn these actions into everyday habits. We continually give prayer the opportunity to lift up others as well as ourselves. Any good that we accomplish is because of God’s grace. He is the one who gave us the motivation to do any good works at all. We try our best to help others but then let God fill in the inevitable mistakes that we make. He can take them a lot further than our advice can. We pray for them to be open to the Lord’s leading and the same for ourselves. Our help can avail much but God can bring about even more power as well as deliverance, restoration, and redemption.

Prayers avail much when they help point people to the God who created them, loves them, and longs to be in a relationship with them.

Praying in a Way that “Availeth Much”
It is key to remember that if we confess our sins to God and to one another, God is faithful and just to forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Then we can be confident that God hears us when we pray for things that please Him (1 John 5:14). When we ask, we will receive from God if our motivations are to keep His commandments and do what pleases Him (1 John 3:22).

Pray that God will shed light onto people’s hearts so that they will be convicted of their wrong actions and thinking. Pray for harmony and peace so that arguments will be doused with God’s living water. Pray that plots of evil and revenge are thwarted. Your prayers can play a part in turning someone toward God.

Doubt less and pray big. Worry less and pray often. Pray more for others than you do for yourself and you will see benefits as well. When you pray like this, your righteous prayers will avail much.

text:
The Cherokee called her the War Woman. She was a tall, red-haired, cross-eyed frontier wife who could not read or write, and according to the most famous story of the Georgia backcountry, she once captured a whole squad of enemy soldiers single-handedly, in her own cabin, with their own guns. Her name was Nancy Hart, and she is the only woman in the history of Georgia to have a county named after her.

Hart lived on the raw Georgia frontier during the Revolution, in a region torn apart by a savage, personal civil war between Patriots and Loyalists. She was a fierce rebel, and she made no secret of it. She spied, she smuggled, and she was known to disguise herself to gather information on the enemy. The Loyalists and their Native allies knew her and feared her temper, and she earned that ominous nickname, the War Woman, with a creek near her home named for her.

The legend that made her immortal goes like this. A group of Loyalist soldiers, five or six of them, came to her isolated cabin one day. They had been hunting a Patriot leader, and they barged in, bragging about their deeds, and demanded that Nancy cook for them. She played the part of the grumbling but obliging hostess. She killed the last turkey, set it cooking, and, crucially, kept the men's cups full of wine and corn liquor. As the soldiers relaxed, ate, drank, and let their guard down, they stacked their muskets against the wall, out of easy reach.

That was their mistake. There was a gap or chink in the cabin's log wall, and as the men grew drunk and careless, Nancy quietly began slipping their muskets, one at a time, out through that opening to the outside, while sending her daughter to signal for help. She got several guns out before the soldiers noticed. When one of them finally realized what was happening and lunged for the weapons, Nancy snatched up a musket, leveled it, and warned them she would shoot any man who moved. One did. She shot him dead. Another rushed her, and she shot him too. Then she held the rest at gunpoint, alone, until her husband and neighbors arrived.

And the ending is grim frontier justice. The surviving Loyalists begged to be treated as prisoners of war. Nancy would have none of it. She insisted, over milder suggestions, that shooting was too good for them, and the captured Tories were hanged.

For a long time this was dismissed by some as pure tall tale, backcountry folklore that grew with the telling, and to be fair, the details have surely been polished over two centuries. But then history offered a chilling footnote. Generations later, in the early 1900s, workers building a railroad near the site of Hart's old cabin dug up a neat row of skeletons in a shallow grave, right where the story said the bodies should be. Bones do not prove every detail of a legend. But they gave the story a weight that has never quite gone away.

Georgia never forgot her. They named a county after her, Hart County, the only one in the entire state named for a woman, along with a lake and a town. Remember Nancy Hart, the War Woman, who did not wait for an army to protect her home, and who proved that on the Revolutionary frontier, some of the most dangerous soldiers around were not soldiers at all.

A single mom friend caught us at church today and said my name came up with her and her son. She and his dad have been divorced for a few years, and the son and the dad do not get along anymore. He still goes over to the dad's house who has remarried, just to keep the relationship going, but his dad basically deals with him and puts him off so he can spend time focusing on his new wife. His kids from the previous marriage are now an afterthought.

He and my 16-year-old grew up together, and I've spent a lot of time with him coaching teams, doing scouts, etc. While the mother and son were in a counseling session they asked him what he wanted from his father. He replied that he didn't need much, he basically wanted his dad to treat him like I treat him. He said that I shook his hand like he was already a man, looked him in the eye, always spoke positively and encouraged him to always do and be his best. He said I saw something in him his dad never saw, and this gave him confidence. 

This is not to toot my own horn, but to show appreciation to all the other men out there who do the same thing. There's no doubt in my mind all the men in this picture have a similar attitude with their families, and really anyone else who they interact with on a daily basis. That doesn't mean we are perfect, but we are all trying to be the man that God wants us to be. If you have a good man in your life, tell him how much you appreciate him. John Polomny cut through the UN noise this weekend. Trump’s “annihilate the Islamic Republic” line is not strategy. It is tribute language. Rebuild on our terms, or we erase you. That is the whole offer.

The conflict is not theology, not latency. It is the core Western mentality of money-hungry power elites. Control the sword. Collect the rent. That drive did not start in 1979. It did not start in 2003. It is the same colonial imperial impulse that has defined the West since the West existed.

I'm wrong if the strait reopens on terms the market believes and the spread stays wide: then it is a barrel story after all. Next: Wednesday's EIA print and the transit counts.

text:
They told you Donald Trump was a Russian asset. 

They told you he was a Nazi. 

They told you, for years, in every major media outlet in America, that the man was an existential threat to democracy itself.

Once you've told a country that, you have justified nearly anything.

So the apparatus went to work. Surveillance warrants on a campaign. A dossier funded by his opponent, laundered into intelligence channels. A special counsel, years of it, and a collusion case that never materialized. Note the sequence. The threat justified the measures. The threat turned out to be fake but the measures stayed.

Now he's back as president, and this time he came prepared. The corrupt agencies are being cleaned out. The pathway that they used last time has been closed.

So here is the question the Canadian press gallery will not ask. When the people are willing to do that to their own president lose the ability to do it from the inside, do they simply stop? Or do they find a new position outside his reach?

Because there is an obvious one. A G7 country. With the longest undefended border on earth. Buried deep in his supply chains. Holding a veto over the industrial states that decide elections. And are entirely beyond the jurisdiction of every agency he just took back.

Why capture an agency when you can capture a country?

But a country is not an agency. You cannot subpoena it or leak to it. To turn one against him you would need the right man at the top, and the specification is brutally narrow.

He could not be bought. A bought man leaves a trail.

You would need the perfect Manchurian candidate. Not a man who knows what he is. A man so thoroughly conditioned by a lifetime inside the old order that he cannot see it. No handler. No instruction. Ask him and he would deny it sincerely, because to him it was never betrayal. It was maturity. The adult position. Sacrificing the smaller thing for the greater good, and never once noticing that the smaller thing was his own country.

He would need to be formed in the institutions that built that order. Central banking. Global finance. The summit circuit. A career teaching him that the nation state is an administrative unit and that real authority sits above it.

He would need to be a technician. Someone who can move a state without appearing to move it.

He would need standing on both sides of the border, so that divided loyalty reads as a résumé.

And he would need to arrive clean. No riding to nurse. No faction that made him. No debts to anyone in the party he was about to lead, and therefore no one inside it with the standing to stop him. Not a politician. An operator.

That man is almost impossible to find.

And yet Canada made him Prime Minister in March.

He took over the Liberal leadership at the worst possible moment for anyone who actually wanted a political career. He captured a radioactive brand at the worst time in its political cycle. He jumped anyway. When a man accepts a terrible deal, you should stop asking what it cost him and start asking what he was seeking to gain.

Three days before he announced, he was not in Edmonton. He was on American television, in full campaign register, aimed at the wrong country. Why would a Canadian soft launch their Canadian political career on an American television show?

Then the pattern fills in. He creates a Chief Operating Officer of the Prime Minister's Office, a position that has never existed in the history of this country, and fills it with a former Hillary Clinton American Democratic operative. The same Hillary Clinton whose campaign paid for the dossier. The one that laundered a foreign spy's gossip into an instrument of the American state. Carney closes a Washington-cohosted summit in Toronto with the Canadian press kept outside the room. His portfolio is ninety-one percent American.

And in August, the trade talks collapsed.

Here is where an honest writer stops and tells you what he does not know. Nobody outside that room knows what Washington actually demanded. It’s never been publicly released. Carney says the Americans asked too much and offered too little. Washington says that is false. Two accounts that are clearly contradictory, and there is no transcript. We are in the fog of war, and we will stay there until the documents surface a decade from now, if they ever do. What we can look at is the convenience of the timing.

But lets set aside the disputed part and look only at what nobody denies.

Carney suspended the talks. Carney recalled the negotiators. And when the retaliation came, Canada did not simply mirror the American tariffs. It selected. Over seven hundred products, and the pain was directed at Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, weeks before the midterm elections.

What do we call a foreign government inflicting targeted economic pain on specific electorates immediately before an election? In any other decade we had a phrase for that.
And what did Canada get?

Elbows up. That was the war cry. So where are the spoils of war? Where is the reindustrialization of Canada’s industrial base? Where is the diversified market access that was supposed to free us from the Americans? Where is the pipelines to tidewater, the expanded ports, the LNG plants? Groceries are not cheaper. Rent is not cheaper. The tariffs still sit on our backs. A full year of the loudest confrontation with our largest trading partner in living memory has bought this country nothing you can point to, photograph, or carry home.

Look closer, though, and we will find that the benefits of the last year do exist, its just that they have accrued in someone else's name.

Every dollar of that confrontation flowed one way. The rhetoric ran north, warm and patriotic, elbows up for the cameras. The structure ran south. A Prime Minister whose portfolio is overwhelmingly American, whose closest operator is an American Democratic strategist, whose summits are convened by Washington, spent a year manufacturing a crisis whose targeted casualties landed in precisely the American swing states that decide who governs from that same city. We paid the tariffs. His faction across the border collected the political dividend. Ask who this actually served and the flag on the podium stops matching the balance sheet behind it.

Set every fact down on its own and each one has an innocent face. The portfolio is just a retirement account from a long career. The progressive American political operator is just a hire. The timing is just the calendar. The targeting of the swing states with tariffs are just how trade math works. That is exactly why it holds. A single coincidence is invisible. It is only when you lay them end to end, all of them pointing the same direction, all of them costing Canada and paying his American allies.

The ambition was never to be our Prime Minister. The office was the means. A credential that let him capture Canada and turn it into a forward operating base, a country pointed south and spent against Donald Trump in an American civil war that has cost the Canadian people dearly and bought them nothing.
You have to ask the question eventually. How many coincidences, at this altitude, in this direction, before you stop calling them coincidences?

He is not governing this country. He is occupying it.

Stop thinking of the United States as a foreign country and start thinking of it as what it actually is, a global American empire that governs through markets, currency, media and defence rather than through legions, and whose provinces keep their own flags and anthems as a courtesy. On that map Canada is not a neighbour. We are the richest province in the system, wired directly into the metropole.

So when Caesar took Rome, Pompey did not surrender. He crossed to Greece and kept the war going from the provinces, because a faction that loses the capital does not stop fighting. It relocates. They lost Washington. They went to the most valuable province they had, the one that was already theirs, and they garrisoned it with a man of their own class who needed no persuading at all. He did not have to be recruited. He was already one of them, and the province came with the office.

Which is why the whole performance has been aimed south. The elbows, the flags, the defiance. It was never Canadian politics. It was American theatre, staged here, for them.
Canada is not being governed. It is being occupied, a province held by the losing faction in the global American empire's civil war.

Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Trump was preparing to resume strikes against Iran after the November midterm elections, Waltz called it “anonymous reporting.”

“What I can tell you is the president will leave all options on the table,” he said.

Waltz said any agreement would have to address Iran’s highly enriched uranium and its ability to restore enrichment, adding that Washington had previously offered to sell Tehran uranium.

text:
Four Scarcities Reshaping Agent Infrastructure Economics

Meta($META ) launched Muse on September 8, a personal AI agent capable of executing tasks autonomously in the background, powered by Muse Spark, Meta's first frontier model that no longer publishes algorithm parameters. Within 12 days, US mobile daily active users reached 642,000, exceeding ChatGPT's 231,000 at the equivalent launch point, and Muse topped both the App Store and Google Play. At Meta Connect on September 23, Zuckerberg outlined the monetization structure: a $20/month Power plan and a $100/month Maximum plan.

These figures invite a growth narrative. But Muse exposes a more fundamental problem: when AI migrates from conversational interaction to autonomous execution, the scarcity structure of infrastructure rearranges. The market currently estimates agent infrastructure demand with a linear model — DAU multiplied by per-user compute — that fails systematically when applied to products like Muse. Not because compute stops mattering, but because no single compute bottleneck determines infrastructure scale. Four interdependent scarcities do, each with a different mitigation path, time constant, and cost elasticity.

From token pricing to cost per completed task.

The unit economics of an agent cannot be read from token prices. Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 pricing is $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens, and $0.15 per million cached input tokens. The Contributor tier — where data is used for training — prices input at $0.10, output at $0.20, and cached input at $0.002. Artificial Analysis estimates Muse Spark 1.3 at approximately $0.55 per task on the Intelligence Index. On the surface, competitive pricing.

But the cost per API call is not the cost per task. An agent task involves tool loops, retries, cache misses, and multi-step reasoning. When an edit succeeds after two failed attempts, total attempts equal three. Cache misses force context re-reads. Browser execution and search calls settle outside Meta's billing system. Research on Cost per Completed Task (CPCT) as a measurement framework shows that token price is a weak proxy for agentic workload economics: in a measured case study, capping tool-output verbosity reduced the cost of an identical task by 88%, an 8.6x swing attributable entirely to operational overhead, not model capability. The economic unit is the accepted work, not the token.

For infrastructure planning, this means Muse's inference demand is driven by the distribution of task complexity multiplied by task volume, not by user count multiplied by fixed token consumption. A user submitting one "research competitor pricing strategy" request may generate 50 to 100 model invocations across search, data extraction, long-context synthesis, and multi-turn validation. A user submitting 20 simple queries may generate fewer than half that. The variance in task complexity distribution, not the arithmetic mean of user count, drives infrastructure demand.

Microsoft's study published in Joule in April 2026 provides the energy distribution baseline. For a typical query (about 300 output tokens), median energy is 0.31 Wh. When response length rises to about 5,000 tokens — long code generation or multi-step reasoning — median energy jumps to 3.91 Wh, roughly 13 times the typical query. More critically, Microsoft found that "a relatively small proportion of expensive requests can dominate total electricity consumption." In a scale projection of 1 billion requests per day, if 10% shift to long-reasoning tasks, electricity demand rises from 0.7 GWh to 1.7 GWh, and even after optimization requires 0.8 GWh. A 10-percentage-point shift in request mix more than doubles total energy consumption.

Layered on Muse's architecture: safety classifiers, routing decisions, and tool-selection steps represent the majority of backend invocations, but if 10% to 20% involve complex planning or multi-turn reasoning, overall energy consumption deviates significantly from what the median suggests. The proportion is unknown at Muse's current stage, but its impact on infrastructure cost is non-linear.

Memory: the server-count determinant that replaces CPU.

In conventional data center planning, server count is set by compute demand, with memory and storage as proportional attachments. In agent inference, this logic inverts.

DeepSeek's DSec sandbox platform, published in September 2026, offers the highest-density production data available: a single production unit of about 160 CPU nodes, 30,000 physical cores, and 250 TB memory, with peak concurrency exceeding 380,000 sandboxes. A single node hosts up to 800 microVMs. But this density rests on two strict conditions: about 90% of instances average no more than 5% of requested CPU, and the platform uses aggressive memory overcommitment — through virtio-pmem with DAX, microVMs skip their own page cache and map host physical memory directly, reducing peak memory consumption by 40.2%.

Muse's persistent environment differs fundamentally from DSec's training sandbox. Training sandboxes are ephemeral. Muse's per-user environment carries browser activity, credential management, database I/O, and long-lived state. Research on agentic browser workloads shows that median sandbox peak DRAM usage is about 0.8 GB, but per-session peak can reach 28 GB during compilation and unit tests. For a 32K-context agent session with a 70B-class model using Grouped Query Attention, the KV cache alone consumes 2 to 12 GB of GPU memory per request depending on model architecture.

Muse's published architecture assigns each environment about 2 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM, and 100 GB storage. Observed memory usage for a single environment was about 3 GB. But including platform overhead, physical memory residency has a floor around 6 GB. An application server with 3 TB memory hosts about 500 active environments at 6 GB each — not the larger number calculated from CPU core count. This means server count may be determined by memory bandwidth and capacity, not compute core count. Raising CPU oversubscription ratios alone will not reduce server count, because memory is the binding constraint.

The supply constraint on memory is tighter than on CPUs. HBM4 per-GB cost has jumped from $17 to $18 in the HBM3E era to $31 to $32, with Bernstein projecting further rises to $53 per GB by 2027. UBS estimates HBM average pricing will rise about 79% in 2027 versus 2026. HBM production consumes approximately 3x the wafer capacity of standard DDR5, with yields in the 55% range versus DDR5's 90%+. The three major manufacturers' HBM capacity has exceeded 355,000 wafers per month, rising from 8% of global DRAM wafer starts two years ago to 23% today. For agent platforms, every additional active user environment increases memory demand in two directions simultaneously: application server DDR5 and accelerator-side HBM.

Storage: the quantity that dwarfs compute in absolute volume.

Agent persistent environments are not only a compute problem. Each user environment must persist file systems, application data, history, and context. Muse assigns 100 GB storage per environment. If 100 million DAU corresponds to 75 million to 100 million retained accounts, at 50% utilization, total storage demand reaches 3.75 EB to 5 EB. This exceeds a substantial proportion of current global data center storage.

The storage constraint has a different structure from memory. Marginal cost per TB is far lower — as of August 2026, a 30 TB TLC enterprise SSD costs approximately $22,600, while an equivalent HDD costs approximately $1,216, putting flash at 18.6x the price of disk per terabyte. HDD prices themselves have risen from $495 in Q3 2025 to $1,216, a 2.5x increase. Seagate and Western Digital have both told investors nearline HDD output is sold out through 2027. A neocloud without a hyperscaler-scale supply agreement is buying at spot prices, which carry a 30% to 40% premium.

This means storage cost optimization depends on tiering efficiency, not on unit cost reduction. DeepSeek's tiered loading strategy in DSec provides a reference: through versioned image layers and on-demand loading, an 8,192-container burst completed startup in about 35 minutes with 57% less disk-write traffic. If agent platforms cannot achieve comparable tiering efficiency, storage becomes a larger-than-expected cost line — not because per-TB prices are high, but because the absolute volume at 1 billion DAU approaches 50 EB at 50% utilization of the 100 GB quota.

Network topology: the constraint that scales with geography.

Muse's architecture requires each user's agent environment to maintain controlled connections with inference infrastructure. When users are geographically dispersed, data residency requirements apply, and latency-sensitive tasks demand edge inference, network topology complexity rises. The industry has converged on a three-tier framework: scale-up (within a rack, typically copper, a few meters), scale-out (across racks within a data center, direct-detect pluggable optics, hundreds of meters to a few kilometers), and scale-across (across data center facilities, coherent optics, tens to hundreds of kilometers).

For agent workloads, all three tiers carry traffic simultaneously. A user in Singapore interacting with an agent hosted in Virginia triggers scale-across traffic on every tool call. An 800G optical transceiver consumes 13 to 16 watts per port. At 100 million DAU with even modest cross-region traffic, the aggregate port count and power draw from optical interconnects becomes a material infrastructure cost that is structurally distinct from compute and memory.

CPO and silicon photonics are the technology paths to reducing this cost. Nvidia's $4 billion in strategic investments in Lumentum and Coherent during 2026, and Ciena's hyper-rail photonics platform targeting 128-fiber-pair density, indicate the industry expects optical interconnect to scale. But the capacity constraint is binding: Lumentum and Coherent together hold roughly 40% of the high-power laser supply critical to CPO deployment, and their combined 2026 capacity is already largely booked. CPO port shipments are projected at 120,000 units in 2026, concentrated in North American and East Asian top-tier compute clusters — insufficient for the agent inference wave. This constraint has a supply-side time constant of 18 to 24 months for laser capacity expansion, longer than memory or storage.

The capital markets gap.

Meta's 2027 capital expenditure has been revised upward by both Citi and Morgan Stanley. Citi estimates $205 billion, raised approximately 22%, tied to Meta's target of about 14 GW compute capacity. Morgan Stanley forecasts $225 billion for 2027 and $250 billion for 2028, up from $145 billion in 2025. Citi warns that all three major hyperscalers will enter negative free cash flow territory in both 2027 and 2028.

Comparing this capex scale against Muse's economics yields an informative judgment. If 15% to 25% of Meta's 2027 capex — $31 billion to $51 billion — is allocated to Muse and related inference infrastructure, the corresponding compute capacity supports tens of millions to hundreds of millions of DAU under reasonable efficiency assumptions. But Meta's capex simultaneously serves AI features across Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, and other platforms, with Muse being one allocation among many. The fixed capex commitment is made against a variable DAU conversion, and the mismatch between the two is where the risk sits — not in the capex number itself.

On the revenue side, Muse's $20 and $100 monthly pricing points imply that at 100 million DAU with 10% paid conversion, split 80/20 between the two tiers, annual revenue is approximately $4.3 billion. The ratio between this revenue and the estimated infrastructure cost requires careful evaluation, particularly given that the task complexity distribution — and therefore the per-user infrastructure cost — is not yet observable.

For semiconductor investors, the implication is that no single "DAU to accelerator" conversion coefficient can underwrite revenue forecasts for NVIDIA, Micron, SanDisk, or optical component suppliers. The four scarcities — energy distribution, memory density, storage volume, and optical network capacity — should be modeled separately, each cross-analyzed against its respective supply constraint. A bottleneck in any one dimension changes the deployment cadence and cost structure for all four. The scarcity that binds first determines the infrastructure buildout pace; the scarcity that binds longest determines the total cost.

text:
Another story that highlights the continued fall of a once formidable business icon. A dynamic economy offers much in the way of innovation and growth, but this doesn’t come without upheavals and changes in how business calculation works…both with consumer tastes and how venues respond to them. While some will succeed in such business, others don’t. This is the outcome of creative destruction. The graveyard is littered with those companies that failed to adapt to the changing economic climate around them, with Kodak, A&P, F.W. Woolworth, Polaroid, Sam Goody, Borders, and Blockbuster being just a few such examples. Another American icon in retailing has joined those ranks. Sears, Roebuck & Co. in it’s heyday was a titan in the annals of shopping. Started by an entrepreneur who had found a way to sell watches, the company ultimately became a department store that was a mecca for many products across various genres. It is perhaps well known for being a pioneer in the mail-order catalog business, putting together a “wish book” upon which customers of all ages could have access to products to their heart’s content. Sears was very much the Amazon of it’s day. For much of the 20th century, Sears dominated the marketplace, with brick and mortar stores across the country and a reputation of hard-earned quality both in customer satisfaction and product endurance.

However, unfortunately for Sears, nothing ever truly lasts in a dynamic economy…at least not without shrewd competitive spirit. Hampered by managerial mishaps and myopic vision, the company began to falter toward the latter end of the century. Changes in quality both in service and product began to drive customers away from stores. Little adaptation with regard to the advancement of e-commerce allowed upstarts like Amazon, Target, Wal-Mart, and others to encroach upon aspects that Sears had once championed. The company has become a shell of it’s former glory, with downsizing store totals and selling brands. It is only a matter of time before the once proud vision of a railroad station agent closes it’s doors for the final time.

Such a story though shouldn’t be overtaken with grief. Indeed, there is the matter of unemployment that will befall Sears employees once that last store closes (although most likely many of them will find work at better retailers…if they haven’t done so already). In the end however, what happened to Sears is hardly something to be blamed on anyone. As a company, over various administrations, it is largely responsible for the morass it finds itself in today. Customers have fled due to value that they weren’t finding, and that ultimately allowed others to rise to the challenge in bringing that value. That is what is important, and a demonstration how a company becoming large isn’t automatically something to fear…for such success will only continue as long as such value is continually provided in a free marketplace instead of regulatory bailout/support. In the end, we shouldn’t waste resources propping up failed endeavors like Sears. We instead should be making sure the marketplace is as open as possible for the next railroad station agent that comes up with a brilliant idea waiting to be shared.
