My top 10 Tech Business News for Sept. 20–26, 2026 week.

1. Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5.5
The company says it performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. API pricing is $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. 
#Anthropic #Claude #AIModels #AIEconomics

2. Alibaba unveils Zhenwu V900 and a 20 GW AI plan
@AlibabaGroup unveiled its Zhenwu V900 accelerator, which it says delivers three times the performance of its predecessor. It plans mass production in early 2027 and wants Alibaba Cloud’s data-center capacity to exceed 20 gigawatts by 2032. 

My take: Alibaba is pursuing full-stack AI economics: models, chips, cloud and physical capacity. 
#Alibaba #AIChips #DataCenters #ChinaAI

3. @SoftBank launches an $11 billion bond sale for @OpenAI
SoftBank launched $10 billion of dollar-denominated bonds and €1 billion—approximately $1.15 billion—of euro-denominated senior unsecured notes. The financing will support its OpenAI investment and replace a bridge-loan facility. 

My take: As I said repeatedly over last 6-9 months, frontier-model economics is moving into public credit markets. Rising rates are not helping either! 
#SoftBank #OpenAI #AIFinancing #CapitalMarkets

4. AMD crosses a $1 trillion market valuation
@AMD surpassed $1 trillion in market capitalization for the first time on September 21. It became the fourth U.S. chipmaker to reach the milestone, following Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron, as investors continued pricing in AI-driven accelerator and server demand. 

My take: The market is pricing in a multi-vendor accelerator ecosystem, and that's a good thing. 
#AMD #Semiconductors #AIInfrastructure #Markets

5. @SnorkelAI raises $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation
Snorkel AI raised $350 million as demand increased for specialized training datasets and reinforcement-learning environments. The company's annualized revenue run rate has crossed $350 million, compared with approximately $20 million a year earlier.

My take: Value is migrating outside the base model toward data, evaluations, environments and domain expertise. 
#SnorkelAI #TrainingData #EnterpriseAI #PractitionerEconomics

6. @Apple targets local AI with high-end Macs
Apple is positioning its latest Mac desktops as an alternative to continuously renting centralized AI compute. The company demonstrated four connected Mac Studios running a trillion-parameter model to identify and fix a graphics-code defect. 

My take: Local inference changes AI economics from perpetual token rental toward owned capacity. I still believe that most of the production/runtime inference will be done from Cloud/Datacenters. 
#Apple #LocalAI #EnterpriseComputing #AIEconomics

7. #Accelevation targets up to a $5.4 billion IPO valuation
Data center infrastructure provider Accelevation Holdings is seeking a valuation of up to $5.37 billion in its U.S. IPO. The 

My take: Yet another AI Infra IPO. Investors must distinguish contracted demand from exposure built mainly around the AI narrative.
#Accelevation #IPO #DataCenters #PowerInfrastructure

8. EU orders data-center energy and water disclosures
The European Commission proposed a common rating system requiring data centers with at least 500 kW of capacity to disclose energy and water efficiency. The proposal does not impose consumption limits or require disclosure of total power usage. European data-center capacity is projected to rise from 12 GW in 2025 to 28 GW by 2030. European Commission 

My take: Data-center externalities are becoming operating disclosures. Efficiency scores may influence permits, financing and customer procurement in the long run, turning water and power performance into competitive business metrics.
#EuropeanUnion #DataCenters #EnergyEfficiency #TechPolicy #Regulatiors 

9. AI leaders take the safety debate to the UN
@OpenAI CEO @sma, @AnthropicAI CEO @DarioAmodei and @HuggingFace co-founder Clément Delangue briefed the UN Security Council on September 23 about increasingly capable AI systems and international-security risks. 

My take: AI governance is moving from voluntary laboratory policies into geopolitics. Global agreement may remain dream, so multinational enterprises should expect fragmented safety, deployment and reporting requirements.
#AISafety #UnitedNations #TechPolicy #Governance

10. Fed asks whether AI is becoming “too big to fail”
Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said regulators need to understand whether the interconnected network of AI companies, contracts and data-center projects is developing into a systemically important ecosystem. 

My take: AI’s systemic risk lies in the network, not one company. Supplier financing, long-duration contracts, leveraged infrastructure and circular customer relationships can transmit a slowdown across model companies, chipmakers, neoclouds, utilities and lenders.
#FederalReserve #AIEconomics #SystemicRisk #DataCenters

==============
AI Model Releases
==============
Qwen-Image-2.1 — Alibaba Qwen
Actual weight release · September 20
A unified image-generation and editing model with a seven-billion-parameter visual-generation component. It supports native transparent-background generation, local editing and as many as 10 reference images. Weights are downloadable, but the Qwen Research License requires separate permission for commercial use. 

Why it matters: Native transparency and multi-reference editing remove production steps, but the restricted license demonstrates that “downloadable weights” does not automatically mean commercially open.

Grok 4.7 — SpaceXAI
Actual proprietary release · September 21
Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model and additional reinforcement learning for coding, agentic tasks and knowledge work. It accepts text and images, has a 500,000-token context window and costs $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. It is available through the Grok API, Grok Build, Cursor and model gateways. 

Why it matters: Grok 4.7 adds further pricing pressure to frontier coding models. Enterprises should compare cost per completed workflow rather than cost per token alone.

MiMo-V2.6 Pro and Flash — Xiaomi
Actual open-weight release · September 21
MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 1.02 trillion total parameters and 42 billion activated per token. Flash uses 309 billion total and 15 billion activated parameters. Both provide one-million-token context and native text, image, video and audio inputs. The Hugging Face model pages label the weights MIT-licensed; hosted access is also available through Xiaomi services and OpenRouter. 

Why it matters: Xiaomi is combining large open weights, omnimodal inputs and long context with public deployment recipes. That increases the ability of enterprises and sovereign AI programs to operate capable models on infrastructure they control.

Claude Opus 5.5 — Anthropic
Actual proprietary release · September 22
The text-and-vision model supports one million context tokens and up to 128,000 output tokens. Anthropic reports lower serving costs, faster output and stronger safeguards than Opus 5. It is available through Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry. 

Why it matters: Anthropic is moving capability previously reserved for premium models into a lower-cost operating envelope, increasing pressure on both closed and open-weight competitors.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna — OpenAI
Actual proprietary release · September 22
Sol targets complex coding and agentic workflows, while Luna targets focused, high-volume workloads. Both accept text and images, offer 1.05-million-token context windows and are available through the API, ChatGPT Work and Codex. Standard API pricing is $2/$10 per million input/output tokens for Sol and $0.10/$0.50 for Luna. OpenAI API changelog | Model catalog OpenAI API

Why it matters: OpenAI is explicitly segmenting intelligence by workload economics. Luna’s pricing makes model routing and high-volume agent orchestration substantially more attractive.

FLUX 3 Action — Black Forest Labs
Actual open-weight release · September 23
FLUX 3 Action is a seven-billion-parameter world-action model for robotics and other embodied tasks. It jointly predicts future frames and actions from camera observations, system state and text instructions. Weights use the FLUX Kommunity License v1.0, while the training code and fine-tuning recipes are public. Black Forest Labs https://t.co/VZGbQz3www

Why it matters: Physical AI is moving beyond vision-language understanding toward models that predict and execute actions. This expands model economics into robots, edge hardware and industrial systems.

Alibaba’s five-to-10-trillion-parameter model
Development plan announced September 22—not a release. Alibaba disclosed plans for a model up to four times larger than Qwen 3.8 Max. No completed model, weights, API, license or release date was announced. It should therefore be treated as a roadmap statement rather than an available model. 

My Work: It was a busy travel week. included 4 days Toronto visit, returning home and attending the #WeAreDevelopers conference in San Jose on Friday. At @WeAreDevelopers, I spoke to @Docker (on camera), @JPMorgan (on camera), @IBM, @AWScloud, and @GoogleCloud folks. My most notable talk (on camera) was with WeAreDevelopers organizers. Will post video this week. 

OpenAI–Anthropic agreement to stress-test each other’s models—closely aligning with this week’s broader safety and governance theme. 

My question to you: Which layer do you think will produce the most durable AI returns: models, chips, specialized data, local compute or infrastructure financing?

The Certainty Premium: How Samsung's P5 Equipment Pre-Buy Is Repricing Memory Capital Allocation

Samsung Electronics is pulling forward P5 Phase 1 equipment installation from late summer 2027 to May–June 2027. The more revealing detail is what the company is willing to do to secure that schedule. Samsung has told equipment suppliers it will accept early tool shipments and warehouse the equipment itself, with some reports indicating the company is open to delivery as early as the first quarter of 2027. In an industry where equipment suppliers typically ship against project milestones, a chipmaker offering to pay storage costs for tools it cannot yet install is not a procurement adjustment. It is a signal about what capital allocation is now optimizing for.

The lead time reality that forces the decision.

Semiconductor equipment lead times have stretched to 1.5–2x normal levels, and critical components face delivery periods up to 40 months. ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, and KLA are simultaneously absorbing expansion demand from Samsung, SK hynix, TSMC, and Micron. Samsung and SK hynix together have committed more than KRW 100 trillion in capex this year, and their combined 800 trillion won expansion is straining tool supply across EUV, etching, photomask, CMP, and deposition.

In that environment, the chipmaker that orders first does not get the tool first. The chipmaker that accepts delivery risk does. Samsung's warehousing offer is effectively saying: we will absorb the cost of idle equipment to remove delivery uncertainty from the critical path. That is a capital allocation decision that prioritizes time-to-capacity over cost-per-unit-of-capacity — a trade-off that the traditional memory cycle framework does not capture.

P5's dual-track configuration reveals a DRAM-NAND divergence.

P5 Ph1 is being built as a 1c nm DRAM and HBM line. Samsung has ordered more than 70 lithography tools from ASML and Canon — approximately 20 EUV systems and 50 DUV tools — at a total value exceeding KRW 10 trillion. P5 Ph2 is more likely to be configured for advanced NAND, including the tenth-generation V10. P5 and P6 combined nameplate capacity could reach 300,000 wafers per month, roughly equivalent to Samsung's current entire DRAM monthly capacity.

The DRAM side has a clear catalyst. HBM4 requires 1c nm DRAM dies, and Samsung is targeting HBM4 mass production in the second half of 2027 with P5 positioned as the core supply base. Samsung plans to double HBM4 and HBM4E capacity from approximately 20,000 wafers per month in 2026 to 50,000 wafers per month in 2027. This is a volume ramp that needs wafer starts, not just design wins.

The NAND side is a more complicated bet. TrendForce projects NAND Flash entering a looser supply environment in the second half of 2027 as new capacity comes online while consumer electronics demand remains weak. Citi estimates the NAND supply-demand gap at approximately 6.1% in 2027, narrowing to 5.5% in 2028. Samsung's decision to configure Ph2 for V10 NAND, if executed on a faster timeline, is not a volume play. It is a positioning move to lock in leading-edge NAND share and margin before the supply window tightens.

What Samsung's own management has said about the shortage.

On its Q2 2026 earnings call, Samsung management stated that demand currently being received cannot be fulfilled this year, that unmet demand will carry into next year and create additional supply burden, and that next year's supply shortage will be more severe than this year's, persisting into 2028. That is not a one-year cyclical call. It is an admission that the industry is structurally short of capacity, and that every quarter of delay in capacity additions compounds the gap.

TrendForce's data supports this view for DRAM. The 2026 DRAM supply-demand gap is approximately -1% to -2%, and the gap is expected to widen in 2027 as demand growth outpaces supply growth. Even as new fabs ramp meaningfully in the second half of 2027, a meaningful supply contribution will not materialize until 2028. The contradiction between TrendForce's looser NAND call and Samsung's Ph2 V10 bet is not a data discrepancy — it reflects the two product lines' fundamentally different capital allocation logics.

The capital allocation regime is shifting from scale to time.

The traditional memory cycle framework says: expand when tight, cut when loose. Samsung's warehousing offer breaks that framework. The question is no longer how much capacity to build — P5's scale is already determined by the cleanroom footprint and tool orders. It is how fast that capacity can be brought online. When lead times are 1.5–2x normal, the only way to compress the timeline is to accept delivery earlier than the facility can accept installation.

This has a direct implication for how to read the equipment supply chain. SEMI forecasts global semiconductor manufacturing equipment sales reaching $165.9 billion in 2026, up 23.2% year on year, and $229.5 billion by 2028. Memory capex specifically is expected to grow 48% in 2026 and 60% in 2027. Equipment suppliers are not just selling more tools. They are selling certainty of delivery, and the pricing power that comes with it.

What to watch.

Samsung's formal P5 Ph1 purchase order confirmation and the timing of the Ph2 investment decision are the two near-term verification points. If Ph2 orders materialize in the first half of 2027, Samsung is positioning for a NAND upside scenario that contradicts TrendForce's looser-supply call. If Ph2 slips to the second half of 2027 or later, Samsung is concentrating capital on the DRAM and HBM side and treating NAND as a watch-and-wait.

SK hynix($SKHY )'s capital expenditure trajectory is equally important. Market consensus puts SK hynix 2027 capex at $37.5 billion, rising to $44 billion in 2028. If SK hynix adopts a similar pre-buy and warehouse strategy, equipment lead times extend further, and the certainty premium becomes an industry standard rather than a Samsung-specific tactic. The Marvell precedent — $1 billion prepayment to lock TSMC A14 capacity with a five-year demand forecast — shows that this logic is already spreading across the semiconductor supply chain.

The memory industry's capital allocation logic is migrating from how much can we build to how fast can we get it running. Samsung is willing to pay to store tools it cannot yet install. That is what a multi-year structural shortage looks like from the factory floor.

text:
Please feel free to copy paste this mail to everyone connected to these poor elephants:
——
This letter confronts a moral obscenity that has been allowed to fester under the cover of tradition and devotion. Elephants—beings you yourselves associate with the divine form of Ganesha, symbols of wisdom, strength, and auspiciousness—are systematically confined, shackled, isolated, dislocated from their natural lives and social herds, and subjected to prolonged physical and psychological torture designed to crush their spirits into submission. This is not reverence. This is not worship. This is calculated cruelty driven by human ego, spectacle, and monetary greed. It is pure evil dressed in ritual clothing.
These animals are torn from their mothers as calves. They are then “broken” through methods that include prolonged beating, starvation, chaining so tight that metal sinks into flesh, and the deliberate infliction of pain with bullhooks, spiked poles, and other instruments until their will is destroyed. After periods of musth, groups of men subject them to extended assaults lasting days in order to reassert dominance. They stand for decades on hard concrete or stone, often in their own waste, developing crippling foot rot, arthritis, abscesses, blindness, and infections. They are denied movement, social contact, natural foraging, and any semblance of the life their biology demands. During festivals they are forced to endure hours or days of deafening noise, fireworks, dense crowds, and extreme heat while carrying idols or standing motionless as living props. Many die young from the cumulative trauma. Others finally snap under the pressure, causing harm—itself a direct consequence of the conditions humans created.
What god demands this? Which scripture, which principle of dharma, which concept of the sacred requires the daily torment of a highly intelligent, emotional, long-lived social animal? Hindu tradition elevates ahimsa—non-violence—as a foundational ethic. The same tradition that sees the divine in all life cannot coherently endorse the reduction of elephants to shackled commodities for temple prestige and festival income. The isolation is solitary confinement. The chaining is immobilization. The beating to “crush” them is systematic psychological and physical destruction. Calling this holy does not make it so; it exposes a profound perversion of the very idea of the sacred. It reveals selfish human egos that prioritize spectacle, status, and revenue over the suffering of beings far more powerful and ancient than the temporary institutions that exploit them.
The karma generated by this practice is not abstract. Every open wound from chains, every hour of enforced immobility, every act of domination inflicted on an animal denied its nature accrues. Those who order it, those who perform it, those who defend it as “culture,” and those who look away while benefiting from the pageantry participate in a cycle of harm that stands in direct opposition to compassion, restraint, and respect for life. No amount of ritual language erases the blood, the scars, the stereotypic swaying of traumatized animals, or the premature deaths. The public record—documentaries, veterinary reports, court observations, activist investigations, and official inspections—has made the conditions undeniable for years. Continuing this system after such knowledge is not ignorance; it is choice.
This must end. Transfer remaining captive elephants to genuine sanctuaries where they can live without weapons, without permanent chains, and with the company of their own kind.

Replace live animals in processions with mechanical alternatives already offered and used by some temples.

REPOST. 

The annual meeting of the 23th Valdai International Discussion Club is opening today and it will be held from September 28 to October 1 in Moscow (this year, due to security reasons, the event was moved from Sochi to Moscow).

The President will as usual be the plenary speaker.  The exact date of his attendance has not been announced yet. 

This year's theme: “Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible, or Limitless Possibilities?”

Verbatim from the Valdai website (please scroll down for Russian):
The Club’s flagship conference will bring together 120 participants from 40 countries, including Algeria, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Iran, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Last year, participants in the Annual Meeting discussed the factors that enable states to remain resilient amid ongoing change. Today, the organisers believe that, despite the crisis in the global order and the unprecedented escalation of conflicts, it is important to continue analysing what the future may look like in order to be able to influence the process of shaping it.

The issue of responsibility for the future has been a central theme, shaping the agenda of Valdai events throughout the year. Participants in the Annual Meeting will continue to discuss the question of how manageable and predictable international affairs can be against the backdrop of the crisis facing multilateral institutions. The organisers propose that participants in the 23rd Annual Meeting consider the possible consequences of escalating the military and political situation, the restructuring of trade and economic ties, and the introduction of new technologies, as well as discuss the responsibility of states and their role in the future international order.

The meeting will open with a presentation of a specially prepared report, “Keep Calm: The State and Responsibility for the Future”.

“The annual Valdai Report in the turbulent and alarming year 2026 offers a blueprint on ways of looking into the future without fear even if the processes unfolding on our watch can be quite unnerving,” write the authors themselves. In their conclusions, they note that the response to contemporary challenges is an increasing role for the state, as well as the return of the individual as a whole, and the state leader in particular, to the centre of international and public life.

The 23rd Annual Meeting will run for four days, with a programme comprising the opening ceremony, the presentation of the report, nine thematic sessions, a special session, and an open discussion. In addition, participants in the Annual Meeting will traditionally meet with representatives of the Russian authorities: Sergey Lavrov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Russia; Maxim Oreshkin, Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration of Russia. On the sidelines of the forum, journalists will have the opportunity to speak with participants in all Valdai events.

Among the international participants this year are Karen Hallberg, Secretary General of the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs (Argentina); Richard Sakwa, Emeritus Professor of Politics at the University of Kent (United Kingdom); Ramzy Ezzeldin Ramzy, Ambassador; Former Senior Deputy Foreign Minister of Egypt; UN Assistant Secretary-General (Egypt); Arvind Gupta, Director of the Vivekananda International Foundation (India); Saeed Khatibzadeh, Deputy Foreign Minister and President of the Institute for Political and International Studies (IPIS) (Iran); Feng Shaolei, Director of the Centre for Russian Studies at East China Normal University (China); Tsogtbaatar Damdin, Member of the Mongolian State Great Khural (Parliament), Chair of the Legal Standing Committee (Mongolia); Majid Ehsan, President of the Islamabad Policy Research Institute (Pakistan); Rasigan Maharajh, Full Professor of Public Affairs, Faculty of Humanities, Tshwane University of Technology (South Africa); Taisuke Abiru, Senior Fellow at the Strategy and Deterrence Program of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation (Japan), and others.

Among the Russian participants are Andrei Fursenko, Aide to the President of the Russian Federation; Alexei Likhachev, Director General of the State Atomic Energy Corporation “Rosatom”; Alexander Dynkin, President of the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO) of the Russian Academy of Sciences; Sergey Karaganov, Academic Supervisor of the Faculty of World Economics and International Relations at HSE University; Victoria Panova, Russian Sherpa to the Women 20 (W20) and Head of the BRICS Expert Council-Russia; Andrey Sushentsov, Dean of the School of International Relations at MGIMO University; Andrei Bystritskiy, Chairman of the Board of the Foundation for the Development and Support of the Valdai Discussion Club; Fyodor Lukyanov, Research Director of the Valdai Discussion Club; Oleg Barabanov, Anton Bespalov, Timofei Bordachev, and Ivan Timofeev, Programme Directors of the Valdai Discussion Club, and others.

С 28 сентября по 1 октября 2026 года пройдёт XXIII Ежегодное заседание Международного дискуссионного клуба «Валдай» на тему «Ответственность за будущее: пределы возможного или возможности без предела?».

Флагманская конференция Клуба объединит 120 участников из 40 стран, включая Алжир, Аргентину, Бразилию, Великобританию, Германию, Египет, Индию, Индонезию, Иран, Италию, Канаду, Китай, Малайзию, ОАЭ, Пакистан, Саудовскую Аравию, США, Турцию, Францию, Швейцарию, Эфиопию, ЮАР, Японию.

В прошлом году участники Большого Валдая обсуждали факторы, благодаря которым государства могут сохранять устойчивость в условиях непрекращающихся изменений. Сегодня, по убеждению организаторов, несмотря на кризис мирового устройства и небывалое обострение конфликтов, важно продолжать анализировать, каким может стать будущее, чтобы иметь возможность повлиять на процесс его становления.

Тема ответственности за будущее была стержневой и формировала повестку Валдайских мероприятий в течение всего года. Участники Большого Валдая продолжат обсуждать вопрос об управляемости и предсказуемости международной жизни на фоне кризиса многосторонних институтов. Организаторы предлагают участникам XXIII Ежегодного заседания рассмотреть возможные последствия нагнетания военно-политической обстановки, переформатирования системы торгово-экономических связей и внедрения новых технологий, а также обсудить ответственность государств и их роль в будущем мироустройстве.

Откроет заседание презентация специально подготовленного доклада «Без паники: государство и ответственность за будущее». «Ежегодный доклад Валдайского клуба в бурном и тревожном 2026 году – о том, как смотреть в будущее без страха, даже если от процессов, разворачивающихся на наших глазах, немного не по себе», – пишут сами авторы. В своих выводах они отмечают, что ответом на современные вызовы становится увеличение роли государства, а также возвращение в центр международной и общественной жизни человека в целом и государственного лидера в частности.

XXIII Ежегодное заседание будет продолжаться четыре дня, его программа включает в себя открытие, презентацию доклада, девять тематических сессий, специальную сессию и открытую дискуссию. Помимо этого, участники Большого Валдая традиционно встретятся с представителями российской власти: министром иностранных дел России Сергеем Лавровым, заместителем руководителя Администрации Президента России Максимом Орешкиным. В кулуарах форума журналисты смогут пообщаться с участниками всех Валдайских мероприятий.

В числе иностранных участников в этом году: генеральный секретарь Пагуошского движения учёных Карен Хальберг (Аргентина); почётный профессор политологии Кентского университета Ричард Саква (Великобритания); посол; бывший старший заместитель министра иностранных дел Египта; помощник Генерального секретаря ООН Эззельдин Рамзи Рамзи (Египет); директор индийского Международного фонда Вивекананды Арвинд Гупта (Индия); заместитель министра иностранных дел Ирана, президент Института политических и международных исследований Сайед Хатибзаде (Иран); директор Центра по изучению России в Восточно-Китайском педагогическом университете Фэн Шаолэй (Китай); депутат Великого Государственного Хурала, председатель постоянного комитета по юриспруденции Цогтбаатар Дамдин (Монголия); директор Института политических исследований Исламабада Маджид Эхсан (Пакистан); профессор кафедры общественных наук факультета гуманитарных наук при Техническом университете Цване Расиган Махарадж (ЮАР); старший научный сотрудник программы «Стратегия и сдерживание» Фонда мира Сасакавы Тайсукэ Абиру (Япония) и другие.

Среди российских участников: помощник Президента Российской Федерации Андрей Фурсенко; генеральный директор Государственной корпорации по атомной энергии «Росатом» Алексей Лихачёв; президент ИМЭМО РАН Александр Дынкин; научный руководитель факультета мировой экономики и мировой политики НИУ ВШЭ Сергей Караганов; шерпа Российской Федерации в «Женской двадцатке» (W20), руководитель Экспертного совета БРИКС – Россия Виктория Панова; декан факультета международных отношений МГИМО МИД России Андрей Сушенцов; председатель Совета Фонда развития и поддержки Международного дискуссионного клуба «Валдай» Андрей Быстрицкий; директор по научной работе Фонда клуба «Валдай» Фёдор Лукьянов; программные директора Международного дискуссионного клуба «Валдай» Олег Барабанов, Антон Беспалов, Тимофей Бордачёв, Иван Тимофеев и другие.

text:
Perversions of Science stands as one of the boldest and strangest experiments in 1990s television, a short lived HBO anthology series that took the twisted spirit of Tales from the Crypt and blasted it into the realm of science fiction with unapologetic sex, dark humor, and moral chaos. Premiering on June 7 1997 and lasting only ten episodes until July 23 of that same year, it arrived right after its parent show ended its legendary run and tried to capture the same late night cable magic by adapting stories from EC Comics titles like Weird Science, Weird Fantasy, and Incredible Science Fiction. What made it immediately different was its host. Instead of the Cryptkeeper’s rotting puns about death, viewers met Chrome, a gleaming computer generated female android voiced by Maureen Teefy. She lounged in a futuristic control room, pressed a nipple to access story files, and delivered every introduction and closing remark laced with pure sexual innuendo. That single choice set the tone for everything that followed. The series never pretended to be wholesome or restrained. It leaned hard into the freedom HBO offered at the time, mixing graphic violence, nudity, and wicked comedy into tales about technology, desire, and human folly.

The overall structure worked like a warped Twilight Zone crossed with soft core sci fi. Each episode opened with Chrome pulling a tale from her database, then dropped the audience into a self contained story that usually ended with a sharp ironic twist. After the story finished she returned for a final smirking comment that tied the moral back to something dirty or clever. The themes stayed consistent across the run even as the settings jumped from dream worlds to outer space to alternate dimensions. Science in these stories never simply advanced knowledge. It always became a tool for obsession, control, or self destruction. Characters chased perfection, immortality, or escape and paid for it in grotesque or darkly funny ways. The series treated sex as both a punchline and a weapon. Chrome herself embodied that blend. Her metallic body and sultry delivery made the framing device feel like a living advertisement for the show’s dual personality of sexy and funny. That combination is rare even now. Most science fiction anthologies either stayed cerebral or went pure horror. Perversions of Science refused to pick one lane and instead crashed them together with the volume turned up.

Look at the guest stars who rotated through those ten episodes and the depth becomes clearer. Keith Carradine played a professor trapped in endless dreams. Jason Lee and Jamie Kennedy shared a 1930s Halloween party that spiraled into panic during a War of the Worlds broadcast. William Shatner appeared as an admiral with very specific ideas about fidelity while directing one episode himself. Ron Perlman, Jeffrey Combs, Heather Langenkamp, Yancy Butler, Sean Astin, Wil Wheaton, Elizabeth Berkley, Kevin Pollak, George Newbern, and Barry Williams all showed up in different installments. Directors included heavy hitters like Walter Hill, Tobe Hooper, Russell Mulcahy, and even Sean Astin stepping behind the camera. Danny Elfman composed the theme, giving the opening sequence that distinctive eerie yet playful energy. The production team carried over key names from Tales from the Crypt including executive producers Richard Donner, Walter Hill, Joel Silver, and Robert Zemeckis. That pedigree alone made the show feel like a high end party that only lasted one summer.

The stories themselves never needed elaborate mythology because the lessons lived inside the actions of ordinary people pushed past their limits by scientific power. In one tale a man cannot wake from layered dreams and discovers that reality itself might be the illusion he fears most. The takeaway sits right there in his desperate thrashing. Control over the mind can become a prison worse than any physical cage. Another episode follows a woman who surgically and temporarily rewrites her body into ideal form then travels into the past only to confront a man equally obsessed with perfection. Their mutual pursuit exposes how the hunger for flawlessness can erase the messy humanity that actually makes connection possible. A space pilot spends years alone with a female android while promising fidelity to a distant fiancée only to learn that technology and authority have already rewritten the rules of loyalty. The humor lands because the situation is absurd yet the lesson about isolation and the commodification of intimacy still stings. Elsewhere a scientist who experiments on people to purge impurity ends up facing a justice system that decides exile is the cleanest solution. The actions of the character force the viewer to ask whether purification is ever pure or simply another form of cruelty dressed in clinical language. A grieving widower volunteers for an experiment that might let him reach another plane where his dead wife still lives and the consequences spiral outward. The desire to undo loss becomes the very thing that multiplies it. Even the lighter episodes carry weight. A suburban family caught between warring robots ends up choosing a patriotic model that promises safety and the choice itself becomes a quiet satire on how people outsource their values to machines.

These lessons never arrive as lectures. They emerge from the choices characters make under pressure. Science offers power and the characters grab it with both hands. Then the power twists. The series keeps returning to the idea that human desire will always corrupt the tools it invents. Whether the tool is a dream machine, a body modification process, a space vessel, or a household robot, the result follows the same pattern. Ambition outruns wisdom. Lust outruns caution. Fear outruns reason. Chrome’s closing remarks usually underline the point with a wink so the audience never feels preached at. The combination of sexy framing and genuine moral sting is what gives the show its particular flavor. It can make you laugh at a chastity belt joke one moment and then sit with the horror of a self destructing spaceship the next.

What makes Perversions of Science stand out from other anthologies is precisely that refusal to sanitize. The Outer Limits of the 1990s stayed more restrained. Black Mirror later perfected the technology gone wrong formula but arrived in a different era. This show arrived at the peak of HBO’s willingness to push boundaries and it used that freedom without apology. The CGI for Chrome looks dated now yet still carries a strange charm because it was ambitious for 1997. The practical effects and production design hold up better than expected. The star power packed into half hour episodes feels almost wasteful in the best way. You get Shatner, Lee, Combs, Langenkamp, and others delivering sharp turns in stories that might have been feature length elsewhere. The short run itself became part of its legend. It never had time to grow stale or formulaic in the public eye. Instead it remains a concentrated blast of 1990s excess that later viewers rediscover and treat like a lost artifact.

The cultural footprint stayed small during its original airing. Ratings never matched Tales from the Crypt and HBO was already shifting toward serialized dramas like Oz. Yet the show refused to vanish completely. Fans of the Crypt series hunted it down. Genre collectors kept the episodes alive through bootlegs and later digital releases. Its cult status grew because it captured a specific moment when cable television still felt dangerous and experimental. The stories about sexbots and robot nannies now look almost prophetic. The satire of media induced panic in the War of the Worlds episode still feels relevant. The body horror mixed with comedy remains distinctive. In an age of endless reboots and safe content, the pure weirdness of a metallic hostess pressing her nipple to start a tale about scientific perversion feels refreshing.

It earns the title of must watch classic not because every episode is perfect but because the whole package is uniquely itself. The uneven quality is part of the charm. Some stories hit harder than others yet the consistent voice of Chrome and the shared DNA of EC Comics keep everything tied together. Watching it now is like finding a time capsule of late century anxiety about technology wrapped in neon lights and leather. The lessons about hubris and desire still land because the characters act them out with full commitment. The funny moments never undercut the darker ones. They coexist the same way Chrome’s beauty and her cold metallic nature coexist. That balance is rare. Most shows choose one tone and stick to it. Perversions of Science kept both plates spinning for ten wild weeks and then disappeared, leaving behind a concentrated dose of sci fi that feels both of its time and strangely ahead of it. The combination of star studded casts, unfiltered adult content, sharp twists, and a host who treated every story like a dirty secret makes it impossible to confuse with anything else that came before or after.

text:
The White House's Xi-Trump meeting readout says interesting things about what each side seems to have reached consensus on. As always, Beijing continues to withhold. Here are a few of my takeaways from a new piece in @moneycontrolcom:

1️⃣ Beijing is setting the floor and ceiling, in that "Constructive strategic stability" is China's phrase, and the latest US fact sheet now builds it on "respect," the one word Beijing has long wanted from Washington. It also says both leaders agreed to call the mega-profile tech "super intelligence" rather than AI. Xinhua still says "artificial intelligence," so Beijing clearly didn't feel bound.

2️⃣ Washington hasn't given up the page entirely. The fact sheet slips in and normalises America's "forward military presence" in a "Free and Open Indo-Pacific." It also sets coal and rare-earth targets for China that Beijing doesn't repeat, but will likely meet if it wants the stability it keeps talking about. We even saw with the 12 mn tonne soybean output that it was met earlier this year, though 6 months after the initial deadline.

3️⃣ The concessions are uneven. Taiwan goes unmentioned, and the ~US$14 bn arms package may slip past APEC in Shenzhen, or even the G20 in Miami. What China offers in return can all be undone -- 10 mn tonnes of US coal a year in 2027 and 2028, fentanyl precursor controls, and tariff "recommendations" on US$30 billion of goods each way.

4️⃣ The deadlines still to watch: the trade truce is extended 2 months beyond 10 November, but nothing has been said about the ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US, whose pause lapses on 27 November. Decrees 834, 836 and 837 are waiting for the 50,000 American firms in the Chinese market that Beijing keeps counting in its readouts.

5️⃣ Trump still has cards. The threat of 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian oil, and the room between today's ~32% tariff and the 20% Xi wants, are both levers.
With midterms a month away, the question for Washington is whether friendship for show is worth the alliances it costs, and whether there is anything here to sell to voters. If the answer to both is no, stability has gone too far.

Read the full piece: https://t.co/kGfIye1z2Q

text:
My wife heard the MRI tech tell someone the machine had been "acting weird all morning" right before her scan.

Scheduled for a brain MRI, routine headache follow-up. She's changing into the gown when she hears the tech on the phone in the hallway.

"Yeah, it keeps shutting off mid-scan. I've restarted it three times... No, the engineer can't come until tomorrow... I know, but we're booked solid. I'm just gonna keep running it and hope it holds."

My wife opens the door. "Excuse me?"

Tech jumps. "I'll call you back." Hangs up, turns to my wife with a smile. "All ready?"

"Is the machine broken?"

"Oh, you heard that? No, just a minor glitch. Completely safe."

"You said it keeps shutting off mid-scan."

The tech tries to downplay it. "It's just a software thing. Doesn't affect the imaging quality."

My wife doesn't move. "If it's shutting off, how do you know you're getting complete images?"

"We restart the sequence. Patients don't feel anything...."

"How many times has it shut off today?"

Tech admits it's happened on four of the six scans that morning. Each time they had to start over, doubling the patient's time in the machine.

My wife gets dressed. "I'm not getting in a broken machine. Reschedule me when it's fixed."

Tech gets the supervisor. Supervisor confirms an engineer is coming tomorrow, tries to assure my wife the images are fine despite the glitches.

"Then why is the engineer coming? If it's fine, why fix it?"

No good answer.

My wife rescheduled at a different imaging center. Their machine worked fine. Got her results in two days.

Original facility called three times to apologize and offer a discount on the rescheduled scan.

She never went back.

"Minor glitch" stops being minor when it's your brain being scanned.

These individuals are navigating a massive disconnect between astronomical capital expenditure and a lack of clear, scalable revenue. https://t.co/PCsyO3BR49 

The Hyperscale Executives (Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon): Behind closed doors, these leaders likely feel the weight of a 'Prisoner’s Dilemma.' Having already committed hundreds of billions to data center infrastructure, they may be privately terrified of slowing down. To pivot now would signal to the market that their core thesis—that generative AI will transform every aspect of enterprise productivity—was premature or overvalued. They are likely calculating how to 'soft land' their hardware investments, perhaps by reallocating capacity toward internal efficiencies or cloud-hosting for third-party developers, while publicly maintaining a narrative of inevitable, world-changing growth. The tension lies in balancing the need to satisfy shareholders who demand AI dominance with the reality of increasing credit risks on their balance sheets.

Privately, they likely recognize the growing trend of enterprise customers favoring cheaper, smaller, or open-weight models that offer more reliability and control. Their push for IPOs—often framed as necessary for liquidity—is likely a strategic calculation to move toward a more transparent (or final) phase of ownership before the 'AI bubble' reality catches up with their long-term lease obligations. Privately, they are likely searching for an exit ramp—a 'Chernobyl event' or market catalyst that forces a correction, allowing them to trim their exposure without being singled out as the ones who 'missed' the tech revolution. The documented reasons differ by offer, but they cluster around the same few issues.

1937 Peel Commission and 1947 UN partition.

Arab leadership rejected both because they opposed any Jewish state on any part of the land. The Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini told the Peel Commission that most Jews would not receive citizenship in an Arab Palestine and that Jews should be expelled if a Jewish state were created. In 1947 the Arab Higher Committee and surrounding Arab states rejected the UN plan - Jews around 33% of the population offered around 55% of the territory, and chose war instead. From the Palestinian/Arab view at the time, the land was already theirs. Partition required them to concede national rights they did not recognize.

Camp David 2000 
Barak’s offer (accounts range from around 91–94% of the West Bank plus Gaza, land swaps and limited Jerusalem arrangements) was rejected without a counter proposal. Arafat’s objections, according to Clinton, Barak and later Palestinian negotiators centered on:

- incomplete sovereignty (Israeli security presence, airspace and border control).

- Jerusalem, especially sovereignty over the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif. Arafat denied any Jewish historical connection.

- the refugee issue: Israel offered only a limited humanitarian intake, not a general “right of return” for 1948 refugees and descendants.  
Arafat also told Clinton that accepting the deal would get him killed.

Olmert 2008
Olmert presented a map of roughly 93–94% of the West Bank with 1:1 swaps, Gaza, a West Bank–Gaza link, shared or international arrangements for the Old City/Holy Basin and a small number of refugees. Abbas later said the gaps were too wide and that he was not allowed to take the map away to study it. The remaining disputes were again refugees, holy sites and whether Israel would be recognized as the nation state of the Jewish people.

The recurring Palestinian position across these episodes is that a state “on their land” was unacceptable if it required permanently accepting a Jewish state, forgoing a mass refugee return into Israel proper, or accepting less than full sovereignty over East Jerusalem and the holy sites. Israeli and some international accounts treat that as rejection of two states for two peoples. Palestinian and some critical accounts treat the offers themselves as insufficient or as requiring them to ratify the 1948 outcome they still regard as illegitimate. Arab settlers from all over the Middle East are now referred to as Palestinians. They never owned the land, they merely settled on it.

Lilith (/ˈlɪlɪθ/; Hebrew: לִילִית, romanized: Līlīṯ; also spelled Lilit or Lilis) is a feminine figure in late-antique Mesopotamian and Jewish mythology. Lilith does not appear in the Hebrew Bible or any other biblical source, although the Hebrew word lilit appears in the Book of Isaiah, specifically in Isaiah 34:14. The meaning of this word is debated by scholars[1] with interpretations ranging from a primordial she-demon[2] to a night bird.[3] The King James translation renders the term in this verse as "screech-owl". Based on medieval Jewish folklore, Lilith is said to have fled from the Garden of Eden because she did not want to submit to Adam.[4]

The earliest known mention of Lilith is in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q510-11),[5] and afterwards in Mandaean and Jewish sources from late antiquity (300 AD onward), in historiolas – incantations that incorporate a short mythic story – that give partial descriptions of her.[6] She is mentioned in the Babylonian Talmud (at Eruvin 100b, Niddah 24b, Shabbat 151b, Bava Batra 73a), and in the Zohar § Leviticus 19a as "a hot fiery female who first cohabited with man".[7] Some rabbinic authorities, including Maimonides and Menachem Meiri, reject the existence of Lilith.[8]

Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").

In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.

text:
Since his return to the White House last year, President Donald Trump has systematically gutted USAID, the government agency that oversees US efforts to improve health and education and fight poverty around the world. Most contracts were canceled, its budget was cut, and what was left of the agency’s functions were folded into the State Department. The Trump administration’s argument: USAID had become bloated, inefficient, and not valuable use of taxpayer money.

But the administration has not abandoned foreign aid it has reshaped it. Washington is channeling foreign aid through bilateral deals, many of which promise the US something in return. The 19 bilateral health agreements signed in Africa in the last year include only a fraction of the assistance distributed largely through USAID, and require many recipient governments to co-finance programs themselves. For example, in Nigeria, the US has offered about $2 billion in aid over five years but only if the government raises its own health spending by $3 billion over the same period. Across the 26 countries around the world that have signed bilateral agreements so far, recipient governments are expected to cover roughly 37% of the nearly $20 billion total package.

The administration’s new model also ties aid more directly to US interests. In Zambia, negotiations linked health assistance to a separate push for access to critical mineral resources a significant departure from the old approach of aid for development and humanitarianism. Post-USAID funding is allocated less by universal development goals than by whether the country serves “America First” interests.
The upside. This shift is being presented by the administration as a move away from dependency and toward sovereignty. For some African governments, that argument has appeal. Many have long objected to an aid system in which foreign NGOs shaped spending priorities and captured large administrative budgets. Direct government-to-government arrangements could, in principle, give ministries more control and better integrate HIV, malaria, and primary care services into national systems.
The risks. In many countries, co-financing demands are arriving at a time of weak growth, high debt, and already constrained budgets. For example, Liberia, and Uganda face particularly high financing requirements. Under the requirements, Liberia needs to increase its own health spending by 23% by 2030 to meet the projected terms of the agreement, at a time when GDP growth has stagnated around 5% since 2023. That raises the prospect that governments will either fail to meet the terms, divert money from other priorities, or accept shoddy standards

Direct democracy, federalism, fiscal discipline, citizen service and strong institutions give Switzerland something most powers lack: cohesion without permanent external antagonism. That is a serious strategic asset.🇨🇭

𝟮. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗦𝘄𝗶𝘁𝘇𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱’𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹.  

Trade, finance, pharmaceuticals, commodities and Alpine transit make Swiss stability useful to others. The objective is not isolation; it is ensuring that neighbours and partners have a stake in Switzerland remaining stable, open and predictable.✅

𝟯. 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺.  

Armed neutrality, credible self-defence, good offices and strategic restraint are not nostalgic ornaments. They are rational doctrine for a small, prosperous, landlocked country.

𝟰. 𝗗𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆.  ✅🇨🇭

Switzerland should not turn sanctions, military posturing or bloc loyalty into substitutes for a clear, independent national interest.

For Switzerland, the “kingly way” is not empty rhetoric. It is the only scalable strategy: be internally legitimate, economically useful, militarily capable, diplomatically trusted—and independent enough that no outside power can cheaply use us as a pawn.✅

Washington increasingly treats interdependence as leverage. Brussels too often mistakes geopolitical signalling for strategy.

Switzerland’s comparative advantage is to resist both temptations.🇨🇭

text:
When Packaging Becomes Accountability: The Strategic Logic of SK hynix's In-House 2.5D Line

SK hynix disclosed at its Global Forum roundtable on September 18 that it has been preparing an in-house CoWoS-L class 2.5D packaging line for two years. The first line will land at its West Lafayette, Indiana facility, which is scheduled to complete cleanroom operations in the second half of 2028 and begin HBM4E volume production in Q3 2029. The information deserves analysis not because SK hynix is doing advanced packaging — Samsung and Intel are also doing it — but because its motivation for entering packaging is different from every existing participant.

Samsung builds advanced packaging to offer a turnkey solution spanning design, foundry, and packaging. TSMC builds CoWoS because it is the packaging bottleneck for the entire AI chip ecosystem, and packaging capacity itself is pricing power. Intel builds EMIB to convert packaging into a differentiated foundry entry point. SK hynix's case is fundamentally different. It has no intention of becoming a foundry and no intention of competing with TSMC on packaging capacity. At the forum, the speaker stated explicitly that the company "won't go where it would overlap with TSMC" and has "no plan to become a foundry just because its base dies are doing well." Unlike Samsung and Intel, SK hynix does not overlap with TSMC in core business.

This means the purpose of SK hynix's in-house 2.5D line is not to expand packaging capacity. It is to answer a question it cannot answer as an HBM supplier: when an HBM fails inside a customer's package and the failure does not reproduce upon return, how is accountability determined?

The economic scale of this problem far exceeds a typical engineering concern. HBM4's package structure is substantially more complex than HBM3E: pin count roughly doubles from approximately 1,024 to 2,048, TSV count exceeds 20,000, base micro-bumps reach 16,148, package size expands from 10×11 mm to 12.4×11 mm, and die Z-height reaches 775 μm. In 2.5D packaging, GPU and HBM connect through a silicon interposer via 1,024 I/Os across 16 channels, with HBM4 doubling bandwidth to 2,048 GB/s.

The problem is that when this package fails in a customer's data center, the failure could originate from an HBM TSV defect or micro-bump anomaly, from interposer warpage, or from thermal stress during packaging. If the customer returns the failed package and SK hynix cannot reproduce the failure in its own test environment, accountability becomes a multi-party dispute. The HBM supplier, the foundry, the packaging house, and the system integrator can each claim their portion is faultless.

At the forum, SK hynix framed it this way: the in-house 2.5D line's first purpose is to "find out firsthand under what conditions the company's HBM fails inside customers' packages," and the place to do that work is the R&D testbed in Indiana. This is not a commercialization statement. It is an accountability statement. SK hynix is building the capability to determine responsibility with first-hand test data rather than speculation at a negotiating table.

The Indiana facility's construction timeline supports this reading. The plant, with over $4 billion invested, will process wafers shipped from Korea into 2.5D/3D stacking and advanced interposer work, with cleanrooms scheduled for H2 2028 and HBM4E volume production targeted for Q3 2029. Before volume production begins, an "advanced packaging R&D testbed" will be built alongside the production line for joint development and rapid prototype validation with customers and partners.

This means the Indiana facility's core output before 2029 is not packaged HBM products. It is packaging failure diagnostic data and failure mode libraries. Commercialization comes after validation. This is not a capacity expansion capex decision. It is a data sovereignty capex decision. SK hynix is moving HBM failure analysis from customer sites or third-party labs into an environment it controls.

SK hynix currently has four parallel 2.5D packaging paths: CoWoS-L/S/R with TSMC, Intel's EMIB-T, the in-house 2.5D line, and continued reliance on OSAT partners such as Amkor. The market typically reads these as "capacity hedging" — more packaging options, more supply security.

The real logic runs deeper. CoWoS-L is reportedly sold out into 2027, with Nvidia estimated to consume more than 60% of global CoWoS capacity and Broadcom and AMD absorbing roughly another 26% between them. Under that allocation, SK hynix's packaging path choice is strongly constrained by its downstream customers, primarily Nvidia. The customer decides which packaging technology to use, and SK hynix must adapt.

Building an in-house 2.5D line changes not SK hynix's packaging capacity but its bargaining position. When SK hynix has its own packaging test capability, it can enter packaging discussions with customers carrying its own test data rather than relying on failure reports provided by the customer. Against an HBM4 yield environment still below 60%, that capability difference directly affects commercial negotiation outcomes.

The valuation implication of this investment does not sit on the near-term revenue side. Indiana's HBM4E volume production does not arrive until 2029, contributing zero to 2027–2028 revenue. The real pricing question is whether failure accountability capability becomes a core competitive dimension in HBM supplier selection. If it does, SK hynix's early investment changes its negotiating leverage in next-generation HBM supply agreements.

The HBM market currently competes on supply capacity and price. As HBM4 packaging complexity rises and failure accountability becomes a customer concern, a competitive dimension may emerge that did not previously exist: who can quickly and quantitatively define the boundary of responsibility when a failure occurs. On that dimension, the diagnostic capability SK hynix acquires through its in-house 2.5D line may be worth more than one additional packaging capacity option. Samsung's turnkey strategy theoretically offers similar accountability capability by integrating design, foundry, and packaging under one roof, but its competitive overlap with TSMC in foundry makes the neutrality of its packaging data questionable to customers.

SK hynix's unique position — not competing with TSMC, not becoming a foundry — gives its in-house packaging line a neutrality that other participants cannot replicate. When SK hynix says "I won't do foundry," it is telling customers that its packaging test data does not serve any foundry business competition. In a market where HBM4 yield is an industry-wide challenge, that neutrality may convert into a material commercial advantage.

The next node to track is 2027. If SK hynix($SKHY )'s Indiana facility begins producing early HBM packaging failure analysis data and uses it to restructure terms in HBM4E supply agreements with major customers, then the $4 billion capital commitment will have been validated as a strategic investment — not because it added packaging capacity, but because it changed SK hynix's position in the HBM value chain.

Core Associations of Mars in Kabbalah

Elon (אֵילוֹן in Hebrew) is a masculine first name, or Jewish surname, which means "oak tree" in the Hebrew language. Variants of the name include Alon, Eilan, Eilon, and Elan; it can also be a variant spelling of Ilan and Ilon (Hebrew: אילן), of the similar meaning "tree".
The given name became more popular in the 2010s (from No. 3,310 in 2008 to No. 885 in 2018 for baby boys in the United States) due to the rise to fame of Elon Musk, though he is not Jewish.[1][2]

The Tree of Life (Hebrew: עֵץ חַיִּים, ʿēṣ ḥayyim) is a symbolic diagram used in Jewish mystical traditions, especially in Kabbalah, to describe divine structure, creation, and the spiritual path of ascent.[1] It is usually referred to as the "kabbalistic tree of life" to distinguish it from the tree of life that appears alongside the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the Genesis creation narrative as well as the archetypal tree of life found in many cultures.[2] It serves as both a conceptual framework and, in later Kabbalistic texts, a schematic diagram linking the sefirot, or divine emanations, to cosmology and human spiritual development.[1]

Simo Parpola asserted that the concept of a tree of life with different spheres encompassing aspects of reality traces its origins back to the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the ninth century BC.[3] The Assyrians assigned moral values and specific numbers to Mesopotamian deities similar to those used in Kabbalah and claims that the state tied these to sacred tree images as a model of the king parallel to the idea of Adam Kadmon.[3] However, J. H. Chajes states that the ilan should be regarded as primarily indebted to the Porphyrian tree and maps of the celestial spheres rather than to any speculative ancient sources, Assyrian or otherwise.[4]

Kabbalah's beginnings date to the Middle Ages, originating in the Bahir[5] and the Zohar.[6] Although the earliest extant Hebrew kabbalistic manuscripts dating to the late 13th century contain diagrams, including one labelled "Tree of Wisdom," the now-iconic tree of life emerged during the fourteenth century.[7]

The iconic representation first appeared in print on the cover of the Latin translation of Gates of Light in the year 1516.[8] Scholars have traced the origin of the art in the Porta Lucis cover to Johann Reuchlin.[9]

Description
The tree of life usually consists of 10 or 11 nodes symbolizing different archetypes and 22 paths connecting the nodes. The nodes are often arranged into three columns to represent that they belong to a common category.[10]

In kabbalah, the nodes are called sefirot.[11] They are usually represented as circles and the paths (Hebrew: צִנּוֹר, romanized: ṣinnoroṯ) are usually represented as lines.[12] The nodes usually represent encompassing aspects of existence, God, or the human psyche.[13] The paths usually represent the relationship between the concepts ascribed to the spheres or a symbolic description of the requirements to go from one sphere to another.[13] The columns are usually symbolized as pillars.[14] These usually represent different kinds of moral values, electric charges, or types of ceremonial magic.[8]

The sefirot are the ten spheres on the Tree of Life. Each sefirah (singular of sefirot) represents a different aspect of the Divine, as well as aspects of human consciousness and existence. These are, from top to bottom:[15]

Keter (crown)
Hokhmah (wisdom)
Binah (intelligence)
Hesed (mercy)
Gevurah (judgement)
Tiferet (beauty)
Netsah (lasting endurance)
Hod (majesty)
Yesod (foundation of the world)
Malkuth (kingdom)
An eleventh sefirah, Da'at (knowledge), appears in some diagrams of the tree halfway between Keter (node 1) and Tiferet (node 6).[16]

The diagram is also used in Christian Kabbalah, Hermetic Qabalah, and Theosophy.[17] The nodes are also associated with deities, angels, celestial bodies, moral values, single colors or combinations of them, and specific numbers.[8]

Subject: Immediate End to the Systematic Torture of Temple Elephants – A Gross Betrayal of Dharma, Ahimsa, and Any Notion of the Sacred
To the Temple Trusts, Administrators, Mahouts, Priests, Festival Organizers, and All Who Enable or Profit from the Captivity of Elephants in Indian Temples:

This letter confronts a moral obscenity that has been allowed to fester under the cover of tradition and devotion. Elephants—beings you yourselves associate with the divine form of Ganesha, symbols of wisdom, strength, and auspiciousness—are systematically confined, shackled, isolated, dislocated from their natural lives and social herds, and subjected to prolonged physical and psychological torture designed to crush their spirits into submission. This is not reverence. This is not worship. This is calculated cruelty driven by human ego, spectacle, and monetary greed. It is pure evil dressed in ritual clothing.
These animals are torn from their mothers as calves. They are then “broken” through methods that include prolonged beating, starvation, chaining so tight that metal sinks into flesh, and the deliberate infliction of pain with bullhooks, spiked poles, and other instruments until their will is destroyed. After periods of musth, groups of men subject them to extended assaults lasting days in order to reassert dominance. They stand for decades on hard concrete or stone, often in their own waste, developing crippling foot rot, arthritis, abscesses, blindness, and infections. They are denied movement, social contact, natural foraging, and any semblance of the life their biology demands. During festivals they are forced to endure hours or days of deafening noise, fireworks, dense crowds, and extreme heat while carrying idols or standing motionless as living props. Many die young from the cumulative trauma. Others finally snap under the pressure, causing harm—itself a direct consequence of the conditions humans created.
What god demands this? Which scripture, which principle of dharma, which concept of the sacred requires the daily torment of a highly intelligent, emotional, long-lived social animal? Hindu tradition elevates ahimsa—non-violence—as a foundational ethic. The same tradition that sees the divine in all life cannot coherently endorse the reduction of elephants to shackled commodities for temple prestige and festival income. The isolation is solitary confinement. The chaining is immobilization. The beating to “crush” them is systematic psychological and physical destruction. Calling this holy does not make it so; it exposes a profound perversion of the very idea of the sacred. It reveals selfish human egos that prioritize spectacle, status, and revenue over the suffering of beings far more powerful and ancient than the temporary institutions that exploit them.
The karma generated by this practice is not abstract. Every open wound from chains, every hour of enforced immobility, every act of domination inflicted on an animal denied its nature accrues. Those who order it, those who perform it, those who defend it as “culture,” and those who look away while benefiting from the pageantry participate in a cycle of harm that stands in direct opposition to compassion, restraint, and respect for life. No amount of ritual language erases the blood, the scars, the stereotypic swaying of traumatized animals, or the premature deaths. The public record—documentaries, veterinary reports, court observations, activist investigations, and official inspections—has made the conditions undeniable for years. Continuing this system after such knowledge is not ignorance; it is choice.
This must end. Transfer remaining captive elephants to genuine sanctuaries where they can live without weapons, without permanent chains, and with the company of their own kind. 

Replace live animals in processions with mechanical alternatives already offered and used by some temples. 

Sincerely:
