This transactional approach signals to regional players that long-term security commitments are subject to sudden bilateral economic negotiations.

Consequently, regional states are likely to hedge their security bets, driving a fragmented defense landscape in the Western Pacific.

The proposal challenges the established bipartisan consensus in Washington, which historically framed Beijing as a primary systemic competitor.

By introducing military sales into bilateral negotiations, the administration attempts to bypass traditional diplomatic channels to force economic concessions.

This tactical maneuver coincides with the release of new product lists for a $38 billion tariff framework targeting Chinese goods.

• The new tariff framework targets key industrial sectors, introducing significant duties on raw materials and manufacturing inputs.

• Beijing has retaliated by preparing reciprocal duties on US coal imports, striking at key domestic energy production sectors.

• Global energy supply chains and technology manufacturing hubs remain the primary battlegrounds in this intensifying economic conflict.

Using military cooperation as leverage in trade disputes demonstrates a willingness to subordinate geopolitical strategy to immediate mercantilist metrics.

This approach risks undermining the institutional continuity of Western foreign policy, replacing predictable containment with volatile bilateral deals.

European and Asian allies are now forced to rapidly adapt to a security environment where bilateral treaties offer diminishing certainty.

The contradiction between official diplomatic denials and ambassadorial disclosures exposes deep structural divisions within the US foreign policy apparatus.

Such policy inconsistencies allow Beijing to exploit divisions in the Western alliance network, offering alternative regional security arrangements.

• European partners are warning that unpredictable US shifts could undermine the collective security posture of the broader Western bloc.

• The deterrence value of the US military presence in the Taiwan Strait is experiencing its most severe credibility crisis in decades.

As the institutional guardrails of global diplomacy weaken, middle powers are seeking localized security coalitions to bypass superpower volatility.

This shift away from centralized alliances toward flexible, ad-hoc coalitions will define the next phase of global geopolitical competition.

The integration of economic tariffs and potential military sales reveals a highly aggressive, unilateral approach to trade deficit reduction.

By leveraging defense assets, Washington seeks to force Beijing into structural economic concessions that conventional trade policy could not achieve.

However, this strategy risks backfiring by accelerating Beijing's drive for technological self-reliance and domestic defense manufacturing.

• Beijing has accelerated its domestic semiconductor development to insulate its military-industrial complex from Western supply chains.

• The regional balance of power is shifting toward a highly militarized, unstable equilibrium where miscalculation risks are elevated.

The erosion of predictable diplomatic red lines increases the probability of localized conflicts escalating into broader regional confrontations.

**SYSTEMIC IMPACT**

The long-term equilibrium of the international system is shifting from a structured, alliance-based bipolarity to a highly volatile, transactional multipolarity.

text:
Warren Buffett Offers Solution to America’s $40 Trillion Debt Crisis: ‘I Could End the Deficit in Five Minutes’ | David Lindfield, Slay News

Billionaire investor Warren Buffett has offered a brutally simple solution to America’s spiraling debt crisis: Make members of Congress personally pay the political price when they fail to control federal spending.

With the national debt surging past an astonishing $40 trillion this summer, Buffett’s proposal puts accountability directly where it belongs, on the politicians responsible for approving Washington’s spending.

“I could end the deficit in five minutes,” Buffett once said.

“You just pass a law that says that any time there is a deficit of more than 3% of GDP, all sitting members of Congress are ineligible for reelection.”

The proposal is remarkably straightforward.

If lawmakers cannot keep the deficit under control, they lose their jobs.

And with Washington now borrowing roughly $2 trillion a year despite collecting more than $5 trillion annually, Buffett’s idea is drawing renewed attention as America’s fiscal crisis reaches another alarming milestone.

America Blows Past $40 Trillion

The United States crossed the $40 trillion national debt threshold this summer, less than a decade after passing $20 trillion in 2017.

The debt now exceeds 120% of America’s gross domestic product.

But the sheer size of the debt is only part of the problem.

Washington must also pay interest on the money it has already borrowed, and those financing costs are consuming an increasingly large share of federal spending.

Investors are demanding higher returns to lend money to the federal government, making America’s borrowing increasingly expensive.

At the same time, the Treasury has relied heavily on shorter-term debt that must continually be refinanced.

The result is a federal government simultaneously financing enormous new deficits while repeatedly refinancing trillions of dollars in existing obligations.

Interest payments on the debt have already grown larger than America’s military spending.

If the current trajectory continues, servicing the national debt could eventually become the federal government’s largest expense.

Washington Collects Trillions and Still Can’t Stop Overspending

The federal government already collects more than $5 trillion from Americans each year.

That is more than the annual economic output of virtually every country on Earth.

Yet Washington still spends roughly $2 trillion more than it takes in.

The problem is not a lack of money flowing into the federal government.

It is Washington’s inability to live within its means.

Estimates place waste, fraud, and abuse throughout the federal government at anywhere from hundreds of billions of dollars to as much as $1 trillion annually.

Congress has also repeatedly avoided serious reforms to massive entitlement programs even as their long-term costs continue to place greater pressure on federal finances.

The political calculation is obvious.

Meaningful spending reform requires lawmakers to make difficult decisions that can anger voters and powerful interest groups.

Borrowing more money allows politicians to delay those decisions and leave Americans with the consequences through higher debt, mounting interest costs, and the erosion of purchasing power.

Buffett’s Plan Changes the Incentives

Buffett’s proposal attacks that political problem directly.

Instead of allowing members of Congress to repeatedly approve deficit spending and then campaign for reelection without consequences, his rule would tie their political careers to the government’s fiscal performance.

Run a deficit exceeding 3% of GDP, and every sitting member of Congress becomes ineligible for reelection.

An even tougher version would require Washington to balance the budget entirely through spending restraint rather than tax increases.

That would prevent politicians from simply reaching deeper into Americans’ pockets to preserve bloated federal spending.

The underlying principle is simple: incentives drive behavior.

Congress currently has every incentive to spend money, distribute benefits, avoid painful reforms, and leave the bill for future taxpayers.

There is little immediate political reward for cutting spending, while virtually every reduction creates a constituency prepared to punish lawmakers for making it.

Buffett’s proposal would reverse that equation.

Congress Created the Crisis

America has the economic capacity to bring its finances under control.

What Washington has lacked is the political will.

Decades of unchecked spending have produced a $40 trillion debt burden while interest payments increasingly consume money that could otherwise fund national defense and other core federal responsibilities.

And every additional trillion dollars makes correcting the problem more difficult.

Americans will ultimately bear the consequences whether Congress acts or not.

The only question is whether lawmakers confront the problem deliberately through spending reform or allow debt, interest costs, and inflationary pressure to impose the consequences later.

Buffett’s solution would give members of Congress a powerful reason to finally make that choice.

If lawmakers cannot balance America’s books, Americans get new lawmakers.

Nothing is new.

Look at that Low cartoon. 

In May 1944, top diplomat, Duff Cooper, produced a remarkably imaginative vision for post-war Britain: lead a Western European grouping, with Britain and France at its core, strong enough to stand alongside America and Russia.

It was not sentimental. It was power. Cooper understood that European organisation need not diminish British influence — it could multiply it.

Eden broadly accepted the strategic logic, though he worried about provoking Stalin and complicating relations with Washington. Churchill was more ambiguous: eloquent about European unity, but never entirely clear about where Britain itself should sit within it until too late.

And by the late 1940s, we were tantalisingly close to what the Europeans offered: the moral and political leadership of the continent.

Britain led the Brussels Treaty, helped create Western Union and the Council of Europe, and for a moment seemed capable of shaping the post-war European order.

Then we hesitated.

When Schuman and Monnet moved towards the Coal and Steel Community, Britain stayed out. The Six went ahead without us.

That became the recurring pattern: Britain complains about the shape of Europe after repeatedly declining to be present when its institutions are being built.

Duff Cooper saw the opportunity.

Eden half-embraced it.

Churchill spoke magnificently about it.

And Britain let it slip.

Eighty years later, the argument is still the same.

text:
NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
From Europe to East Asia, US allies face a hard question: how far would Washington go to defend them? NATO’s Article 5 offers a revealing place to start.
Published 27 Sep, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/hHC4UXnKjW
By Dmitry Trenin, a president of the Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC) and a lead research fellow at the Institute of World Economy and International Relations. He is also a research professor at the Higher School of Economics.
--------
There are few myths as captivating and durable as that of Article 5 of the 1949 Washington Treaty. Proponents of the myth are convinced that, thanks to this provision, NATO is like Alexandre Dumas’s Three Musketeers, in which an attack against one is an attack against all, and the US would automatically come in full force to the rescue of any of the allies under attack.
It’s debatable and essentially unknowable to what extent that would have worked in the situation of the Cold War, when the US genuinely feared the Soviet/Communist threat, because the bloc was never tested to that extent. But it certainly is utterly false under present conditions and likely future circumstances, and America’s allies and partners need to pay attention and be careful.
The wording of the article itself is deliberately ambiguous. Clearly, there’s no automaticity there in the use of force, and such careful formulation was a condition for the treaty’s ratification by the US Senate because American policymakers at the time abhorred entering into entangling alliances.
So much for the automatic use of US military force.
Later, after the Soviet Union developed intercontinental ballistic missiles in the mid-to-late 1950s, American military strategy sought to avoid a direct nuclear exchange. Nuclear war, if it were to be fought, was to stay limited, confined to Europe, east and west.
So much for the US nuclear umbrella.
During the Cold War, recurrent crises around West Berlin were considered in Washington as a likely casus belli, but West Berlin was formally an occupied territory, rather than an allied country. It was safeguarded by American, British, and French military garrisons, and a move against the city (which was never attempted) would have been an attack on US military personnel. The situation along the German-German, Czechoslovak-West German, or Norway’s and Türkiye’s borders with the Soviet Union, though tense, was invariably stable. Elsewhere, NATO and the Warsaw Pact were separated by wide swaths of neutral territory.
So much for the likelihood of military conflicts which would have triggered Article 5.
The current US National Defense Strategy doesn’t view Russia as a major threat, with the Trump administration busy shifting the focus of US forces to East Asia and the Pacific. President Donald Trump has shifted the burden of NATO’s defense onto the European members themselves. If his performance in the Ukraine conflict is a gauge, he has no wish and no inclination to commit US forces to defending America’s allies and clients. Selling arms to them and sharing intelligence is the limit.
Washington also probably takes seriously Moscow’s warning that a NATO-Russia war would be different from the Ukraine conflict, and that it “would be short.” This logically means, in plain English, that it would be nuclear. Americans who studiously avoided a nuclear war with the Soviet Union when they felt genuinely threatened cannot be expected now to allow themselves to be dragged, on behalf of their European allies, into a nuclear conflict with Russia – still the only country in the world that has the capability to annihilate the US.
In his time, President Joe Biden said the US would defend Taiwan if China tried to achieve national reunification by force, but Trump is far more circumspect. To contain China, as with Russia, his administration pushes its allies to the fore, and the Philippines and Japan are the top candidates. As for Taiwan, after its semiconductor industry is safely relocated to America, the island’s significance for America will greatly diminish.
US security guarantees, though admittedly not Article 5-type, have been exposed as less than hollow in the ongoing US war against Iran. Instead of protecting the Gulf Arab countries, the American bases in the region acted like magnets, drawing Iranian drones and missiles which damaged the host countries’ infrastructure. Those in Eastern and Northern Europe who think they will be better off hosting American (or French, for that matter) nuclear facilities should think again.
Ukraine lost its way and brought untold calamities upon itself when its leaders made NATO membership their goal. They didn’t realize that Washington never intended to give them even a symbolic guarantee of protection. Security in the 21st century world can’t be delegated to foreign powers, it can only rest on one’s own resources and stable relations with neighbors. This is the lesson not just for Ukraine and Europe, but also for the Gulf Arab states and East Asia.

text: Bill Gates’s recent warning was not that a model will spontaneously end civilization. It was that advanced AI is “powerful enough to drive events that… cause a billion deaths,” and that “there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools.”  THE STRESS FALLS ON 'MALICIOUS HANDS.'  Capability plus intent.   He used that framing to reject industry self-regulation and to argue that politicians and law enforcement must impose mandatory safeguards.  Gates claim is easy to overread.    Hostile actors can already cause large-scale harm with existing computers, weapons, and state programs. Ordinary software did not wait for frontier models to enable cybercrime.  The distinctive argument is narrower.  These systems do not invent new physics so much as they compress expertise—planning, iteration, scientific reasoning—that used to reside in small specialist communities.   For well-resourced states, AI is often an accelerator. For weaker actors, it may enlarge the set of people who can attempt harms previously out of reach. Gates’s line is a capability claim about that combination, not a forecast that anyone with a laptop can produce catastrophe.    The policy leap is harder.  If self-regulation is insufficient, someone must write binding rules.  In the United States that someone is Congress, which then delegates to agencies. Members are not model evaluators. They vote; staff and briefers supply the substance. On a technology this expensive and opaque, the people who can explain the details, draft language, and remain in the room are disproportionately the firms already at the frontier. That is ordinary public-choice dynamics.   AI lobbying has become a permanent Washington operation. Frontier labs spend record sums shaping safety rules, infrastructure policy, export controls, and whether states may regulate at all.   Capture can cut two ways. Rules may be too weak: reporting theater, friendly auditors, monitors who depend on the same companies for access.  Or rules may lock in incumbents.  Licensing, large compliance teams, and capital-heavy safety processes raise fixed costs that only current leaders can pay.  Closed labs have floated frameworks—compute thresholds, embedded evaluators, pre-release review—that smaller and open-weight developers call moats. A closed government review shared mainly with the largest firms would bake that advantage in.    A second risk is geopolitical. A unilateral American pause does not pause Beijing. U.S. models still lead on peak capability, but the gap is measured in months, not years. China is already competitive on price, open weights, and much real-world usage.   If Washington delays training while Chinese labs do not, the ceiling narrows. If it only protects closed U.S. labs, it can keep the benchmark crown and still lose the cheap stack other countries install. Export controls try to preserve a lead without stopping American labs; they leak and have not kept Chinese models from drawing close.   A negotiated slowdown with China is the only version of “pacing” that would stop the race. It's not on offer.    None of this proves Gates wrong that malicious use of powerful tools is a public problem.  It does show that “put it in Congress’s hands” transfers the same fights—expertise, money, incumbency, and China—into a venue easier to lobby than a laboratory and slower than the models.    The live questions are more specific than regulate-or-not: who has independent technical capacity; whether rules attach to capabilities or to a short list of firms; whether compute thresholds are safety filters or barriers to entry; and whether open development is a risk or a check on the closed frontier.    Ignore those, and a warning about ill intent becomes an argument for a statute written by the people who already hold the tools.

text:
Life. You need to know when to walk away, know when to run and when to hold steady.

On July 26, 1977, in a New Orleans hotel room, Robert Plant answered a phone call that would tear his life in two

He was twenty-eight years old, leading the most powerful band on the planet, living among private jets, packed stadiums, and seemingly limitless success. Then he heard the voice of his wife, Maureen. And in an instant, everything fell apart.

Karac, their five-year-old son, was dead. A stomach virus, swift and merciless. No warning, no chance to intervene. While Robert sang on the other side of the ocean, his "little mountain man" was gone.

The tour stopped immediately. Plant flew to England in a state of shock that no amount of fame could allay. He found his son in the quiet of the Midlands, surrounded by a grief beyond words. That day, he looked for his bandmates. John Bonham was there, as devastated as he was. Jimmy Page and John Paul Jones were not. They did not show up at the funeral. Years later, they would talk about "respecting space," but for Robert, it was an absence that left a deep scar.

Something inside him cracked. He returned to his farm, stopped drinking, stopped taking drugs, stopped living like a rock star. He said he didn't want to be in Led Zeppelin anymore, that he just wanted to be with his family. He even applied for a job at a teachers' college, ready to leave music forever.

The only one who managed to bring him back was Bonham. Not with pressure, but with friendship. He'd show up at the farm driving a limousine, wearing a chauffeur's hat to make him laugh, and take him out for a quiet drink. He'd remind him that they were friends first, and musicians second. So Robert agreed to give it one last try.
In Through the Out Door was born, an album marked by an undisguised pain. Inside was All My Love, the most intimate tribute Plant ever wrote for his son.

In 1980, they were about to go back on tour. But tragedy wasn't over. On September 24th, during rehearsals, Bonham began drinking like never before. Forty shots of vodka in twelve hours. The next morning, he was dead. He was thirty-two years old.

Led Zeppelin issued a brief, almost terse statement: without Bonham, they couldn't continue. And they kept their word. No farewell tour, no replacement, no nostalgic outing. The biggest band in the world simply stopped.

For the next forty years, promoters from half the planet offered Plant astronomical sums for a reunion. Hundreds of millions for a single tour. Each time, he refused. Fans accused him of selfishness, of stubbornness. But Plant knew something they didn't: the "Golden God" had died in 1977, along with Karac.

Since then, he has built a new musical life. He explored folk, bluegrass, North African rhythms, sang with Alison Krauss, lowered his voice, let go of the cry that had made him immortal. He said he could no longer be that man, because that man no longer existed.
His story overturns the common idea of strength. It's not about moving forward at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop, when to protect what remains of truth. Plant chose his humanity over legend, life over myth.

Today he's seventy-six. He still plays, still creates, tours small venues. But he's never looked back. And perhaps this is his greatest lesson: you can buy everything except the past. And sometimes the bravest thing is to let go of what made you famous to save what made you human.

Police now say the five men at Fairford are British nationals from London, in their 20s. That is being used as a full stop. It is not.

“British national” is a legal sticker. It covers people born here, people naturalised after asylum, people given citizenship after a few years’ leave, and dual nationals whose other loyalty is never tested. None of that finer status has been released. Names are still withheld. Heritage, naturalisation route, travel, and handlers are still withheld. The public is told to accept the passport and move on.

That is the easy-touch problem. Citizenship here is treated as a shield, not a standard. Once the word “British” is out, questions about how someone ended up in the country, who granted them status, and whether they should keep it are waved away as prejudice or “operational.” A suspected plot against a bomber base used to strike Iran is exactly when those questions matter. If any of these men were naturalised, granted protection, or allowed to stay after a weak claim, that is not a side issue. It is how a hostile actor gets to live among the people he is accused of targeting.

Asylum and settlement have been run as a volume process: arrive, claim, wait, appeal, stay. Citizenship follows. Checks on ideology, foreign-state links and travel are thinner than the threat. The Channel route made that worse. Officials spent a day letting the small-boat rumour run, then offered nationality as if it closed the file. It does not. It hides whether the system manufactured the suspect.

Names should be public on a plot of this scale. So should the route to status: born here or made here, and on what evidence. Until that is out, “British from London” is a bureaucratic comfort, not an answer. A state that will not say how these men came to hold its nationality is a state that has already decided the public does not own the citizenship it is expected to trust.

The official police report was completely devastating for Brandon and his mother. Combined with the full emergency dispatch recording and the clear audio files pulled directly from the baby monitor’s internal memory card, which had miraculously survived the smash on the floor, the local prosecutor built a rock-solid criminal case.

The audio recordings explicitly captured my husband and his mother conspiring together to deprive me of sleep, physically assault my body, forcibly seize my newborn infant, and false-imprison me inside the house to break my mental health.

They had foolishly thought they were playing a subtle game of psychological control over an exhausted mother. Instead, they had laid out a premeditated roadmap of felony domestic abuse.

Faced with a mountain of digital evidence, my visible physical injuries documented at the local hospital, and the clear emergency dispatch audio, the district attorney offered no favorable plea bargains. Brandon, completely unable to smooth-talk his way out of serious felony charges, pled guilty to domestic battery, false imprisonment, and criminal conspiracy.

He was sentenced to four years in a state penitentiary. His mother, despite her frantic attempts to use her advanced age and fake concern for her grandchild as an excuse, received a two-year sentence as an active accessory and co-conspirator.

During the subsequent divorce and child custody proceedings, the family court judge viewed the baby monitor evidence with visible disgust. An emergency permanent protective order was granted immediately. I was awarded full legal and physical custody of my son, with zero visitation rights granted to my ex-husband or his family.

The house, the very building where they thought they could trap and control me, was ordered to be sold by the court, with all net proceeds awarded directly to me as financial compensation and ongoing support for my child’s future.

Six months later.

I sat on the sunny wooden deck of a small, bright apartment overlooking a green community park. The afternoon air was crisp and smelled faintly of fresh rain. In my arms, my son, who was now six months old, healthy, chubby-cheeked, and bright-eyed, giggled happily as he reached for a colorful hanging toy.

My swollen cheek had healed completely long ago. The dark purple bruises on my shoulder and thigh had faded away into distant memories. The burning pain in my scalp was completely gone.

Sometimes, in the quiet dark of the night, the ghost of those three soft knocks on a locked wooden door would echo briefly in my mind. However, it no longer brought a freeze of pure terror to my body. It brought a quiet, fierce reminder of the exact moment I chose never to surrender to abusers.

They had thought my physical exhaustion was a weakness they could easily exploit. They had thought my deep love for my newborn son was a leverage point they could use to break my spirit. They had thought that by simply lowering their voices and acting calm, they could rewrite reality to suit their needs.

They had fully expected a helpless victim who would apologize for being hurt.

They got a mother who protected her child at all costs.

I gently kissed the smooth top of my son’s head, breathing in his sweet baby scent, and watched the bright afternoon sun break through the white clouds. The balcony door behind us was completely unlocked, the windows were open wide, and for the very first time in my life, I was entirely, beautifully free.

THE END.

text:
Suor Maria Celeste (Virginia Galilei) was the eldest daughter of the renowned Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei. Her story is one of profound intellectual brilliance, deep religious faith, and unwavering devotion to her father during his most turbulent years. Though cloistered behind convent walls, she served as Galileo’s confidante, domestic manager, and emotional anchor... 

Born Virginia Galilei in 1600, she was Galileo’s daughter with Marina Gamba. Because Virginia and her sister Livia were born outside marriage, Galileo believed marriage prospects would be difficult and arranged for both girls to enter the convent of San Matteo in Arcetri.

Virginia was only 13 when she arrived.

The convent was poor. Food was scarce, conditions were difficult, and once she took her vows, Maria Celeste would spend the rest of her life behind its walls.

Yet from inside that enclosure, she became one of Galileo’s closest companions.

More than 120 of her letters to him survive.

They reveal a woman who was affectionate, intelligent, practical and deeply involved in her father’s everyday life. Maria Celeste repaired his clothes, managed requests, worried about his health and prepared remedies using the convent’s apothecary knowledge. She sent him pills, tonics and candied fruits, while asking him for supplies the impoverished sisters desperately needed.

Then, in 1633, Galileo was tried by the Roman Inquisition for defending the motion of the Earth.

Maria Celeste could not leave the convent to help him.

So she wrote.

Her letters offered encouragement as her aging father faced interrogation, condemnation and house arrest. After Galileo was ordered to recite penitential psalms, Maria Celeste even obtained permission to perform the spiritual obligation on his behalf.

Galileo returned to Arcetri, living close enough to the convent that father and daughter could finally be near one another.

It did not last.

In April 1634, Maria Celeste died after a sudden illness. She was 33.

Galileo was devastated.

History remembers the man who looked toward the heavens and changed humanity’s understanding of them.

But behind the famous astronomer was a cloistered daughter who mixed his medicines, mended his clothes, prayed for him through his darkest crisis and chose a name that joined her devotion to the Virgin Mary with the celestial world her father loved.

In this episode of Going Big!, host Kevin Gentry sits down with Josh Grainer, inaugural winemaker at Lost Mountain Vineyards in Delaplane, Virginia, to explore the unlikely journey that led him into winemaking and the vision behind one of Virginia’s most serious wine projects.

Josh traces his path from growing up around agriculture and studying ecology to a transformative spring break trip to Tuscany, working in restaurant kitchens, and eventually apprenticing under legendary Virginia winemaker Jim Law. He shares how persistence opened a door that initially seemed closed, and how an unexpected opportunity at a young age led him to Lost Mountain.

The conversation goes deeper into the philosophy of craftsmanship, mentorship, risk-taking, and building something exceptional in an unlikely place. At Lost Mountain, a hillside once considered unsuitable for agriculture because of its rocky soil became the foundation for a distinctive approach to Virginia wine. Josh’s story offers lessons for anyone trying to discover their contribution, take a meaningful risk, and spend a lifetime getting better at their craft.

Returning to Bucharest in September 1944 alongside the advancing Red Army, Pauker emerged as the undisputed ruler of postwar Romania. Dominating the ruling Politburo, she drove the forced abdication of King Michael, orchestrated the collectivization of agriculture, and crushed the democratic opposition. Appointed Foreign Minister in November 1947, she commanded international stature and domestic terror. Yet despite her hardline image, archival records reveal striking nuances: she opposed rapid, violent farm collectivization and quietly facilitated the emigration of tens of thousands of Romanian Jews to Israel. These policies, combined with her Jewish heritage and independent prestige, ultimately marked her as a target.

Total submission to Moscow offered no protection when the dictator turned on his loyalists. In the early 1950s, as Stalin unleashed an antisemitic purge targeting Jewish party leaders, Romanian rival Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej moved to destroy her. Accused of cosmopolitanism and Zionism, Pauker was stripped of her ministerial posts in 1952 and expelled from the party. In February 1953, the secret police dragged her to Malmaison prison, preparing a show trial that would end before a firing squad. She was saved only by biological chance: on March 5, 1953, Joseph Stalin suffered a fatal stroke, halting the trial and sparing her life.

Released into strict house arrest, Pauker lived out her final years in a modest Bucharest apartment, working in obscurity as a translator. When news of Stalin’s death had reached her cell, she had wept, still revering the man who had executed her husband and imprisoned her. She died of breast cancer in June 1960 at sixty-six, largely erased from official state memory. Ana Pauker had surrendered her marriage, her morality, and her conscience to an ideological machine, only to prove that totalitarianism demands the complete sacrifice of its most faithful disciples before casting them aside.

text:
Her father ran an illegal street lottery because nobody would hire a Black bricklayer, and Louise Meriwether wrote the book of her life and put him right in the title. Not a hustler, not a criminal. She called him Daddy, the softest word she had, and hundreds of thousands of people bought it. She printed hers on the cover.

His hands were made for brick.

Marion Lloyd Jenkins had laid it down in South Carolina, straight and level, the work of a man who took pride in a wall that would still be standing after he was gone.

In Harlem those same hands took nickels and dimes off strangers on a corner, wrote a number on a slip, and carried it to the man who held the bets.

There was no steady work for a Black bricklayer in the Depression. So he ran numbers, the poor man's stock market, an illegal street lottery that half of Harlem played on a penny and a dream.

People picked their three digits out of dream books, turning a nightmare or a stranger's face into a bet, and men like her father collected the slips before the winning number came out at night.

His daughter watched him do it.

And decades later, when she wrote the book that made her name, she refused to hide him. She put him in the title, and she called him Daddy.

Her name was Louise. Born in Haverstraw in 1923, the third of five children and the only girl.

After the crash of 1929 the family joined the Great Migration north, chasing work that kept sliding out from under them. Philadelphia, back to Haverstraw, then Brooklyn, and finally a room in Harlem on Fifth Avenue between 116th and 117th.

Somewhere in there came a Brooklyn schoolroom where she was the only Black child in the class.

She walked out of that school carrying what she later called a deep feeling of shame, and she did not set it down for a long time.

So she decided to read past it. Then she decided to write her way, in her own words, out of the wilderness.

There was a library on 124th Street with a colored section, and that is where a girl of ten or eleven spent her afternoons in 1934, working through whatever they would let her have.

Huckleberry Finn first. Then Claude McKay and Jessie Redmon Fauset, the Black writers a Harlem branch stocked only a few of. She read them down to the spine.

She finished Central Commercial High School downtown, took a job as a secretary, and went to New York University at night for a degree in English.

That was how a girl like her got one. In the dark, after work, tired.

She married a Los Angeles teacher named Angelo Meriwether and moved west. That marriage ended, and a later one to Earle Howe ended too, and she carried the Meriwether name through both.

In her forties she went back and earned a master's in journalism from UCLA.

She was already writing about her own people by then, filing pieces for the Los Angeles Sentinel on an opera singer named Grace Bumbry, on a lawyer named Audrey Boswell, on Vaino Spencer, the first Black woman to win a judgeship in California.

One of the writers she interviewed as a young reporter was James Baldwin. They became friends, two Harlem children who had found a way out.

By the time she finished the master's she was overqualified for everything but a newsroom or a classroom, a Black woman with two degrees and almost no doors that opened.

Then Universal Studios called.

The year was 1965. Watts had just burned for six days, more than thirty people dead, and a nervous Hollywood was suddenly interested in a Black woman with a good eye.

They hired her as a story analyst. She sat in the story department and read the scripts as they came in, and she decided which ones held a story worth telling and which ones did not.

No Black woman had ever held that chair. She was the first, weighing the whole industry's ideas about who mattered, inside a business that had spent forty years telling stories with almost no room in them for anyone like her.

She read other people's stories for a living. Her own was still sitting inside her, unwritten.

Around then a new magazine for Black women was starting up, called Essence, and they offered her the top job. Editor in chief.

She turned it down. She would rather write for them than run them, she said, and she wrote the cover story for the very first issue instead.

The thing that finally pulled her own story out of her was a room in Watts.

After the riots, the screenwriter Budd Schulberg opened a workshop there for Black writers, and Meriwether went. She began setting her Harlem childhood on the page, a twelve-year-old girl named Francie in a family holding on by its fingernails.

Then she made a choice about the title that most people in her position would not have made.

She could have named the book for Francie, or for Harlem, or for the Depression, for anything respectable. The man at the center of it ran numbers, and a numbers runner was exactly the kind of relative a family climbing toward respectable was supposed to keep quiet about.

She named the book Daddy Was a Number Runner.

Not a hustler. Not a criminal. Daddy, the tenderest word in the language for the man the country had reduced to taking bets on a corner.

The girl in it, Francie, speaks the saddest true line in the whole book. That they were all poor and Black and apt to stay that way, and that was that.

Baldwin was not a stranger doing her a favor when the manuscript reached him. He read the book his old friend had written, and he wrote the foreword himself.

He said the book told everyone who could read or feel what it meant to be a Black man or woman in this country.

Paule Marshall reviewed it in the New York Times and called it a most important novel. It sold hundreds of thousands of copies.

It arrived alongside Toni Morrison's first novel and Maya Angelou's first memoir, and together the three of them cracked something open. A generation of Black women who had been told their lives were not literature.

Writing was never the whole of her.

She called herself a peacenik and meant it for eighty years. In her twenties she chaired her union and marched in the May Day parades, and she remembered plainly having rotten eggs thrown at her head for it.

She helped start a group with the historian John Henrik Clarke to fight South African apartheid from a base in Harlem.

And when a studio moved to film William Styron's novel about Nat Turner, a book that twisted the rebel into someone he never was, she helped organize the writers who killed the project. They bought a back page in the Hollywood Reporter and warned every Black actor away from it.

After the novel she turned to writing history for children, small biographies of Robert Smalls, of Rosa Parks, of the surgeon Daniel Hale Williams.

She said why in a line worth keeping. Leaving Black people out of American history, she explained, damaged the children of both races, building "a feeling of inferiority" in one and "a myth of superiority" in the other.

She lived to be a hundred years old.

She died in a Manhattan nursing home in October of 2023, of nothing more dramatic than age, having outlasted nearly everyone who ever doubted her.

Go back to that Brooklyn schoolroom, and the poor girl who swore she would write her way out of the wilderness.

She did it. And the door she walked through was a book with her father on the cover, the bricklayer who took bets on a corner because his country would not let him lay brick.

She had every reason to be ashamed of him. She looked at the man the Depression had reduced, and she reached for the softest word she owned, and she set it first.

Daddy.

text:
Diverse autism genes converge to disrupt shared biological pathways, study finds | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A new mapping of how proteins interact in the brain suggests that many different genetic mutations linked to autism spectrum disorder end up altering the same underlying biological networks. By determining how specific mutations rewire these protein connections, the research offers a potential roadmap for finding targeted treatments for neurodevelopmental conditions. The findings were published in Science.

Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by varying challenges with social communication and repetitive behaviors. The genetics underlying the condition are highly complex, with hundreds of different genes implicated. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 found that thousands of genes might contribute to the condition in different ways. Despite identifying so many risk factors, scientists have struggled to understand how such a wide variety of genetic changes leads to similar developmental outcomes.

“Over the past 15 years, large-scale sequencing studies have identified hundreds of genes associated with autism,” study co-author Nevan J. Krogan, a researcher at the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at the University of California, San Francisco, told PsyPost. “That progress was initially very exciting; in 2012, only a few genes had been clearly implicated, whereas today the list includes several hundred.”

“However, identifying genes and mutations has not, by itself, produced a sufficiently detailed understanding of autism biology or led to many new therapeutic strategies,” Krogan continued. “A list of genes is somewhat like a parts list for a machine. To understand how the machine works, and what happens when one part is altered, you also need to understand the proteins those genes produce and how those proteins interact inside cells. That was the gap we wanted to address.”

To bridge this gap, scientists look to proteins, which are the microscopic machines that carry out most of a cell’s functions. Proteins rarely act alone. Instead, they bind to one another to form larger complexes, much like interlocking puzzle pieces. A 2026 study showed how a single autism-linked mutation can physically disrupt the binding between two partner proteins, impairing how brain cells communicate. Similarly, a 2026 preprint study that has not been peer-reviewed indicated that turning off different autism-associated genes in human brain cells disrupts shared biological pathways.

Mapping these physical connections can be highly useful for medical research. In fact, research covered by PsyPost in 2022 used protein interaction networks to identify existing medications that might counteract the biological processes underlying autism.

Building on this concept, a research team that included Krogan and lead author Belinda Wang sought to map the physical interactions of proteins associated with autism risk genes at a massive scale. They wanted to see if different mutations might converge on the same biological complexes, selectively rewiring how these proteins connect rather than simply destroying their function altogether.

“Through this work, we generated what we believe is the largest protein-protein interaction map assembled for a neuropsychiatric disorder,” Krogan said. “The map provides a molecular framework for understanding how autism-associated mutations may disrupt cellular systems. Importantly, it has also revealed potential therapeutic directions that would not have been visible from genetic information alone.”

“We are now following up on several of those opportunities through drug-development programs,” he noted. “The broader goal is to move beyond cataloging autism-associated genes and toward understanding the underlying biology well enough to identify new strategies for treatment.”

The team focused on 100 genes identified as high-confidence risk factors for autism. They introduced the protein versions of these genes into human embryonic kidney cells. This cell type is widely used in laboratories because it is easy to grow and allows for large-scale analysis of protein interactions. Using a technique called affinity purification and mass spectrometry, which acts like a microscopic fishing hook to pull out a target protein along with everything attached to it, they identified which other proteins bound to their targets.

The resulting map uncovered 1,881 total interactions, 87 percent of which had never been reported before. On average, each autism risk protein interacted with 11 other proteins. The researchers observed a highly interconnected network, meaning that the different autism risk proteins tended to bind to the same central hubs.

To determine which proteins touched directly rather than indirectly, the team used AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence system that predicts the three-dimensional shapes of proteins. They then tested one of the central hubs, a protein complex involving the molecules DCAF7 and DYRK1A, in living systems. They edited the genes of Xenopus, a type of frog often used to study early development, as well as human neural progenitor cells, which are stem cells that develop into brain cells.

Disrupting this shared protein complex impaired the multiplication of the progenitor cells and resulted in a smaller forebrain size in the frog models. This provides evidence that different autism risk proteins work together in the same physical machinery to regulate early brain growth.

The researchers then looked at the impact of the disease-linked mutations themselves. They introduced 54 specific genetic mutations derived from autistic patients into 30 of the risk proteins. They repeated their protein-fishing experiment to see how these mutations changed the interaction network compared to the typical, unmutated proteins.

The mutations caused 253 interactions to be altered, with some connections strengthening and others weakening. The researchers found that completely different mutations often caused the exact same changes in the protein network. For example, three different mutations in a gene called FOXP1 all caused its resulting protein to lose its connection to a partner protein called FOXP4.

To see how this specific severed connection affects brain development, the team grew human forebrain organoids. These are miniature, three-dimensional bundles of brain tissue grown in a dish from stem cells, which mimic the early stages of human brain development.

In organoids carrying the FOXP1 mutations, the loss of the FOXP1 and FOXP4 connection led to the partner protein attaching to the wrong sections of DNA. This biological misstep caused the brain cells to mature too early. The premature maturation altered the proportion of specific types of neurons in the organoids and increased their overall electrical activity.

This overlap in downstream effects was exactly what the researchers were looking for. “The most surprising finding was the degree of biological convergence,” Krogan noted. “We began with roughly 100 genes associated with autism, but the corresponding proteins were not acting independently. Many were connected within a smaller number of shared biological networks.”

“That suggests we may not need a separate treatment for every individual genetic mutation,” he added. “A smaller number of therapies targeting common pathways could potentially benefit multiple groups of patients. That possibility has significant implications for future drug development.”

The findings provide independent researchers a new lens to interpret the thousands of rare mutations identified in recent years.

Lisa Bradley, a senior research associate at The Centre for Applied Genomics at The Hospital for Sick Children Research Institute who was not involved in the study, noted that the research complements existing genomic efforts. “This large-scale study of bona fide high-risk genes specifically looks at the very real possibility that ASD-associated mutations rewire specific protein-protein interactions,” she told PsyPost. “For me, the key takeaway is that this strategy provides a way to move from many different ASD-associated genes toward a smaller number of convergent molecular mechanisms, which otherwise could have remained hidden.”

Bradley found the study’s experimental validation using human forebrain organoids particularly persuasive. “For me, the FOXP1 story was the most convincing because they took an ASD-associated mutation from disruption of a specific protein interaction with FOXP4 through to downstream effects on gene expression and neuronal development in brain organoids,” she said. “Other ASD studies have implicated altered cortical layer development, so this provided an important proof of principle that altered protein interactions can translate into meaningful cellular neurodevelopmental consequences.”

As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The initial protein mapping was conducted in kidney cells rather than brain cells. While the researchers validated key interactions in brain-specific models later, the initial environment might lack some specialized proteins found only in developing neurons.

Bradley cautioned that the findings offer early-stage evidence for molecular mechanisms, “rather than demonstrating that they are causal mechanisms.” She added, “Some of these genes and mutations could also be associated with complex ASD, including co-occurring intellectual disability, so the molecular changes identified may include broader NDD [neurodevelopmental disorder] biology rather than mechanisms unique to autism etiology.”

The study focused on 100 high-confidence autism risk genes, but hundreds more have been linked to the condition, meaning the current map represents only a fraction of the total biological picture. “In this study, we examined a small number of genes and mutations in depth using stem cells, neurons and brain organoids,” Krogan said. “We have now built a pipeline that allows us to apply the same approach more systematically and at a larger scale. Our next goal is to identify which autism-associated mutations and biological pathways are most suitable for therapeutic development.”

Before new therapies can be developed, these molecular interactions must be observed in broader behavioral contexts. “While the molecular and mechanistic evidence is very compelling and is likely to be highly relevant to complex ASD etiology, I would like to see this tested in a mammalian developmental model where social and ASD-relevant behaviors can be examined alongside learning and cognitive impairments,” Bradley said. “This would allow more direct tests of causality for the FOXP1-FOXP4 interaction and how these molecular changes ultimately translate into social behavior.”

Additionally, artificial intelligence predictions of protein structures are estimates and sometimes miss the nuance of how proteins bend and fold in a living organism. Beyond refining these models, future research could expand this network and test additional drug candidates that might stabilize these weakened protein connections. The researchers believe the principles established in this study could eventually stretch to entirely different fields of medicine.

“The concept of biological convergence may extend beyond autism,” Krogan pointed out. “We are applying these tools to other neuropsychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder, to look for shared pathways. We are also seeing overlap between some genes and proteins implicated in autism and those studied in cancer.”

“Because drugs already exist for certain cancer-related targets, there may be opportunities to investigate whether some of those compounds could be repurposed for neurological or psychiatric conditions,” he continued. “That possibility is still at an early stage, but it opens an unexpected avenue for collaboration and therapeutic research.”

Ultimately, the research team views this extensive protein map as a foundational resource for the scientific community, moving the field past simple catalogs of genetic risks.

“This is an important step between identifying a genetic change and developing a potential treatment,” Krogan concluded. “It is not the final step, and new therapies will still require years of research and testing. That said, our study provides a clearer biological framework for identifying therapeutic opportunities that were not apparent before.”

Nebius is building the first neoscaler. (AI native hyperscaler)

The neocloud bucket is a very lazy classification mixing completely different business models. 

- You have bare metal hardware players like CoreWeave and IREN. 
- You have software layers like Fireworks. 
- And you have vertically integrated platforms combining hardware, software, and services.

Nebius is the third. Comparing it to the other two categories misses the point of the company entirely.

Serving this broad horizontal market as ONE PLATFORM means solving consulting, hardware and software integration on an full stack ecosystem basis. 

As seen at Inflection 2026, close partnerships on every level, early installs of the newest hardware, and deep co engineering are standard practice.

That depth explains why Nebius regularly wins business against legacy hyperscalers (which face an innovator’s dilemma in allocating resources and capital expenditure) and ordinary neoclouds, and why it holds a direct development and research partnership with $NVDA at the same time. 

They meet builders with a native machine learning experience and a single platform running training, post training, and inference together.

And that unified stack is a growing moat.

Teams take (open) models (via token factory) into production (inference) and then come back to post train them on proprietary data. Because Nebius unifies training, inference and agentic loads on the same platform it owns the loop.

They are not simply selling isolated compute or services. (which they still can and do) They are selling a one stop intelligence platform.

The Tavily acquisition is a clear proof of that stack logic. Marc has been blunt about why it was brought in. Agentic search is a cornerstone capability for AI builders and Tavily adds another layer so developers do not have to stitch vendors together. 

Token Factory handles reasoning. Tavily grounds agents in live information. Together they turn infrastructure into a production system rather than a pile of GPUs.

The Palantir partnership fits the exact same map as well. It is a direct route into enterprises needing more than raw capacity. Digital natives are a rapidly growing customer layer which perfectly fits $NBIS one stop / higher margin offerings.

That means $NBIS serves two extremes at once. 

1) Deep frontier software and hardware expertise for AI natives. -> Usage based

2) Intensive guidance for enterprises / digital natives just discovering AI helping them turn ideas into working business models. -> Outcome based

Beyond that infrastructure Nebius is also building a community for frontier research and production builders. The calendar is not decoration. It is the distribution engine. 

Events and initiatives like Inflection, Nebius Science, the Inference Frontier Program, the Serverless AI Builders Challenge, the Nebius and NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon, Robotics and Physical AI Awards etc. pull ambitious researchers, founders, and operators into the exact same orbit.

Management anticipates a builder community of more than one million in the forseeable future. 

That community is a go to market weapon. Marc has seen this mechanism before at Twilio and Cloudflare. 

Developers adopt first. They integrate. They become the internal champions who later decide which vendor the company standardizes on. 

Once a builder is in the stack switching costs explode. The people writing the agents, the evals, and the production pipelines are the very people who later influence procurement.

If Nebius owns that density it does not just win the cluster deal today. It shapes the vendor shortlist of tomorrow.

Calling it a Silicon Valley for AI sounds ambitious. The mechanism however is highly familiar. Exceptional people cluster around the best infrastructure and partners who turn ideas into running systems.

If Nebius becomes the trusted place for that intersection the moat runs on steroids. 

$NBIS offers exposure to a future AI infrastructure cycle that is only just beginning to take shape.

text:
The Democrat in me is thrilled about the Supreme Court’s decision in the Missouri election case. But I’m still amazed that the Court keeps reaping what it sowed — and then complains about the harvest.

As wrong as the Eighth Circuit may have been on procedure and merits, I sympathize. The Supreme Court’s emergency‑docket rulings rarely explain themselves, leaving lower courts guessing.

It’s hard to fault the Eighth Circuit for not divining that the justices were done entertaining stays. When the Court offers no rationale, how can anyone infer what “no” means? Maybe they were saying “thread the needle differently.”

Liberals aren’t exasperated with the Shadow Docket just because of outcomes like Texas HB‑8. Even conservative commentators admit it creates confusion and more work for everyone — especially lower courts.Kavanaugh and Gorsuch once scolded a Massachusetts judge for defying an unsigned order that simply said the government was “likely to succeed.” In Missouri, the Court didn’t even give that much.

Someone needs to give the justices the classic spouse speech: “Honey, I can’t read your mind.”

I’m grateful for the Missouri outcome. But if the Court wants less chaos, it should stop complaining about the messes it made and start explaining itself to those still willing to listen.

text:
Catholic Church’s Saint of the Day commemoration for September 28:
Saint Wenceslaus (c. 907–935)
Title: Duke of Bohemia and Martyr
Liturgical Rank: Optional Memorial (General Roman Calendar)
Feast Day: September 28
Patronages: The Czech Republic, Bohemia, Prague, brewers, and peacemakers

Biography & Spiritual Significance
 
A Royal & Saintly Heritage: Born near Prague around 907 A.D., Wenceslaus was the son of Duke Vratislaus I of Bohemia. His early Christian education was entrusted to his holy grandmother, Saint Ludmilla, who formed him in scripture, Latin, and deep personal piety. Following his father’s death, an anti-Christian pagan faction led by his mother, Drahomíra, seized power and murdered Ludmilla.

 A Christian Sovereign: Around 924, Christian nobles placed Wenceslaus on the ducal throne. His reign was distinguished by a radical commitment to gospel justice, charity, and the protection of the vulnerable:
 
He personally tended vineyards and harvested wheat with his own hands to produce communion wine and hosts for the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass.

 He walked through the snow at night in disguise to distribute firewood, food, and warm clothing to orphans, widows, and impoverished prisoners. (These acts of winter mercy later inspired the famous 19th-century Christmas carol, "Good King Wenceslas").

He promoted reconciliation within Bohemia, supported Christian missionary priests, built the original basilica of Saint Vitus at Prague Castle, and negotiated peaceful diplomacy with neighboring Germanic territories to protect his people from war.

Fratricide & Martyrdom: Wenceslaus’s policies of peace, Christian morality, and Roman Catholic alignment angered pagan nobles, who conspired with his ambitious younger brother, Boleslaus ("the Cruel"). In September 935, Boleslaus invited Wenceslaus to Stará Boleslav (Alt-Bunzlau) under the guise of celebrating the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. On the morning of September 28, as Wenceslaus walked to church for morning prayers, Boleslaus and his henchmen ambushed and mortally wounded him on the church threshold. As he fell, Wenceslaus forgave his assassins, praying: "May God forgive you, brother. Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit."

Patron of the Nation: Wenceslaus was immediately acclaimed a martyr. His relics were translated to Saint Vitus Cathedral in Prague, where the "Crown of Saint Wenceslaus" became the sacred symbol of Bohemian sovereignty and national identity.

Also Commemorated Today: Saint Lawrence Ruiz and Companions, Martyrs
Sharing the liturgical date of September 28 on the General Roman Calendar is the Optional Memorial of Saint Lawrence Ruiz and companions, martyrs |

•••The Protomartyr of the Philippines: A Filipino husband, father, and parish calligrapher from Binondo, Manila, who sailed to Japan in 1636 alongside Dominican missionaries
•••The Witness at Nagasaki: Arrested during the Tokugawa shogunate's persecutions, he endured the brutal torture of the pit (ana-tsurushi) on Nishizaka Hill, professing:
“I am a Catholic and whole-heartedly do accept death for God; had I a thousand lives, all these to Him shall I offer."
•••Canonized in 1987 by Pope Saint John Paul II as the first canonized Filipino saint, alongside fifteen Dominican priests, brothers, and consecrated laywomen.

You Cannot Build Freedom on Submission

Submission to a faith and to God is living in control. Surrender to a faith and to God is living in trust.

The words sound alike. The reality behind them does not.

Submission means bowing to something that stands above you and watches you. The rules become the goal in themselves. How you pray, what you eat, how you dress, who you may marry, what you may say out loud. Everything is decided in advance. 

That offers a kind of security, because you never have to carry the responsibility yourself. But it is a security built on fear. You obey to avoid punishment. And when fear is the foundation, control becomes necessary. Over yourself and over everyone around you.

Surrender is something else entirely. You give yourself over because you trust the one you give yourself to. You keep your conscience and your free will. You are allowed to doubt. You are allowed to wrestle with God. 

That is exactly what the name Israel means... the one who wrestles with God. Abraham bargained with God over Sodom. Job cried his pain up toward heaven. Jesus prayed in Gethsemane to be spared the cup and surrendered anyway. That is not a subject obeying. That is a human being in relationship.

That relationship is what the West was built on. The idea that every person has a conscience no state and no priest can own. That freedom is a gift from God, not a rebellion against him. That the law exists to serve man.

Islam means submission. That is not my interpretation, it is the meaning of the word. And the system follows the name. Sharia is faith, law and social order in one package, with no separation between what you believe and what you must do.

And we don't have to guess what happens when Islam gains power. History has told that story for 1,400 years. Islam was invented around 610 AD, roughly six hundred years after Christianity. Wherever it has taken power since, the pattern repeats. Those who will not submit end up as second-class citizens in their own land.

Judaism and Christianity also have commandments and discipline. But at the bottom lies a covenant between God and man. In Islam lies a master and a subject.

That is why the two cannot coexist as the foundation of the same society. You cannot build freedom on submission. It has never worked, and it never will.

It should be simple enough for a teenager to understand. Yet we have governments across the West deliberately submitting to the very faith that will eventually rip the Western foundation out by its roots.

The worst part? Naive, uninformed people keep voting for them.

Have you lost your minds? You are complicit with your suicidal empathy. Wake up. Or do you or your children have to submit on your knees to Allah before you see it?

Let me enlighten you. By then it will be TOO LATE!

text:
I’d make the people **clearly illustrative rather than implying real people achieved invented financial results**. Here’s a more engaging version with names, emojis, stronger storytelling, and natural requests for comments and shares:

### 🚨 YOU DON’T NEED 100,000 FOLLOWERS TO BUILD A REAL ONLINE BUSINESS.

Imagine three people.

👩 **Sarah** has 75,000 followers.

👨 **David** has 12,000.

👩 **Aisha** has just 4,500.

Who has the strongest business?

You can't tell from the follower count.

Sarah might generate thousands of likes but very few customers.

David might have a smaller audience but a clear service people actually need.

Aisha might have only 4,500 followers—but an engaged community that trusts her recommendations.

📌 **Follower count is visible. Business fundamentals aren't.**

That’s where many entrepreneurs get distracted.

They chase:

❌ Followers 
❌ Likes 
❌ Views 
❌ Viral posts 
❌ The newest AI tool 
❌ The latest “business opportunity”

Instead of building something much more important:

🔥 **A SYSTEM.**

AI and automation can help small businesses operate more efficiently—but they don't guarantee customers, revenue or profit.

Here’s a more practical way to think about building online 👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 🎯 1. SARAH STOPS TRYING TO SELL TO EVERYONE

Imagine Sarah wants to start an online business.

Her first idea is:

> “I'll create something everybody can use.”

Sounds good.

But there's a problem.

If everybody is your customer, your message can become so broad that nobody feels like you're speaking directly to them.

So Sarah changes her approach.

Instead of asking:

❌ “What can I sell online?”

She asks:

🔎 Who specifically am I helping? 
🔎 What are they struggling with? 
🔎 What have they already tried? 
🔎 What costs them time or money? 
🔎 What would make their lives easier? 
🔎 What are they already willing to pay for?

Now she has somewhere to start.

**PERSON → PROBLEM → SOLUTION → OFFER**

Simple.

But powerful.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 💡 2. DAVID DOESN’T START WITH A PRODUCT

David wants to make money online.

He could immediately create:

📘 An eBook 
🎓 A course 
🛒 An e-commerce store 
💻 Software 
📱 A membership 
🤝 A consulting service

But David does something different.

He doesn't start by asking:

**“What product can I create?”**

He asks:

**“What useful problem can I solve?”**

🔥 That changes everything.

Because customers generally don't care whether your solution is 37 pages, 137 pages or 300 pages.

They care about whether it helps them accomplish something meaningful.

**Don't fall in love with the format.**

❤️ Fall in love with solving the problem.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 🤖 3. AISHA USES AI—BUT DOESN’T EXPECT AI TO BUILD THE BUSINESS FOR HER

Aisha discovers AI.

Suddenly she can accelerate:

🔎 Research 
✍️ Writing 
💡 Brainstorming 
📧 Email drafts 
🎬 Video scripts 
📊 Data analysis 
📱 Social content 
⚙️ Workflow organization 
🛍️ Product descriptions 
💬 Customer-support drafts

That's powerful.

But she quickly learns an important lesson:

⚠️ **AI IS NOT THE BUSINESS.**

AI can give Aisha 100 product ideas.

She still has to decide which are worth testing.

AI can draft an advertisement.

She still needs something people actually want.

AI can create content.

She still needs something useful to say.

AI can increase speed.

🧠 **Human judgment still determines direction.**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 📱 4. THEN THEY NEED ATTENTION

Imagine David creates an excellent service.

Nobody knows it exists.

His first month's sales?

**$0.**

Not necessarily because the service is terrible.

Nobody discovered it.

That's why distribution matters.

David could build his audience through:

𝕏 X 
🎬 YouTube 
📱 TikTok 
📸 Instagram 
💼 LinkedIn 
🔎 Google 
📧 Email

But here's where another mistake happens.

People think they need to dominate ALL of them.

They don't.

🎯 **Master one before trying to manage seven.**

Create content that:

📚 Educates 
🎯 Solves problems 
🎬 Entertains 
💡 Demonstrates ideas 
🤝 Builds trust 
💬 Starts conversations

Eventually, the right person should discover your content and think:

**“This person understands my problem.”**

That's when attention becomes useful.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 📊 5. NOW IMAGINE AISHA GETS 42,000 VIEWS

Sounds impressive.

But let's look deeper.

This is a **hypothetical example**, not an income claim:

👀 42,000 content views

↓

🌐 1,600 website/profile visits

↓

📧 310 leads

↓

🛒 28 customers

↓

💵 Average purchase: $145

That would equal:

**$4,060 in revenue.**

Now imagine Aisha spent approximately $1,750 on advertising, software, contractors, payment processing and other operating costs.

That leaves approximately:

**$2,310 before taxes and any additional expenses.**

⚠️ These numbers are only an example.

Actual businesses can perform much better, much worse, or lose money.

But here's the lesson:

🔥 **42,000 views weren't the business.**

The business happened here:

**ATTENTION → INTEREST → LEAD → OFFER → CUSTOMER**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### ⚙️ 6. DAVID BUILDS A CUSTOMER JOURNEY

Instead of randomly posting every morning and hoping somebody buys something, David creates a process:

📱 CONTENT

↓

👀 ATTENTION

↓

🌐 WEBSITE

↓

📧 LEAD

↓

🤝 FOLLOW-UP

↓

🎯 OFFER

↓

💳 CUSTOMER

↓

⭐ GOOD EXPERIENCE

↓

🔄 REPEAT BUSINESS

↓

🗣️ REFERRALS

Now David isn't simply:

**“Posting on social media.”**

He's developing a customer-acquisition system.

Big difference.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 📧 7. SARAH REALIZES FOLLOWERS AREN’T ENOUGH

Sarah builds 30,000 followers.

Great.

But those followers are on somebody else's platform.

Algorithms change.

📉 Reach changes.

⚠️ Policies change.

Platforms change.

Accounts can sometimes be restricted.

So Sarah starts developing assets beyond social media:

📧 Email subscribers 
🌐 Website traffic 
👥 Customer relationships 
📊 CRM contacts 
🤝 Communities 
🛍️ Existing customers

Think about it this way:

📱 **SOCIAL MEDIA MAKES THE INTRODUCTION.**

🤝 **YOUR BUSINESS BUILDS THE RELATIONSHIP.**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### ⚙️ 8. THEN AUTOMATION BECOMES USEFUL

Here's another misunderstanding:

Automation doesn't mean:

❌ Press one button 
❌ Go to sleep 
❌ Wake up rich

That's marketing fantasy.

Useful automation is much more boring—and much more practical.

It can help Sarah, David and Aisha with repetitive processes such as:

📧 Welcome emails 
📅 Appointment reminders 
🛍️ Order confirmations 
📊 Reporting 
📱 Content scheduling 
👋 Customer onboarding 
🔔 Internal notifications 
📝 Lead capture 
💬 Basic FAQ routing

That frees time for things machines aren't necessarily good at:

🧠 Strategy

❤️ Relationships

🎨 Creativity

🤝 Customers

📈 Decision-making

🔥 Growth

**Automate repetition—not trust.**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 📊 9. THE NUMBERS BECOME THE SCOREBOARD

Imagine David's monthly funnel looks like this:

👀 **50,000 impressions**

↓

🌐 **2,500 website visitors**

↓

📧 **400 leads**

↓

🛒 **35 customers**

↓

💰 **$5,250 revenue**

↓

💸 **$2,200 operating and marketing costs**

↓

📈 **$3,050 before taxes and additional expenses**

Again:

⚠️ **This is a hypothetical example—not a promise, forecast or typical result.**

The interesting part isn't the $3,050.

It's what David can learn.

What if 50,000 people see his content but only 300 visit the website?

🔎 Investigate the message.

What if 5,000 people visit but almost nobody buys?

🔎 Investigate the audience, offer, pricing, positioning and trust.

What if sales increase but costs increase even faster?

🔎 Investigate the economics.

🔥 **DATA TELLS YOU WHERE TO LOOK.**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 🚀 10. NOW THEY CAN THINK ABOUT GROWTH

This is where many people make another mistake.

Something starts working...

So they immediately add:

5 new products.

4 new social platforms.

3 new employees.

7 new automations.

And 15 new problems. 😂

Instead:

🎯 If one offer works → improve it.

📱 If one platform generates customers → strengthen it.

🎬 If one video format performs → study why.

📧 If one email sequence converts → improve it.

👥 If one customer segment repeatedly buys → understand them better.

🔥 **DON'T SCALE CHAOS.**

**Scale what the evidence says is working.**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 🤖 HERE'S THE ENTIRE SYSTEM

👥 **AUDIENCE**

↓

😩 **PROBLEM**

↓

💡 **SOLUTION**

↓

🎯 **OFFER**

↓

📱 **CONTENT**

↓

👀 **ATTENTION**

↓

📧 **LEADS**

↓

🤝 **FOLLOW-UP**

↓

💳 **CUSTOMERS**

↓

⭐ **CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE**

↓

🔄 **REPEAT BUSINESS**

↓

🗣️ **REFERRALS**

↓

📈 **SUSTAINABLE GROWTH**

AI can potentially help at almost every stage.

But remember:

❌ AI + no demand = faster failure.

❌ AI + a poor offer = more efficient disappointment.

❌ AI + no strategy = automated confusion.

A stronger combination is:

🔥 **AI + HUMAN JUDGMENT + USEFUL OFFERS + SYSTEMS + CONSISTENT EXECUTION**

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

### 💭 SARAH, DAVID AND AISHA ARE FICTIONAL EXAMPLES.

But the decisions they're facing are real.

Building an online business isn't about finding a secret button that prints money.

It's about learning how to:

**BUILD → TEST → MEASURE → LEARN → IMPROVE → REPEAT**

Some ideas will work.

Some won't.

Some campaigns will make money.

Others may lose money.

Some content will perform.

Some will disappear without anyone noticing.

That's business.

💡 **The opportunity isn't “get rich with AI.”**

The opportunity is using modern technology to research faster, test faster, create more efficiently and learn from customers faster.

And that's far more sustainable than chasing the next overnight-success story.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

text:
II. The new divinities

What replaced Buddhism in India was not one creed. Durant’s four common marks: caste and Brahman leadership; reverence for the cow; karma and rebirth; new gods in place of most Vedic ones.

The working triad is Brahma (creator, little worshiped), 
Vishnu (preserver), 
Shiva (destroyer). 

Vishnu’s popular form is Krishna: prison birth, wonders, poor and sick helped, favorite disciple, disputed death stories, descent and return. 

Durant lines these up with the Gospels. The parallels mix later Puranic Krishna with Christian narrative; they are not evidence that the two figures are the same man.

Shiva is destruction and also generative force. Durant, following Marshall on Indus seals, calls Shivaism possibly the oldest living cult. Kali, Shiva’s shakti, is mother and killer: skulls, blood, sword, and blessing hands at once. Animal and even human sacrifice belonged to her cult into recent centuries.

Below the great gods Durant puts a crowd of local, animal, and planetary deities. Souls pass through beasts; therefore beasts can be divine. 

The cow is first among them: free in the streets, dung and urine used in rite, slaughter forbidden. He offers the practical guess that the taboo once saved draft animals, then froze into holiness. 

The “thirty million gods” figure is a popular flourish, not a count. He notes that polytheism and a philosophic monism lived side by side: many forms, one Brahman behind them.

text:
Osogbo Food Store Disappears After Collecting Pre-Orders From Hundreds of Customers

Panic broke out in Osogbo, Osun State, after a foodstuff store allegedly disappeared after collecting pre-order payments from hundreds of customers and traders attracted by heavily discounted food items.

The store, located around Odi Olowo, opposite the NEPA office, had reportedly been selling food items at discounts of up to 80 per cent for several months.

A 50kg bag of rice, which normally sold for about ₦60,000 to ₦70,000, was reportedly offered for as low as ₦20,000 to ₦30,000. A carton of Indomie reportedly sold for between ₦5,000 and ₦7,000, depending on the quantity ordered.

Other food items, including semovita, vegetable oil, beans and spaghetti, were also reportedly sold at discounts of at least 50 per cent.

Customers were required to place their orders in advance, with a seven-day processing period before collection. The business reportedly promoted its latest round of sales on social media, attracting hundreds of customers from different parts of Osun State.

However, when customers arrived at the store on the scheduled collection day, they reportedly found the premises empty.

Attempts to reach the business through the phone numbers provided to customers were also reportedly unsuccessful, sparking panic among those who had paid for food items in advance.

The development prompted some of the affected customers to seek police intervention, with victims calling for an investigation and the recovery of their money.

The incident has also drawn attention because it reportedly occurred in the same Odi Olowo area where the controversial Hero’s Merchant, also known as Hero’s Capital, previously operated a similar food-related scheme before collapsing.

A similar incident was also reportedly recorded in Auchi, Edo State, in July last year. In that case, a seller reportedly offered ₦60,000 bags of rice for about ₦20,000, claiming the discounted prices were linked to Federal Government subsidies and palliatives.

The Auchi seller reportedly attracted more than 1,000 customers before disappearing after collecting payments, with victims later alleging that they had collectively lost between ₦20 million and ₦30 million.
