text:
This idea that Jamaicans cannot access their beaches is retarded.

Jamaica is an island surrounded by the Caribbean Sea, with thousands of beaches, plus countless rivers, springs, waterfalls, canals and other bodies of water that locals enjoy every day.

Jamaica’s economy is heavily dependent on tourism. Tourists stay in resorts and privately owned villas, all of which have their own private or restricted access beach areas. Why would a resort want people who aren’t guests freely entering the property and using its facilities?

And Jamaicans aren’t barred from enjoying those resorts. Hotels offer heavily discounted local rates, and Jamaicans routinely book all-inclusive resorts for staycations and enjoy the same amenities and beaches as tourists.

There are also private islands all around Jamaica with beautiful beaches that we yacht to every time I visit, as well as countless local beaches that aren’t resort-owned. Nothing that locals enjoy or anyone recommends visiting in Jamaica is restricted. All the popular spots, all the fun spots are Jamaica’s. 

Go to Palm Beach, Florida and try accessing the Breakers’ beach without spending $3000 per night to stay there, and see how quickly they have you removed for trespassing.

The only reason you think it’s unusual is because you never stay anywhere nice. 

The average  Jamaican is unaware they have limited beach access because they’ve always had access to their local beaches and any out of town beach they want to visit. 

Plus, Jamaicans have an entirely different relationship with the beach. Tourists go to the beach to lay out and tan. Jamaicans go to the beach to eat fresh fish and lobster and dance. 

Using your Jamaican passport, your hotel rates are usually just around $150 while using your American passport will cost you $750 for the same room. 

Stop spreading your foolishness online about Jamaicans not having access to their beaches. Jamaicans cannot stay at 5 star all-inclusive hotels without paying so therefore they don’t have access to resort beaches unless they’re a guest.

text:
🚨🦶 TODAY IN BIGFOOT HISTORY — SEPTEMBER 28

In 1976, the FBI wrote to Bigfoot investigator Peter Byrne offering to examine alleged Sasquatch hair. Decades later, the file became public. On this same date, witnesses reported a fogbound Kentucky encounter and tracks in New York.

Here’s what happened on September 28 across the records I could date:

🦶 1976 — FBI: Assistant Director Jay Cochran wrote Byrne that the bureau had no record of an earlier hair analysis Byrne had asked about. He offered to have the FBI Laboratory examine material Byrne could provide. The hairs tested later were identified as deer.

🦶 1998 — COLORADO: A rockhound reported finding his car’s windshield wipers flipped up. He then noticed a dark figure watching from the trees. When he shut his car door, he said it stood and ran over a quartz outcrop.

🦶 1998 — NEW YORK: Near Eagle Lake, a solo camper reported finding a roughly 12-inch footprint with four visible toe impressions. From his tree stand that evening, he heard repeated blows against wood and calls from different hillsides. He did not see their source.

🦶 2004 — OREGON: At Eagle Rock Campground, two brothers reported calls across the river and movement around their campsite. One heard what he described as grunting beside his van. Neither saw an animal or found tracks.

🦶 2008 — KENTUCKY: In heavy fog near Green River Lake, a witness retrieving a trail camera reported a broad-shouldered figure about 80 feet away. He said it bellowed and approached. Frightened, he fired two shots toward the ground, then accidentally discharged another inside his vehicle as he left.

🦶 2008 — ILLINOIS: Near Taylorville, a motorist reported that a large, dark-haired figure walked across Route 48 and stepped over a guardrail. A BFRO investigator later spoke with her.

🦶 2013 — MICHIGAN: Near Cedar Springs, a hunter reported hearing howls and grunts through his closed windows at about 12:30 a.m. He said his horse grew agitated. No creature was seen.

🦶 2015 — MISSOURI: Three coworkers near Arcadia Valley reported hearing an unfamiliar howl lasting 10–15 seconds. An investigator noted that they remembered the date because it was the night after a lunar eclipse.

🦶 2017 — NATIONAL ARCHIVES: The Archives opened an exhibit of the 1959 “Yeti Memo,” a U.S. Embassy dispatch describing Nepal’s rules for expeditions seeking the Yeti. The exhibit opened September 28; the memo was written decades earlier.

Seven dated witness reports across seven states, plus two documented government-history events. Which account would you pull the original records on first?

text:
THE PRE-BELL BOUNCE HAS ONE ADDRESS, AND IT IS THE NASDAQ:

Half an hour before the 9:30am ET opening bell, U.S. stock futures still point to a lower start, but since 7am the selling has eased in only one place. Nasdaq-100 futures are at 30,728.25, -161 / -0.52% since Friday's close; at their low near 5am they were down 358 points, at 30,531. Dow futures are at 51,894.00, -269 / -0.52%, and their lowest point of the night came around 8am, at 51,829 - an hour after tech had started climbing.

The verdict for the open: the rebound runs on one company's cash and a step back in oil, not on any relief in interest rates, and the parts of the market most tied to borrowing costs have not joined it.

Futures are contracts that trade nearly around the clock and point to where the big indexes may start. The other two sit in between: S&P 500 futures at 7,776.75, -27.00 / -0.35%, and Russell 2000 futures, which track smaller U.S. companies, at 2,844.20, -15.10 / -0.53%. Each contract at 7am ET, and now:
- Nasdaq-100: 30,584.50 -> 30,728.25, +144 points / +0.47%
- S&P 500: 7,761.50 -> 7,776.75, +15 points / +0.20%
- Russell 2000: 2,840.60 -> 2,844.20, +3.60 points / +0.13%
- Dow: 51,888 -> 51,894, +6 points / +0.01%

Two things landed within minutes of each other near 7am.

The first was a buyback. At 6:56am ET, Nvidia (NVDA) at $225.07, +$0.49 / +0.22% on Friday, and $229.48 premarket, +$4.41 / +1.96% from that close, added $150 billion to its authorization to buy back its own shares, bringing the total to $235 billion. Yahoo Finance called the addition the largest single buyback authorization in history. For scale, $150 billion is about 2.7% of the $5.54 trillion the company was worth at Friday's close. An authorization is a ceiling, not a promise. The stock traded between $223 and $225 from 4am until the announcement - a 5am launch of a safety product for AI agents barely moved it - and was at $228.45 by 7:15am.

Nvidia is the most valuable U.S.-listed company, so it is the heaviest single member of the indexes behind the Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 contracts, which weight members by size. The Dow contract tracks an index that weighs its 30 members by share price instead, so a $229 Nvidia share has far less pull there. Nvidia is not a current pick on any of the six Len5es: at about 28 times the last year of profit, its price carries none of the discount the value-minded Len5es look for.

The second was oil backing off. U.S. crude oil futures peaked at $96.54 a barrel just after 7am ET and have slid to $94.33, +$1.92 / +2.08% since Friday's close as of about 8:50am ET - more than half of the overnight jump is gone. Brent, the international benchmark, is at $106.30, +$1.98 / +1.90%, off an overnight high of $108.83. No new headline has been confirmed as the reason. The weekend news stands: President Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf passage that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, and says he expects more talks. No date is set.

What has not eased is the cost of money. The 10-year Treasury yield - what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years, and the anchor for mortgage and business loan rates - was 5.217% at 9am ET. That is up 3.6 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) from Friday's 5.181%, and less than 2 basis points under its overnight high of 5.234%. The 2-year yield, the one most tied to where traders expect the Federal Reserve to go, is 4.912%, up 4.8 basis points. The Fed raised its benchmark rate a quarter point on September 16, to 3.75%-4.00%, and CME Group's FedWatch tool puts the odds of another quarter-point increase at the October 27-28 meeting near 70%.

That is why the rebound is lopsided. Smaller companies lean harder on borrowing, much of it at rates that reset quickly, so a 10-year yield still near its high gives them little to rally on. Gold, which pays no interest, is still at $4,178.50 an ounce, -142.70 / -3.30% since Friday's close. The VIX - the options market's gauge of how much traders expect stocks to swing - is at 16.02, +1.15 / +7.73% as of 9am ET: higher, but still below its long-run average near 19.

Premarket trading is thin, and overnight moves often shrink or flip once the opening bell brings full volume. Some of that fading already happened before the bell: the Nasdaq contract has erased more than half of its worst loss. Whether the rest of the market follows is what the first hour decides.

Today, in Eastern time:
- 10:30am: the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas releases its Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey for September. Its general business activity index read 11.6 in August - above zero means more Texas factories reported improving conditions than worsening. No firm forecast yet. It rarely moves markets alone, but it is an early look at factories in an oil state with crude above $94.
- 1:25pm: Fed Governor Lisa Cook speaks on emerging technologies.
- 1:30pm: Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin holds a fireside chat. A comment on rates from either would hit that 2-year yield first.

Later this week:
- Wednesday, 8:30am: the Bureau of Economic Analysis releases Personal Income and Outlays for August, with the PCE price index, the inflation gauge the Fed watches most. Forecast: prices 3.8% above a year earlier. Wednesday is also quarter-end, when funds rebalance and late-day moves can reflect bookkeeping more than news.
- Friday, 8:30am: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' September jobs report. Forecasts center near 90,000 new jobs, with unemployment holding at 4.1%.

By 9am the premarket had sorted itself into two camps: the market's biggest company, with $235 billion set aside for its own shares, and everything that runs on borrowed money, still priced against a 5.22% Treasury yield.

Not investment advice.

text:
Sept 28 Iran war update

Trump turned down Tehran's "seven-day" offer this weekend, and he was right to. Iran said it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks in a week, but only if the U.S. first lifted its naval blockade, waived oil sanctions, released Iranian assets and agreed to a ceasefire that also covers Lebanon. That asks America to give up its leverage before Iran does anything. "They overplayed their hand," Trump said. The terms, he said, are what the U.S. might have accepted a year ago. Sen. John Kennedy called it "not a serious offer."

The pressure is working. Even Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said this weekend: "we sank their navy." U.S. aviation sanctions are cutting Iran off from its neighbors, and on Friday airports in Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniya in Iraq stopped accepting Iranian flights. President Pezeshkian now says Iran would let U.N. nuclear inspectors in as part of a long-term ceasefire deal. Trump expects more talks this week, with Axios reporting indirect contacts through Qatari mediators as early as today. He hasn't ruled out more strikes, and his bottom line hasn't changed: Iran will not get a nuclear weapon.

Tehran is still making threats. The IRGC claims it captured a U.S. underwater drone in the Strait. CENTCOM rejects Iran's account and says it has "positive control" of all its operational drones. An IRGC official also threatened to go after American ships in the Indian Ocean if heavy fighting resumes. Trump has also told Xi Jinping that any Chinese help to Iran, including intelligence, parts or equipment, is unacceptable.

Oil is moving. Trump says more than 20 million barrels left the Strait over the weekend, the most since the war began. Prices still jumped Monday after the rejection, and Brent hit its highest level since mid-September. Getting the Strait fully open on America's terms, not Iran's, is what brings prices down for good.

text:
And again, no one said anything about Paul being lawless.

That is an assertion you're adding to my argument that I never made. Reading comprehension is needed on your part here. Let's stick to what was actually said.

The question is whether Paul's personal practices, or Paul preaching in synagogues on the Sabbath, proves that the apostles COMMANDED Gentile believers to observe the seventh day Sabbath.

Acts 15 directly addresses whether Gentile believers should be commanded to keep the law of Moses.

Acts 15:5 says some were teaching that it was necessary "to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses."

Peter asks why they would "put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples." Acts 15:10.

James then says:

"Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God." Acts 15:19.

Then the apostles write concerning those saying the Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law:

"to whom we gave no such commandment." Acts 15:24.

And they conclude:

"For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things." Acts 15:28.

Acts 21 confirms the same distinction.

The Jewish believers were described as "zealous of the law" in Acts 21:20, but concerning the Gentiles they say:

"But as touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication." Acts 21:25.

Now Acts 25.

Before Paul says what you're quoting, Acts 25:3 says there was a plan to kill him. Acts 25:7 says his accusers brought "many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove."

THEN Paul answers:

"Neither against the law of the Jews, neither against the temple, nor yet against Caesar, have I offended any thing at all." Acts 25:8.

That's Paul defending himself against accusations. It is not an apostolic command telling Gentile Christians to keep the Mosaic law.

Acts 26 makes Paul's message even clearer.

Paul tells Agrippa that Christ sent him to the Gentiles "to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light." Acts 26:17 through 18.

He preached that they "should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance." Acts 26:20.

Paul then says the Jews seized him and tried to kill him. Acts 26:21.

And what does Paul say Moses and the prophets testified about?

"That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles." Acts 26:23.

Then concerning your claim that Gentiles "kept the Sabbath 84 times," let's not add assumptions to Scripture. We are instructed not to add to or take away from God's Word.

Acts 13:44 actually tells us why they gathered:

"And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God."

They gathered TO HEAR THE WORD OF GOD.

The text does not say those Gentiles were observing the Sabbath as a commanded Christian ordinance, nor does it say they "kept the Sabbath 84 times."

So the question remains:

Where does Paul or ANY of the apostles COMMAND the GENTILE believers to observe the seventh day Sabbath?

Acts 15 directly addresses whether Gentile believers should be commanded to keep the law of Moses.

Show me the command. Not added assumptions. If not sit down yourself and be quiet. Making a bunch of useless noise and not proven anything

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Leanne Morgan

Overview
Leanne Morgan’s career is a case study in delayed payoff: nearly three decades of stand-up, repeated network deals that collapsed, and years earning roughly the same modest fee before a single video changed everything. The throughline is not luck but self-investment arriving late, after a childhood outside Nashville, an abusive first marriage, a long marriage to Chuck Morgan, and three children. Fame at this stage is surreal, family is often the last to register it, and the work itself remains exhausting. Running underneath is a harder claim: steady, unglamorous partnership and stubborn persistence tend to outperform flash, even when the world only notices the flash.

Key Themes
- A career can sit stuck for twenty years and then move in weeks once the right audience finds the work.
- Hiring social media marketers was framed as one of the first times she invested in herself, and it preceded sold-out shows across the country.
- Family is frequently the last to understand how big a career has become, because they never see the work happening out in the world.
- Chuck Morgan’s identity was tied to being the provider, so her success forced a hard renegotiation of the marriage.
- An abusive first marriage was built on love-bombing, isolation, and erosion of confidence, and leaving in secret was the turning point.
- Waiting tables functioned as performance training, since every table is a new audience and a new set.
- Stand-up experience is unusually strong preparation for sitcom work because it trains speed and recovery.
- Southern life is defended against coastal stereotypes, and tradition is framed as compatible with working women and happiness.
- Long-delayed success raises the stakes on self-policing, since the workload now extends years into the future.

Detailed Summary
Leanne Morgan describes sudden fame later in life as something she still cannot fully absorb, saying every day she is just like what in the world. A recurring tension is that family is often the last to grasp it. One theory offered is that families simply do not see the work happening out in the world. Her husband Chuck’s identity had been tied to being the provider and an overachieving executive, and when her career blew up he said, “You don’t need me anymore.” She says she does need him, but their different family models made the shift hard. Her parents had a business together; Chuck came from a family where the dad took care of everything.

The long plateau is central to the story. She spent about twenty years making the same pitiful amount of money through corporate gigs, breast cancer fundraisers, clubs, and Chamber of Commerce lunches. Even during those years Hollywood was coming after her. She had about five sitcom deals over the years, and one made it. For roughly two decades she earned around $30,000 to $50,000 annually from comedy, often about $2,500 per gig, and felt stuck below the $5,000 mark. She says she did not invest in herself. She got two head shots in twenty-some years, and a friend did her website. A Dry Bar Comedy special, initially dismissed by her manager, produced one clip with 55 million views but did not translate into selling tickets.

Before all of that, the first marriage nearly defined her. She describes an abusive relationship with an older man who love-bombed her, then said terrible things and tried to reduce her confidence. He was twenty-seven, beautiful, smart, charismatic, built like an NFL wide receiver, and is no longer alive. He told her people thought her accent made her stupid and that she needed diction lessons. She remembers thinking, no, they’re not. She says she believed most of his criticisms except that one. He isolated her after they were together and living together, and she describes walking on eggshells every day.

He left her in a restaurant before Christmas when they had ordered a diet coke or tea, and she had no money. A waitress told her not to worry, and Morgan felt the waitress understood from experience. That kindness became a defining moment that helped her decide the marriage was over. She left secretly in the middle of the night, went to a friend’s house where he would not find her, and was scared because he was volatile. He later cried and begged her to return, and she never looked back. Her parents had been nervous about the wedding, and after the divorce they supported her and did not make her feel bad about it. She says she wanted children and a good life, and believed God did not want her in the marriage.

She later returned to university, majoring in child and family studies and crisis intervention counseling, and was 26 when she would graduate. Her father told her she would be 26 anyway. She worked at Grady’s as a waitress and met Chuck Morgan there. Grady’s was a popular, lucrative place to work, especially on University of Tennessee ball game Saturdays, and was later bought by a big chain and ruined. Chuck Morgan was 6 foot 4, in a training group at Grady’s, and had returned to school for an MBA. She had been in therapy after her divorce, was messed up, cut her hair off, and did not want to date. She says Chuck fell in love with her early, but she did not know it because he does not talk.

Waitressing is framed as formative training for performing, because every table is a new audience. She contrasts her chatty, rapport-building style, fewer tables and better tips, with Chuck’s quiet, task-focused style, more tables and fewer tips, which nonetheless earned him waiter-of-the-year recognition through side work and reliability. His courtship is described as acts of service rather than love bombing. He did her side work, cleaned ketchup bottles, cleaned the women’s bathroom unasked, bought her flowers, brought things to her apartment, changed her oil, filled her gas tank, and rotated her tires. She told him she was damaged and not ready. He was a mobile home salesman and does not take no for an answer.

She was told she could not have children, and she says being a mama was what she wanted most besides Hollywood. After graduating, Chuck bought a used mobile home business refurbishing mobile homes, despite never having been in one, during a weak job market tied to the first Bush and Iraq period. They moved to Bean Station, Tennessee, in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains. She sold jewelry at home parties to earn her own money while wanting to be home with and nurse her babies. She had never been to a comedy club until Chuck took her to see her sister in Huntington Beach, and she wanted to do the hearse tour of old Hollywood murder sites.

Seeing live standup at the Comedy Store was the moment she felt she could do standup, because she saw unfinished, experimental performances rather than only polished acts. She had previously seen polished performers such as Richard Pryor and Richard Lewis. Her first real opportunity came through a Sunday school connection. After moving to Morristown, Tennessee, a class member in the Kuanas club asked her to MC the Kuanas Capers. A sandwich shop owner with a stage then offered her an hour of standup. Before that first hour-long set she was so scared she saw an ENT thinking she had a tumor, and the doctor said she was just scared. She prepared using a kindergarten tablet, writing down words for stories she already knew. Chuck had the babies in the minivan during her first set, three babies under five, with about fifty people attending.

A comedy club owner told her she had talent but could not build a comedy career while raising three babies on the road. Brian Dorman, now her concert promoter, said yes when she cold-called Zanie’s in Nashville and asked to come perform. She opened for Billy Gardell at Zanie’s without knowing what an opener was. Dorman told her she had something but said Roseanne would have had her kids in a station wagon in the parking lot. Comedy Central, Montreal, and Aspen never selected her. The first pilot deal was with ABC and Warner Brothers when her son Charlie was in sixth grade, and the writer strike hit and ended it. She experienced what she calls clinical depression after that pilot deal collapsed.

The low point came around age fifty or fifty-one, unable to sell tickets and playing poorly paid road gigs, feeling nothing was going to happen after more than twenty years of hope. After a dinner with Chuck where she cried and considered quitting comedy, possibly opening a hardware store, or focusing on being a grandmother, she noticed Nate Bargatze was about a year and a half ahead of her and attributed his success partly to social media people. That motivated her to hire social media marketers from Plano, Texas, who knew her voice and had a mom like her. She believes television and local news and newspapers were no longer effective ways to reach audiences. A video about Def Leppard, Journey, and aging rock bands resonated, and audiences began asking what else she had. She describes the shift as somebody turned a light on in a dark room. After one video resonated, ticket sales changed rapidly, from being unable to sell tickets to selling out across the United States within weeks.

She reflects that not making it earlier may have protected her from the pressures of fame, and that being in her own lane allows her freedoms others in Hollywood may not have. She notes health and lifestyle tradeoffs, including eating white flour and sugar, concerns about dementia, and taking fish oil and magnesium. A discussion about hair loss includes mentions of Propecia and the popularity of hair transplants in Turkey, and she jokes that Chuck took Propecia without telling her. She estimated losing about forty percent of her hair in four months after her daughters pointed it out in a vacation photo.

The acting transition was terrifying. She was scared out of her mind and did not know what a table read was, so she called a friend who explained it. Reese Witherspoon helped her get the film role, personally encouraged her, and later provided Opry tickets to the hosts. In the film she replaced scripted profanity with milder southern expressions because she is a mother and grandmother, and Nick Stoller told her she knew her character better than he did. She describes the set as unusually kind, with Will Ferrell as beautiful and benevolent, Witherspoon taking care of her, and Stoller as precious. Rory Scovel played her brother, Celia Weston played her mother, and Blake Clark plays her father in her sitcom.

Chuck Lorre sent her special to her manager, then flew to Knoxville via Warner Brothers to meet her. He told her he could tell she put in 10,000 hours and was the real deal, and offered a show without a pilot, which reassured her after five previous deals that did not make it. Lorre is described as quiet, reserved, serious, brilliantly funny, and intimidating, and Chuck Morgan is also quiet and intimidating, and they connected. She initially felt overwhelmed and thought she had a gastrointestinal disease for six weeks, and almost quit but felt it was right. She is now doing an arena tour and finds herself ranked alongside Dave Chappelle in Netflix numbers. She has met Jerry Seinfeld, who gives her advice, and David Letterman asked how she did it with three babies.

The tradeoff between career and family recurs. Delaying a TV deal allowed her to raise her children rather than relocate them. Matt Williams warned her not to move her family or have her husband quit his job because the show would likely be cancelled, and Ray Romano is mentioned as someone who did a similar long-distance arrangement for a while. She says she has about 150 shows running through 2027 and will owe Netflix another special. She wrote a book a couple of years ago and has been offered small movie roles, and appeared in a Judd Apatow movie with Glenn Close, playing a dean who flirts.

The Opry is framed as a uniquely special, comforting institution linked to country music history. She grew up going because her parents had a meat processing plant and did meat for country music stars and Opry leadership, which led to free tickets every year. She saw Dolly Parton, Porter Wagoner, Roy Acuff, and Minnie Pearl there as a child. The Ryman is treated as legendary and emotionally significant, with backstage pictures of Elvis and Patsy Cline. She was raised right outside Nashville in Adams, Tennessee, on the Kentucky-Tennessee border, thirty-five minutes north of Nashville, a town of about 600 people. Her school was K through 12 with 650 students, she ate lunch with kindergarteners, and she went to church with all her teachers.

She describes Southern life against coastal stereotypes, arguing Southerners are educated, hip, eccentric, family-oriented, and community-minded, and rejecting the idea that traditional family structures equal oppression, saying the women she knows work and are happy. She also pushes back on the idea that women do not need men. Nashville is described as attracting LA and New York people, with a Nordstrom shifting from orthopedic shoes to Gucci. Moving there required proving they were not those Californians. She was married at 21 to her first husband, and has been married to Chuck for 34 years. Her children are now 30, 33, and 28 and are described as tickled and loving it now. Her baby child is her makeup artist, trained in makeup for television and film and in the union. Season two of Leanne comes out on Netflix on Thursday, August 27th.

FED GOVERNOR MICHELLE BOWMAN SPEAKS BEFORE THE BELL. TRADERS ALREADY SEE A 70% CHANCE OF ANOTHER HIKE:

U.S. stocks are set to open lower, and the reason is a barrel of oil. Crude jumped overnight after President Trump turned down Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that jump pushed interest rates up with it. Nasdaq-100 futures are at 30,636.00, -253 / -0.82% since Friday's close. S&P 500 futures sit at 7,768.25, -35.50 / -0.45%, and Dow futures at 51,870.00, -293 / -0.56%. Futures are contracts that trade nearly around the clock and point to where the big indexes may start at 9:30am ET.

The verdict for this morning: a measured pullback led by technology, driven by what oil does to the odds of another Federal Reserve rate increase - not a scramble for safety. And it is not fading. At 5:42am ET, Reuters had the S&P 500 contract down 0.49%. More than two hours of European trading later, it is down 0.45%.

The trigger came over the weekend. Iran offered at the United Nations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz - the narrow Gulf passage that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil - within seven days, if the U.S. lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports and its sanctions on Iranian oil and agreed to a ceasefire. Trump rejected it, while saying he expects talks to resume this week. No date is set. U.S. crude oil futures are at $95.65 a barrel, +$3.24 / +3.51% since Friday's close.

Why one commodity matters this much to a stock index right now: over the past 60 days, U.S. stock futures have tracked oil more closely than at any point since late May, Reuters calculated this morning. For now, the price of a barrel is doing much of the work of setting the market's mood.

The path from oil to stocks runs through interest rates. Costlier fuel and shipping feed inflation. The Fed already raised its benchmark rate a quarter point on September 16, to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase since 2023. Traders in rate futures now see about a 70% chance of another quarter-point increase at the October 27-28 meeting, Reuters reported. Treasury yields - what the U.S. government pays to borrow - moved with those odds:

- 2-year: 4.92%, up from 4.86% at Friday's close. This is the one most tied to where the Fed goes next.
- 10-year: 5.22%, up from 5.18%. This one anchors mortgage and business loan rates.

Technology takes the first hit because so much of a fast-growing company's value sits in profits years away, and a 5.22% government bond raises the bar those far-off profits have to clear today. Russell 2000 futures, which track smaller U.S. companies, are at 2,841.00, -18.30 / -0.64%. Smaller companies carry more debt at rates that reset quickly, so a higher-for-longer Fed reaches them fast.

What is missing is panic. The VIX - the options market's gauge of how much the S&P 500 is expected to swing, often called the fear gauge - is at 16.25, +1.38 / +9.3% so far this morning. That is a sharp jump, but to a level still below its long-run average near 19 to 20. Gold, usually a wartime refuge, is at $4,181.00 an ounce, -$140.20 / -3.24% since Friday's close. Investors are pricing a more expensive cost of money, not running for cover.

Europe, now in its afternoon, has mostly looked past the oil jump. London's FTSE 100 is at 10,728, +33.06 / +0.31% so far in Monday's session, trading now. Germany's DAX is at 25,424, +15.03 / +0.06%, barely above flat. France's CAC 40 is at 8,105.30, +27.50 / +0.34%. The notable story is British housing. The government unveiled a "Your First Home" plan letting first-time buyers in England buy a newly built home with a 2.5% down payment plus a government loan covering another 20% of the price, with details due in next month's Budget. UK housebuilder shares jumped, several by 10% or more. Energy producers rose with crude; precious-metals miners fell with gold.

What to watch before the bell, and just after it:

- 8:15am ET: Fed Governor Michelle Bowman speaks. Every voting Fed official who has spoken since the September 16 hike has stuck to one message - more tightening is likely needed - as Reuters' Mike Dolan notes. Governors vote at every Fed meeting, so her words can move those 70% odds either way.
- Oil: a date for renewed talks with Iran is the one development most able to pull crude, yields, and tech futures back before 9:30.
- 10:30am ET: the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas publishes its Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey for September, an index where a reading above zero means more factories growing than shrinking. August read 11.6; a firm forecast has not settled.
- This afternoon: Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin speak.

The bigger tests land later this week. Wednesday at 8:30am ET, the Bureau of Economic Analysis releases August's Personal Income and Outlays report, carrying the PCE price index, the inflation gauge the Fed watches most. Core prices, leaving out food and energy, are expected +0.3% for the month vs +0.2% in July. Wednesday is also quarter-end, when funds rebalance and prices can move for reasons that have nothing to do with news. Friday at 8:30am ET, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the September jobs report: estimates run from about 84,000 to 100,000 new jobs, vs 162,000 in August, with unemployment at 4.1% last month. It is the only jobs report before the October Fed meeting.

One honest limit: premarket trading is a thin slice of what changes hands once the bell rings, and moves this size can shrink, grow, or reverse by 9:30. Nothing above is a forecast for how Monday ends.

The question hanging over the open is whether 70% odds of another rate increase are a cost stocks have finished paying, or one they have only started on.

text:
Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within 7 days. President Trump said no.

Here is what was actually on the table. Tehran's price for reopening: the US ends its naval blockade, lifts economic pressure, and releases frozen Iranian assets. Accepting would hand back the world's most important oil chokepoint in exchange for unwinding the exact leverage that forced Iran to make an offer at all.

Brent crude (the international oil benchmark) spiked as high as $108.83 Monday before settling near $107, up 2.7%. That is the visible cost of holding the line.

The invisible cost is in inventories. Energy analysts warn the world is 'living off borrowed barrels': importing nations have been draining strategic stockpiles to cover supply lost since the strait closed. Stockpile draws are a buffer with an expiration date. The longer Hormuz stays shut, the less cushion remains under the next shock.

Markets are already pricing a return of US strikes after the November midterms. Tehran's opening bid just bought nothing, and every week the strait stays closed, the pressure math tilts further toward Washington.

Podcast Summary | Candace: WE WERE RIGHT! UVU Releases Their Independent Review. | Ep 394

Overview
The release of UVU's independent review into the September 10 security failures inverts the public narrative that dominated for a year: a third-party review by the Lake Force group concludes no UVU employee or agent acted in bad faith or with willful disregard for safety, while key Turning Point USA affiliated figures declined to cooperate with the very process they publicly demanded. The review documents how venue control, ticketing, and access decisions were effectively deferred to TPUSA, leaving UVU without reliable attendance data and with roughly a week to plan protest and crowd control for an event that drew about 3,000 people into an outdoor fountain courtyard. The host argues the findings confirm prior criticisms, expose Brian Harpole's public claims as inconsistent with the evidence, and set up a broader timeline connecting Charlie Kirk's final months, internal TPUSA money tensions, and the pressure campaign he faced over the Epstein files.

Key Themes
- The independent review reportedly clears UVU of bad faith or willful disregard for safety, directly contradicting the Kirk family and TPUSA narrative that UVU security was to blame.
- TPUSA-affiliated individuals declined to cooperate with the review despite public demands for transparency; Brian Harpole spoke on Sean Ryan's podcast but did not respond to the review team.
- Security authority was quietly outsourced: TPUSA chose the fountain courtyard and used its own national ticketing system, so UVU lacked real-time attendance data and reliable crowd estimates.
- The event followed an abnormal approval path, with a TPUSA field representative directing a club president to request the event rather than a chapter requesting Charlie Kirk through National.
- UVU raised documented concerns about venue, protests, crowd management, and access control weeks out, but TPUSA insisted on the outdoor location and its own vendor process.
- Event-day coordination between TPUSA security and UVUPD was minimal, including no TPUSA security member joining the police command post during the event.
- The review identifies structural gaps: no documented venue modification requirements, no real-time camera monitoring assignment, no mutual aid requests, and no structured pre-event briefing.
- The host frames the findings as proof that a year of blame directed at UVU and at her was gaslighting, and promises a wider timeline tying Charlie Kirk's personal and political pressures to the event.
- The final arc shifts to the Croft case dismissal, TPUSA internal money disputes, and the claim that Charlie Kirk expected to die and proceeded anyway.

Detailed Summary
The review was conducted by a third-party group, the Lake Force group, at UVU's request and focused on security protocols for the September 10 event. Its executive summary reportedly states that no UVU employee or agent acted in bad faith or with willful disregard for safety, while identifying actions and omissions to improve future campus event security. The review's project team reached out to Brian Harpole of Integrity Solutions, Dan Flood of TPUSA, Macy Crofts of TPUSA, and the then-head of the UVU TPUSA club. Outreach included phone calls, voicemails, certified letters, and emails to senior TPUSA staff in Phoenix. A Utah risk-management official reportedly urged TPUSA-associated individuals to cooperate. There was no response. The host frames this as especially suspicious because Harpole spoke publicly on Sean Ryan's podcast about the event.

The report says key security decisions were deferred to Turning Point USA, including holding the event outdoors and using TPUSA's own ticketing system. That limited UVU's control and real-time attendance information. The review concludes UVU should have retained decision-making authority over venue selection, ticketing, access control, and other safety-related conditions because the event was on its campus. TPUSA's choices reduced UVU's control and its access to reliable attendance and crowd information.

The event originated unusually. On July 10, 2025, TPUSA's field representative, Macy Crofts, directed a club president to request the event, rather than a chapter requesting Charlie Kirk through TPUSA National, which is a reversal of the normal process. The club president, Caleb Chiliket, reportedly did not know why he was requesting the event and was not in control of ticketing. TPUSA National handled registrations. The normal process has chapters request speakers, with National weighing factors like prior visits, university size, and club performance, typically planning a semester ahead. The July 18 request described a Charlie Kirk appearance on current events, with ticketing handled externally.

The Major Events Assessment Committee process began August 21. UVU staff raised concerns about the outdoor fountain courtyard venue and TPUSA's ticketing process. TPUSA told UVU to expect 600 attendees and offered to connect UVUPD with TPUSA security, stating no risk factor for safety or security. That same day, event services emailed required parties for the major events committee. This was the first time Chief Jeff Long became aware of the event. UVU's free speech committee flagged the event, anticipating protests based on prior TPUSA appearances, including a 2019 Charlie Kirk event at UVU.

On August 25, the major events assessment committee met. No TPUSA security members attended despite UVU raising concerns about the outdoor courtyard, attendance, protests, crowd management, and access control. TPUSA still insisted on the fountain courtyard and cited roughly eight security personnel. UVU suggested alternative locations, including the Fulton Library, the quad, or interior locations with more controllable access. Crofts reportedly said Charlie Kirk had previously spoken on campus and TPUSA was familiar with Fountain Courtyard. Robin Emer, UVU's director of emergency management and safety, expressed reservations. The committee allowed the event in the requested location and allowed TPUSA to manage ticketing. The final approval came August 27, very late relative to the September 10 event. Chief Long requested contact with TPUSA security leadership on August 25, fifteen days before the event.

On September 3, Chief Long and Dan Flood had their first phone call, lasting five minutes and twenty-eight seconds. Flood focused on arrival and departure and parking logistics, including a clean exit for Charlie's SUV, and said TPUSA typically has eight to ten security personnel. A follow-up call lasted forty-eight seconds. Flood said TPUSA national was handling ticketing and ticket totals were unavailable. The last attendance number UVU had was 600, despite roughly 3,000 ultimately attending. The host contends TPUSA and figures like Harpole advanced a false narrative that text communications about the canopy area were about rooftops broadly. The transcript says they were actually about the Hall of Flags pedestrian walkway above Charlie Kirk's canopy.

On September 8, TPUSA security raised concern about pedestrian walkway access above the area where Charlie Kirk's canopy was to be placed. Dan Flood initiated a text exchange. Chief Long replied "We got you covered" regarding the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway. Harpole reportedly told Shawn Ryan his first meeting about the September 10 event was August 24, one day before the UVU MEAC meeting. Harpole said Dan Flood was a security guy for Turning Point and did not share specific security concerns or threats during pre-event planning. Harpole said his team arrived a few hours before the event, surveyed the area, and believed the venue location was horrible, specifically citing the risk of someone in an elevated position having a 180-degree view of Kirk's speaking area. Harpole described the venue setup as ignorant and a security fail but said Charlie Kirk liked the venue. Harpole claimed UVU selected the venue and told TPUSA it had to be there. The review says multiple interviews indicated UVU expressed concerns but ultimately agreed to TPUSA's requested location.

Harpole also discussed drones. He said TPUSA's video team used small drones before the event, but his team did not use drones during the event due to FAA restrictions related to Provo airspace. The host says the drone restriction claim is false because the event location is not within five miles of Provo Airport's Class D airspace. The review states drone operations are restricted within a five-mile radius of Provo airport in Class D airspace and that a drone from neighboring Orem Police Department could have been requested but wasn't. The review notes Chief Long did not initiate a mutual aid request to Orem PD or other local public safety partners before the event, and no additional external resources were requested after crowd size became apparent. The review notes there was no dedicated real-time security video monitoring assignment for UVUPD dispatch or another operational location during the event. There was no structured pre-event briefing or site walk-through on September 10 between Harpole, Flood, and UVUPD.

On event day, Chief Long contacted Utah SIA regarding an anonymous threat about EMPs at 7:23 a.m. The Utah SIAC reportedly said it was not credible and that the tipster had provided similar unreliable information previously. Security arrived on campus at 9:00 a.m. Chief Long did not meet them until then. At 9:04, Dan Flood texted Chief Long that the rest of security had arrived. Chief Long and Flood exchanged texts focused on individuals on the Hall of Flags pedestrian walkway across from Aloi Center. Additional Charlie Kirk staff arrived at 9:28 and 10:28. At 10:49, Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet at the Hall of Flags outdoor area at 11:00, but the meeting did not occur. At 11:00, after observing crowd size, UVUPD staffing was increased beyond Chief Long, one patrol officer, and one reserve officer. Between 11:20 and 11:30, officers went to the Hall of Flags and dealt with protesters. Protesters moved away and officers blocked them off with security tape. At 11:30, Chief Long went to the second floor of the Fugal Gateway building to establish a command post with visibility over the event area. No TPUSA security member joined him. The review credits Officer Bagley as the first to suggest going to the Lozi Center after the shooting and to identify the elevated roof as a possible shooter location. His body cam was not working. Officer Bagley found a screwdriver and disturbed gravel on the roof consistent with a possible prone shooting position.

Turning Point USA National handled registration, not actual tickets. There was no ticket verification, credentialing, screening, designated entry and exit points, or restricted access areas. The review raises unanswered questions about who the wristband recipients were. The host argues Harpole's podcast interview contained multiple lies and that TPUSA and Charlie Kirk's organization cannot make him the sole fall guy because an employee provided him the text message used on Shawn Ryan's show. The project team sought to speak directly with Harpole because his statements conflicted with evidence and interviews. He reportedly declined to clarify.

The host then builds a July 2025 Charlie Kirk timeline. July 7 to 9, BBNet and Yahoo visited America and recorded a podcast with the Elk Boys in Washington DC. July 10, after they left DC, TPUSA's Macy Crofts asked the UVU club president to organize an event. The president was told Kirk needed to be in the amphitheater. July 11 to 13, the Student Action Summit took place in Tampa. Kirk's first speech was at 4 p.m. Tucker Carlson spoke on July 11 and donors "freaked out." Kirk told him to "go Max" and called out Jeffrey Epstein. Kirk reportedly called daily for release of Epstein files and asked Megan Kelly and Tucker Carlson to speak about it. Carlson said people who serve in foreign armies should be stripped of citizenship and questioned Bill Ackman's wealth. He later said he didn't know what came over him. On July 11, Frank Turk deleted his website, which had remnants of an expedition looking for Noah's Ark remnants. On July 12, according to the New York Times, Trump called Charlie Kirk angry and scolded him about the prior day's event. Kirk announced on July 14 that he was done talking about Epstein for the time being, saying he would trust friends in the administration and figures like Kash Patel, Dan Bongino, Pam Bondi, and Todd Blanche.

Charlie and Erika Kirk faced pressure over the Epstein coverage, including donors pulling money. Erika Kirk traveled by private flight to Long Beach, California on July 14 and spoke at James Kattis' Calvary Chapel Church. Kattis is described as radically pro-Israel. Charlie vacationed in Maine, the first time Mikey McCoy and Elizabeth joined him. They captured final footage of Charlie and Erika. Charlie and Erika landed in Bedford, New York on August 3 for the Hamptons Retreat. The retreat occurred August 5 to 6 and was sponsored by Bill Ackman. Charlie described the Hamptons retreat as an intervention and later discussed it on the Megan Kelly show. Netanyahu called Charlie and made an offer, according to Andrew Kovette. Erika Kirk claims there was no offer and it was just a follow-up to a letter Charlie wrote in May. Netanyahu invited Charlie to Israel, and Charlie declined. Charlie also declined to have Netanyahu on his show.

The final section turns to the Croft case. A former high school football coach's criminal case was dismissed before trial after prosecutors said newly discovered information undermined their ability to prove intent, a required element of the felony charge. The dismissal turned on a factual dispute over whether the classroom door was locked. Prosecutors did not argue the underlying conduct did not happen. The dispute centered on the child's version of events, the coach's version, and establishing intent for a child to see him. The coach was arrested in June. In November 2025 his attorney argued for dismissal, saying the door was locked and he was trying to conceal his actions when the minor walked in. The judge denied the November dismissal request and said there was enough evidence to send the case to a grand jury. The minor testified students regularly left backpacks in the classroom and picked them up after extracurricular activities. She went in to get her backpack and came upon the incident. Canyon County prosecuting attorney Alana Minton told the judge new information had come to light: the classroom door may have been locked at the time. Prosecutors said the new information prevented them from proving sexual abuse of a child under 16 even by probable cause, let alone beyond a reasonable doubt. The state explored a lesser misdemeanor indecent exposure charge but said it was not permitted to modify the indictment. The judge granted the state's oral motion to dismiss the indictment before a jury could hear it. Croft's no-contact order covering all minors was lifted and he was released from all pre-trial restrictions. Croft's attorney said his client was never guilty and the dismissal proves that. The teen's father said the outcome left the family feeling unheard and that they were disappointed the truth did not get out. The host claims TPUSA did not want to participate in an independent review even though it was willing to speak to CBS News, ABC News, and official spokespersons. The host names Caleb Chilikut and says he did nothing wrong and was told what to do by headquarters. The host says Macy was likely told what to do by Andrew Cipher, who was promoted shortly afterward to a chief position. The host says there were rumblings early on that money was missing, particularly from Turning Point Action, which Tyler Boyer controls. The host says Mikey McCoy expressed that Charlie Kirk wanted to fire Tyler Boyer, and that Tyler Boyer introduced Charlie and Erica. The host closes by accusing influencers and former allies of betraying Charlie, lying, and gaslighting, motivated by power and money rather than truth. She predicts they will all fail. text:
Podcast Summary | This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von: #685 - Joey Diaz

Overview
Leaving Los Angeles for central New Jersey was a pre-pandemic decision, not a reaction to one, and it doubles as a test of manhood: living in a community and raising a child without drama, arrest, or DUIs. The sharpest thread running through the conversation is contrasts, between city comedy chaos and a calmer home life, between immigrant-style discipline and looser households, and between comfort and manufactured hardship. Childhood instability, a gambling mother, an absent sense of safety, is framed as formative rather than merely tragic, and it shapes both parenting strategy and material. The closing arc turns to gratitude, forgiveness, and late-life reinvention: moving to Austin for stage time, streaming GTA as an earned social outlet, and treating recovery as an ongoing counterweight to isolation.

Key Themes
- Leaving LA was a deliberate exit on one's own terms, meant to prevent overstaying or getting cocky rather than to escape a crisis.
- Jersey and Philadelphia represent the working side of comedy paired with a peaceful home life, not a retreat from ambition.
- Parenting is treated as deliberate exposure, bringing a daughter into green rooms and shows so she grows up comfortable around men and street smart.
- Childhood shame, poverty, and chaotic households are reframed as formative, producing observant storytellers rather than only damage.
- Breaking the cycle is presented as a conscious act: no alcohol-centered parties at home, smoking outside, checking yourself at the door.
- A mother's gambling and drinking are linked to divorce, poor health, and emotional pain, and her death is described as a broken heart disguised as a heart attack.
- The struggle years of comedy, buses and hotels and not getting paid, are framed as world-class education worth repeating.
- Seeing someone from a similar background succeed opens a mental door: if they did it, you can do something too.
- Austin's comedy scene is unusually efficient, and isolation and boredom are named as real risks that social contact, gyms, and boxing counter.

Detailed Summary
Leaving Los Angeles was planned before the pandemic. A house was bought in April, the school year finished, and the move happened in August, with the pandemic only accelerating the timeline. At 57, the reasoning was simple: more had happened career-wise than anticipated, so it was time to take the winnings and leave. Growing up two hours from Asbury Park and coming from North Jersey made the return feel less like exile and more like a homecoming with better terms.

Joey Diaz frames his own move to New Jersey differently. He wanted his daughter to absorb lessons from his upbringing, even knowing her experience would never match the hardship he faced. Both men share a strong preference for comfort over ruggedness. Burning Man gets dismissed as a fancy club moved to the desert, largely wealthy and trust-fund types, and Diaz calls himself anti-anything where he cannot wash properly. Wrestling comes up as comedy with physical danger: bombing on stage versus someone throwing a chair at your head.

Asbury Park threads through the conversation. Diaz grew up two hours away and came for concerts as a kid, including Iron Maiden opening for Judas Priest around 1981. A bottle was thrown at his car before that show, so he and his friends parked on the other side. Jim Florentine was at the same concert and has told a story about being thrown out for throwing smoke bombs, with his mother picking him up. Diaz now lives two doors down from Florentine in New Jersey, in a house Florentine's sister-in-law sold him, and describes the Florentine crime family as big and constantly partying.

The Jersey-to-New York comedy rhythm is laid out in practical terms. Go into the city on Tuesday and do four spots, because returns diminish after four. A brother and childhood friend in Morganville, about ten minutes from where he now lives, introduced him to the area. Back in those days he helped with a fish company, getting in the car at 4 a.m. to pick up fish at the Fulton Fish Market in Manhattan, and would do three or four weeks at clubs like Rascals and Bananas. After deliveries, done by 10:30 or 11, the day turned serene: shower, pool, grilled fish in the afternoon. He compares the city-to-Jersey contrast to living near LA but in Calabasas.

Home life now has its own ritual: an Archie Bunker-style chair, a blanket, a remote, a small refrigerator with drinks, and peptides. Philadelphia is described as uniquely unfiltered, with audiences and public behavior that are raw and real. Jersey and Philadelphia women are repeatedly characterized as especially funny and tough. There is a Phillies game with his then-eight-year-old daughter, preceded by a warning that she would see and hear things she had not before, and she pointed out a large spray-painted phallic image on a wall. At a 76ers game, two men were making out and were soon approached and told there were too many kids around. He once jumped into a Philadelphia casino audience during a set and they caught him; he thinks he messed up one guy's shoulder.

Travel preferences lean toward history and museums over clubs and restaurants, especially in East Coast states. Betsy Ross's house and Philadelphia museums come up, along with George Washington-related history at Fort Lee under the George Washington Bridge. There is a story about walking the bridge to avoid car searches, since cars left under the bridge on the New York side would disappear.

Military service recurs as a road not taken. Looking back, it could have provided structure, benefits, and a second life, and wasted years are regretted. His mother was strongly pro-America and wanted him to become a Marine, but her death and his drug use derailed that path. He spoke to a recruiter in her honor, then missed the blood test after getting coked up. The counterfactual is spelled out: 20 years in the Marines means getting out at 38 with a pension, medical benefits, and a second life.

His mother's gambling escalated after she sold her business and became bored. She bet on horses, dogs, and pigeons, went from daytime racing to cooking dinner, then to the Meadowlands at 8, and if that was not good, took another cab to Yonkers for night racing until around 2 a.m. At one point she invested in a jewelry company but was buying jewelry for herself. Her gambling and drinking are tied to divorce, separation, poor health, and emotional pain. She died when he was 16, and he found her at 15 after initially not going downstairs when she called. Her death is described as a broken heart disguised as a heart attack. Forty-seven years later it still causes daily pain, and he uses that to urge a friend to repair his relationship with his own mother. As a teenager he coped by imagining she had gone to Cuba and would come back, calling it the biggest lie he ever told himself. He was a sophomore in high school when she died, and around 17 he would secretly sit on the steps of their childhood home hoping a mistake had been made. About two months after her death he went to her grave high on cocaine and other substances and tried to dig with his hands for roughly an hour and a half, only about an inch. She had a rule that he had to call by 11 if he would be late, and once smacked him at 15, later explaining it was because he would need to be responsible to a wife someday.

Another throughline is parenting as deliberate exposure. He takes his daughter to standup shows and has brought her to green rooms since she was about 11 or 12, including Rogan's green room. The goal is for her to see what men think and talk about so she will not be in shock when she enters the world at 18. He calls her sassy with a Cuban attitude and says she has a similar body type to his mother. When he hugs or kisses her, he feels he is also connecting to his dead mother. He drives her to practices and attends softball games, prioritizing being part of her life over staying in Austin.

Childhood shame is examined from both sides. One speaker was embarrassed by his older father, which kept him away from him during ages 14 to 16. His father bought a Delta 88 or Cutlass for about $800, with speakers in the trunk that played Paul Harvey and Rush Limbaugh with heavy bass, and the passenger-side doors did not open, so they had to jump in through the window. His father delivered candies for vending machines, and melted chocolate in the car got on the kids while dogs licked them. He sometimes fell asleep in the carpool line. His mother once threw chicken wings and bones at Rusty Staub at a Mets game after losing $800 when Staub did not make a catch, and the stadium moved her to the other side rather than throwing her out. She allegedly paid a guy $20 to move people with real tickets and give her better seats. She stole a church or school bell, took it to Mets games for good luck, then gave it to him after the Mets lost to the Cincinnati Reds in 1973, calling it voodoo.

Strict household discipline is contrasted with looser white household dynamics. A mother came to a pool party, yelled his real name Jose Antonio, tried to climb the fence, chased him for about 20 minutes, hit him with a stick, and later burned his hands with a lit bounty roll for raising his hands to her. Kids could not talk back at the table, and a friend who told his dad at dinner that he did not believe in God was punched repeatedly in the face. Another speaker says his mother made him clean whites and colors at age four and then took them to McDonald's as a reward, where she would shush them and order a McFish as if it were a special menu item, which he saw as a weird superiority.

Chaotic homes are framed as formative for becoming observant and a storyteller. One speaker emphasizes consciously breaking the cycle: no alcohol-centered parties at home, smoking pot outside, checking himself at the door so his kids do not inherit that environment. He left his own house in sixth grade to sleep at friends' places in Union City because he could not sleep at home. His mother and stepfather were involved in two different bookmaking operations, adding pressure. He reflects on his mother's difficult upbringing, her father erratic and avoiding the front door for months with food slid under it, as context for her behavior. The gratitude theme lands here: he is grateful his mother made him, and while early life was not up to him, it is up to him now.

His mother cooked large late-night meals around 3:30 to 4 a.m., steak, eggs, black beans, lobster tail. Uncles and people in the house would be up at 2 to 4 a.m., sometimes coked up, and would give him $20 for school. The late-night noise made the house unlivable for him. He moved to Union City for sixth grade, left school at 3, did karate or basketball, ate dinner at his mother's bar, got clothes, showered, and walked to school from Union City rather than sleeping in North Bergen. Now he keeps no alcohol parties at home, does not smoke pot inside, has not watched porn since he was 13, and describes his home life as a regular American family life with no butlers or nannies.

Greyhound travel is presented as formative and story-generating. He took buses as a feature act before headlining, including the LA bus to El Paso and the Monday Night Express at 11:45, arriving at a hotel around 1:00 the next day. On one bus pulled over by immigration cops with dogs, he snorted about three grams of cocaine in one swipe and sweated heavily through the stop. He met a stripper on a bus to Buffalo who said an STD would go on her stripping license and prevent her from dancing until she saw a doctor. He once had sex on a bus and paid the driver $40 to drive slowly. Luggage theft and lack of customer service round out the experience. Both men say they would do comedy all over again, including the struggle, hotels, buses, and people not paying them, framing the education as world-class and worth it. They miss the struggle and still do not like things being easy, because having something to chase and prove is motivating.

Seeing someone from a similar background succeed opens a mental door. Shoplifting turkeys and coconuts with Ralphie May is used as an example of a peer who later achieved visible success, living in a penthouse on Wilshire Boulevard with three pounds of weed on the coffee table, reinforcing the idea that if he did it, you could do something too. Michael Jordan's freshman start at North Carolina is cited as a door-opener for a kid from Jersey City, and thinking about Jordan happens about once a month, with a wish to thank him. Jordan's mother Rosie is described as an Irish single mom and waitress. Pistol Pete Maravich lived in the same town, with a unique house that had a half court in the attic, and Lee Harvey Oswald went to their middle school. James J. Braddock paid kids a couple of bucks to shovel snow from his driveway and is described as a regular neighborhood guy whose kids became cops.

The closing arc turns to late-life reinvention. Austin offers better stage time and more spots per night, rather than maintaining without improving in New Jersey. The shift was gradual, from twice a year to monthly, doing three spots a night Tuesday through Thursday, and now streaming GTA twice a week. He has rented an apartment in Redban's building on the 44th floor, with sauna, cold plunge, poker room, supermarket, and Amazon returns, and does a monthly show that covers rent and plane fare. Streaming GTA has become a regular social outlet, framed as earned late-life fun since he never played video games as a kid. At 63 he says he still does not know what he wants to do when he grows up, and after 20 years of not staying out past 1 a.m., he stayed out until 4:30 a.m. in Austin with friends. Touring and life stress disrupted his recovery program, and things got choppy this summer but have improved, with AA described as better for him now. Isolation and boredom are named as major risks, especially with age, and communication, gyms, boxing, and social contact are the counterweights.

In her interview with Newsweek, Anita Orbán said that the new Hungarian government wants to establish the same kind of solid institutional relationship with the United States as the one that existed under the previous government.

This would be desirable for Hungary, so we can only hope that people in Washington did not hear them mocking the current administration at every opportunity during the campaign - but let’s not be naive.

Moreover, they can also see how the new government is aligning itself with Brussels’ expectations in every area of life: for example, how it is conducting a political campaign to eliminate right-wing parties, just as other Brussels-aligned parties are doing in their own countries (see Germany and France). 

It may also be difficult to pretend that Hungary remains an attractive investment destination while taxes are being raised, new ones are being introduced, and a Communist-rooted system of wealth confiscation is being created. What can I say, I have seen better offers from an investor’s point of view…

The question is: what can be preserved from the previous government’s foreign policy achievements if the strategy behind them is completely changed? It is a strange diplomatic idea to expect the same results while systematically dismantling the political foundations necessary to achieve them.

Over the past sixteen years, one of the most important tasks has been to figure out how a small, open economy can diversify its energy supplies, financing and export markets while fulfilling its alliance commitments.

Maintaining this balance was also a serious diplomatic challenge in our relations with Washington. One of the fundamental dilemmas of Hungarian foreign policy was precisely how to maintain close Western alliances while preserving independent economic room for manoeuvre in a world where great-power competition increasingly determines trade and investment relations as well.

As for the new government’s answer…

Anita Orbán was given the task by Péter Magyar of bringing Hungary back into the Brussels mainstream. It is a fact that politically this is an easier task. Hungary will probably appear less often on the front pages of Western European newspapers accompanied by harsh criticism. But the Hungarian people will lose as, under the Tisza Party, “step by step,” everything that put Hungary on the map globally and in Washington is thrown out of the window: its sovereign foreign policy, its firm anti-woke position, and its investment-friendly economic policy.

The European Union is currently the most isolated major power centre in the world, in serious conflict with every major power, and every European government is suffering the negative political, social, economic and energy consequences of this confrontation. Those national governments that actively support this failed common foreign policy are particularly poor at representing the interests of their own citizens.

Madam Foreign Minister, this is going to be difficult.

text:
UPTOBER 2026: SEASONAL EDGE OR THE WRONG PART OF THE BITCOIN CYCLE?

Every year, as September ends, the same expression returns to the crypto market: “Uptober”.

There is a statistical reason for it. October has historically been one of Bitcoin’s strongest months. But seasonality is only one variable, and October 2026 arrives with BTC well beyond the immediate post-halving phase, interest rates moving higher again, oil above $100 and geopolitical risk still influencing inflation.

So the relevant question is not whether Uptober exists.

It is whether the conditions that produced previous Uptobers still exist today.

1️⃣ October genuinely has one of Bitcoin’s strongest historical records, although the sample remains relatively small. From 2013 through 2025, BTC finished October higher in 10 of 13 years. The average gain was roughly +19.1%, while the median was about +13.8%. Even the more recent period was impressive: from 2019 through 2024 Bitcoin produced six consecutive positive Octobers. That is enough to identify seasonality, but not enough to treat October as a mechanical trading signal. A few enormous early-cycle gains also inflate the historical average considerably.

2️⃣ October 2025 provided the perfect warning against turning seasonality into a belief system. Bitcoin reached a new all-time high above $126K early in the month, yet October eventually closed around 4% lower, breaking a positive streak that had lasted since 2019. A sudden escalation in U.S.–China tariff tensions triggered massive crypto liquidations while uncertainty over monetary policy intensified the risk-off move. In other words, even one of Bitcoin’s strongest seasonal months was overwhelmed by macroeconomics and politics. The calendar created a statistical tailwind; it did not protect the market from an external shock.

3️⃣ The most important difference in 2026 is where we are in the Bitcoin cycle. The April 2024 halving occurred approximately 29 months ago, while Bitcoin’s ~$126K high came almost one year ago. The usual “post-halving Uptober” comparison is therefore misleading. A more interesting historical comparison is with the later-cycle Octobers of 2014, 2018 and 2022, which occurred roughly two years or more after their respective halvings. Those months returned approximately -11.6%, -4.7% and +5.9%. It is a tiny sample and halving dates differ, but the average was actually negative. Cycle position has historically mattered at least as much as the month printed on the calendar.

4️⃣ Bitcoin is also entering October from a very different market structure than it entered the great Uptobers of 2017, 2020, 2021 or 2023. BTC currently trades around $83–84K, roughly one-third below the 2025 peak. September itself has been positive rather than producing the classic September washout that sometimes precedes a strong fourth-quarter recovery. This makes October 2026 less a story of price discovery and more a test of whether the market can transform a recovery from the post-ATH correction into a durable higher-timeframe trend.

5️⃣ The strongest argument in favour of another Uptober is institutional demand. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs absorbed approximately $2.39 billion during the September 21–25 week, their strongest weekly inflow of 2026, with positive flows across all five trading sessions. BlackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for about $1.16 billion. This is an important structural difference from older Bitcoin cycles. Before spot ETFs, institutional exposure was considerably more fragmented. Today there is a regulated channel capable of absorbing billions of dollars without retail investors necessarily displaying traditional signs of speculative euphoria.

6️⃣ The biggest argument against blindly expecting an Uptober is monetary policy. On September 16, the Federal Reserve raised the federal-funds target by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00%, explicitly stating that inflation remains elevated. The Fed’s September projections put 2026 PCE inflation around 3.7% and core PCE around 3.4%, well above the 2% objective. The next FOMC meeting falls on October 27–28, and markets are currently assigning a substantial probability to another rate increase. Bitcoin therefore enters October with the possibility that the month ends under tighter financial conditions than it begins.

7️⃣ Energy is the variable connecting geopolitics directly to Bitcoin. Brent has returned above $105 and briefly traded around $107 today as U.S.–Iran negotiations remain unresolved and uncertainty persists around Gulf energy flows. Higher energy prices feed transport, manufacturing and ultimately inflation, making it harder for central banks to ease monetary policy. At the same time, long-duration Treasury yields are moving higher; the U.S. 30-year yield is again around 5.5%. For a non-yielding, high-volatility asset such as BTC, rising real yields and a stronger dollar represent genuine competition for capital. An Uptober becomes much easier if oil falls than if another energy shock develops.

8️⃣ The political and social environment adds another volatility layer without necessarily determining market direction. The United States enters October only weeks away from the November 3 midterm elections, while household concern about the cost of living remains elevated. Meanwhile, Washington and Beijing have extended their trade truce into January and agreed to reduce tariffs on $60 billion of bilateral trade, reducing one immediate source of risk compared with October 2025. That is constructive, but the Iran conflict, energy costs and campaign-period policy announcements mean headline sensitivity is likely to remain unusually high. October 2026 is unlikely to be a month in which Bitcoin can ignore politics.

9️⃣ This creates two very different paths toward the end of October. The constructive scenario requires ETF inflows to remain persistent, oil to stabilize or retreat, bond yields to stop rising and BTC to continue absorbing long-term-holder supply without losing its recovery structure. Under those conditions, seasonality could become an amplifier rather than the original cause of the rally. The adverse scenario is equally clear: another oil shock, renewed inflation pressure, a more hawkish Fed and a reversal in ETF flows could recreate the mechanism that defeated Uptober in 2025. The month itself offers no protection against that combination.

🔟 My view is therefore constructive on the possibility of Uptober, but considerably more cautious about the narrative than the historical statistics alone would suggest. The 10-positive-Octobers-out-of-13 record deserves respect, yet October 2026 is occurring late in the current halving cycle and under tighter monetary conditions than most of the strongest historical examples. At the same time, ETF demand has introduced a source of structural buying that did not exist in previous late-cycle periods.

For me, this means October should be treated as a month with a historical statistical advantage, not as a forecast.

The strongest bullish case is not “October always goes up”. It is that seasonality, renewed institutional accumulation and an improving Bitcoin structure could reinforce one another if macro pressure begins to ease.

The strongest bearish case is that the cycle is already mature, real yields remain restrictive and geopolitical energy inflation forces central banks to keep tightening.

In previous cycles, liquidity generally decided which Bitcoin narrative survived.

I expect 2026 to be no different.

If BTC rises because capital returns, ETF demand persists and macro conditions improve, we may legitimately call it another Uptober.

If those conditions do not materialize, history has already shown that the calendar alone is not enough.

Seasonality can provide the wind.

It cannot decide where the ship goes.
