text:
Jamie Wall was sitting at Dulles International Airport, surrounded by six weeks of luggage from a trip covering the All Blacks through South Africa and the United States, and he was, in his own words, "f***ing almost crying." His flight home to New Zealand had already been cancelled. His passport was gone. It had slipped out of his shorts somewhere on the Silver Line Metro train, during a trip into Washington DC he'd taken just to pass the hours before his flight. Now he was looking at an embassy visit the next day and at least one more night stranded in the US.
Then his phone rang. It was a staff member from Air New Zealand, calling to say a man in Virginia had found the passport. "I was like, 'Oh, God, I love you,'" Wall said.

The man was Park Wollam, a retired army veteran and former State Department worker. He had picked up the passport off the train floor and, with nothing more than that document and Wall's boarding pass, spent an hour on hold with Air New Zealand trying to track down its owner. Wall put it simply enough afterward: "I can't think of a better person to find your lost passport than this guy because he'd literally spent a career issuing them and visas and stuff."

Wollam offered to bring the passport all the way out to Dulles, over an hour away by train. Wall wouldn't hear of it. "I said, 'No, please, you've already done enough.'" So instead, dragging his gear the whole way, he made his way to Wollam's front door in Alexandria, Virginia.

"I pulled up to the house, he opened the door, and he's like, 'Oh, you've walked all this way with all your gear,'" Wall recalled. Within minutes he was on the couch with a beer, watching the Washington Commanders play the Philadelphia Eagles, surrounded by people he'd met five minutes earlier. "All of a sudden I'm sitting on the couch with a beer," he said. "We just start talking, and they're all super friendly people. It was him, his wife, his two daughters and daughter's partner."
He got up to leave at halftime. They wouldn't let him. He stayed for the second half. Then he stayed the night.
The next morning, Wollam took him on a personal tour of Alexandria, past the high school that once fielded the 1971 football team that inspired the movie Remember the Titans. Back at the house, Wollam showed him a room full of memorabilia: antique weapons, and a photograph of his own father shaking hands with Raúl Castro. Park Wollam Sr. had been the American consul in Santiago de Cuba during the revolution, one of the diplomats who negotiated directly with Castro's brother over the release of kidnapped US citizens in 1958. "I was just like, man, this is fascinating," Wall said. "I'm not even going to bother going to a museum. I'm in one."

It struck Wall as almost funny that trouble had waited until the very last scheduled day of a six-week trip to find him. But he doesn't describe it as some sudden conversion, some door thrown open on humanity he hadn't believed in before.

"I have faith in humanity, so I wouldn't say it restored it," he said, "but it certainly made me feel pretty good about people and their kindness."

Separately, China's factory profits grew just 4.2% in August from a year earlier, down from 11.2% in July and the weakest this year, with energy costs among the reasons given.

text:
Brussels isn't passively waiting for London to change its mind. The aftermath from 2016 to 2020 left deep scars—constant brinkmanship over Article 50, heated disputes over the Irish Protocol, repeated UK attempts to undo signed agreements, and a domestic debate that saw the EU as both vital and adversarial. Officials may claim to keep an “open mind” if Britain seeks a customs union, but they firmly stress that the UK won't get a better deal than EU members or Norway and Switzerland. They reject cherry-picking and prioritize Ukraine’s accession, competitiveness, and industrial policy—making clear Britain won’t receive a second special status.
Any move toward rejoining or creating a comprehensive single-market or customs arrangement would look vastly different from 2015. It would resemble an accession, involving adopting the acquis, paying contributions, allowing free movement, ensuring dynamic alignment, and involving the Court—marking a substantial shift in relations. That’s why “polite hostility" aptly describes the current stance. The EU isn't afraid of Britain’s trading might; it fears another decade of exceptionalism, veto battles, and Britain leaving abruptly after the next election.
Beneath the rhetoric lie two key constraints:
Domestic politics. Burnham’s political position and regional dynamics explain why he avoids reopening the rejoin debate, even as others talk about reentry. Pledging to rejoin without a referendum would be seen as disguising a second referendum.
And then there’s the asymmetry of need. The UK demands access to SPS, youth mobility, electricity markets, and defence cooperation. Meanwhile, the EU has already secured most of its priorities through the Trade and Cooperation Agreement and Northern Ireland alignment. It can afford to wait and set the terms for access.
The reality is clear: the notion that “Britain’s future is European” remains a British declaration, not an EU offer. Until London explicitly clarifies what it’s willing to accept regarding movement, finances, judicial cooperation, and replacing the pound with the euro—and until Brussels feels the wounds have healed enough to reopen negotiations—the goal isn’t a treaty but just words today.

A DRIVER’S PERSPECTIVE | MONDAY TRUCKING BRIEF
September 28, 2026

DRIVERLESS TRUCKING

Kodiak is running daily preparation trips between Dallas and Houston and says it plans to remove the safety observer by year’s end. Right now, a person is still in the cab. Its new Fresno–Los Angeles produce runs in California also have a safety driver.

These trucks are hauling freight, but Kodiak has not launched driver-out service on either route. My question is what happens to the driving jobs already there, especially on Dallas–Houston, a lane that can offer steady work and home time.

Kodiak and PrePass have also begun connecting autonomous-truck inspection results with roadside screening in Texas and Louisiana. Which inspection sites can use that process today? And what happens when an unmanned truck needs an inspector or mechanic at the roadside?

DIESEL AND FREIGHT

AAA puts the national diesel average at $6.4531 a gallon today, down from $6.5107 a week ago. That is relief from the September 22 record, but the cost is still heavy. At 6.7 mpg, the national pump average equals about 96 cents per mile for fuel alone, before discounts.

Are fuel payments keeping pace with what drivers actually pay?

DAT’s latest dry van spot linehaul average was $2.17 a mile, down 3 cents for the week. That figure excludes fuel. ATA also reported that August for-hire truck tonnage fell from both July and a year earlier.

Higher rates on some lanes do not automatically mean more freight is moving. For a small carrier or owner-operator, the number that matters is what remains after fuel, empty miles, and the rest of the operating bill.

DRIVER LABOR

Attorneys say they now represent at least 45 Mexican commercial drivers alleging deceptive recruitment and coercive working conditions involving a recruiter and several carriers. Twenty-nine are plaintiffs in a pending federal lawsuit. Those allegations have not been proven in court, and carriers dispute liability.

The records worth examining are the recruitment promises, dispatch instructions, handling of drivers’ documents, deductions, and settlement statements. Who controlled the work, and who benefited from it?

REGULATORY WATCH

FMCSA’s fuel-hauler hours-of-service waiver remains in effect through December 16. Eligible drivers may drive up to 16 hours in a 24-hour period under its conditions. The waiver also says a carrier must allow a driver who requests immediate rest to find a safe place to stop and take at least 10 consecutive hours off duty. That protection deserves as much attention as the longer driving limit.

The three leads I’m following this week: the jobs behind the Dallas–Houston driverless plan; what high diesel prices leave in a driver’s settlement; and who controlled the working conditions alleged in the Mexican drivers’ case.

— Will Cook
A Driver’s Perspective

Kirk Bangstad, owner of Minocqua Brewing Company in Wisconsin, says his Madison taproom will likely close by the end of the year after state officials revoked the company’s alcohol permits, a fallout from a Facebook post pledging free beer on the day President Donald Trump d*es.

The brewery, known for selling politically themed beers such as “Resistance Pilsner,” posted in January that it would offer “free beer, all day long, the day he d*es,” adding that customers should show the post “when it happens in a few months and we’ll make good on that promise.” The Wisconsin Department of Revenue moved in July to revoke the company’s Brewer’s permits at two locations and an Alcohol Beverage Warehouse permit at a third, with the revocation set to take effect August 4. Officials said the action followed the seizure of canned beer from the company in June, which regulators alleged had been transported from Illinois without the required permits and taxes paid.

A spokesperson for the department said the state’s Division of Alcohol Beverages is “dedicated to the fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverages regulations in Wisconsin” and that it is “required to follow and implement state law, including ensuring permit holders and licensees follow all applicable laws and regulations.” Bangstad, a liberal activist who also runs a progressive super PAC, has rejected the state’s rationale and said in a Substack post that he was “not taking this lying down,” adding that officials would “have to pry me out of my taprooms before I stop selling beer to thirsty progressives who come to visit us.” He has set up a legal defense fund and vowed to fight the revocation “tooth and nail.”

Bangstad has said he believes the state is targeting the brewery over its politics, while the Department of Revenue maintains the action is tied strictly to alleged transport and tax violations. The dispute remains unresolved as the Madison taproom’s future hangs in the balance.

Upside vol in tech is trading at the bottom of its range, which changes how I'd play a breakout.

One-month vol on the Qs is down around 18 and a half and three-month's about 20. In the summer both of those were mid to high twenties. Two-month vol is cheap on the box plot too, and the upside strikes are priced at the lowest vol on the surface as usual.

So exposure to a break higher is being offered cheaply, with the index sitting right on the cusp of one.

That's where I'd look at a call ratio backspread. Sell the 40 delta call, buy two of the 20 delta behind it, costs next to nothing. No delta today, and if we break it buys itself delta and vega as it goes. If the vega reprices a couple of vols higher on the move, you get paid twice.

The risk is we grind up and vol gets offered into it. With the next round of mega-cap earnings coming I don't think that's the likely path in tech, but that's the thing that would make me wrong.

Markets are opening the week on softer footing, with early selling pressure developing as elevated oil prices remain front and center. Higher energy prices can quickly revive inflation concerns, so traders will be watching whether crude continues to push higher—and whether that starts to pressure rate-sensitive growth stocks and broader risk appetite.  This week’s macro narrative will likely be driven by any fresh U.S.–China headlines, particularly around trade policy, technology restrictions, tariffs, and supply-chain developments. These headlines can create fast rotations across semiconductors, industrials, energy, China-exposed names, and the broader tech complex.  The other major catalyst is Micron (MU) earnings later this week. MU has become an important read-through for the AI infrastructure trade, especially demand for high-bandwidth memory, data-center spending, and the broader semiconductor cycle. A strong report and constructive outlook could reinforce momentum in chips and AI-related leaders; disappointment could spark a more meaningful shakeout after a strong run.  My focus remains on the market’s current leadership. AI names have controlled the tape for much of the past month, and until that relative strength breaks down, that is still where I want to concentrate my watchlist. Rather than forcing trades during early weakness, I’ll be watching for:  AI leaders holding key support and showing relative strength versus the indexes  Semiconductors reacting constructively into and after MU earnings  Whether oil strength broadens into energy-sector leadership or becomes a drag on the overall market  U.S.–China headlines that could trigger quick sector rotations  Pullbacks that offer controlled-risk entries rather than chasing extended momentum  The key question is whether this is simply a routine pullback within an AI-led uptrend—or the beginning of a broader shift in market leadership.

Overall Bias

My bullish bias remains intact heading into Micron’s earnings report this week. MU has the potential to be a major catalyst for an already red-hot memory and semiconductor trade, especially as investors continue to focus on AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory, DRAM, NAND, and data-center infrastructure.  A strong quarter—and, more importantly, upbeat forward guidance—could add fresh fuel to the group and reinforce the current momentum across chip leaders. Micron’s commentary on AI memory demand, supply discipline, pricing trends, and hyperscaler spending will likely matter just as much as the headline earnings numbers.  I’ll be watching MU closely for a constructive reaction after the report, along with relative strength across the broader semiconductor complex. text:
Podcast Summary | Huberman Lab: What Humans, Animals and Plants Tell Us About Consciousness | Michael Pollan

Overview
Consciousness remains one of science’s deepest unsolved problems, and the common assumption that it simply emerges from brain complexity lacks strong support. Michael Pollan explores an alternative: the brain may channel or receive consciousness rather than generate it, much like a radio or television receiver. Drawing on plants, animals, microbes, and psychedelics, the conversation widens the question of who or what is conscious, how sentience differs from self-awareness, and why the mind-body split is increasingly untenable. The through-line is practical as much as philosophical: humility about what we know, and a willingness to test mystical insight against its usefulness.

Key Themes
- Consciousness is poorly understood, and the idea that it is an emergent property of brain complexity lacks strong traction; a receiver or filter model remains a serious alternative.
- Subjectivity is the common criterion: if there is something it is like to be a creature, that creature is conscious.
- Sentience and consciousness are distinct; sentience may be widespread across life, while elaborated self-awareness and metacognition appear narrower.
- Plants display flexible problem-solving, roughly twenty senses, and responses to anesthetics, challenging purely reflexive or genetically programmed explanations.
- Self versus other recognition recurs as a key organizing rule across cells, neurons, roots, and organisms.
- Psychedelics can produce ego dissolution or ego inflation; dissolution offers perspective on the ego but is not a permanent state.
- Homeostatic feelings in the brain stem, not cortical thought, may be where consciousness begins, implying far more conscious animals than cortex-centered theories allow.
- The microbiome influences mood, sociability, and behavior, framing humans and microbes as engaged in a two-way street.
- Hope must be deliberately built into dark stories about food and environment, because people need hope to act.

Detailed Summary
Neuroscientists were historically discouraged from studying consciousness, which was considered risky or career-damaging unless one was already established. Thomas Nagel’s essay “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” supplied a durable criterion: if there is something it is like to be a creature, it is conscious. Subjectivity, not intelligence or complexity, sits at the center of the definition.

A distinction is drawn between sentience and consciousness. Sentience is basic awareness and response to environment and may be universal, a property of life potentially including plants and single-celled creatures. Consciousness is described as how humans do sentience, with added capabilities such as self-awareness, metacognition, and emotion. Human consciousness may not be the universal standard; different creatures may have consciousness shaped by their body, senses, and scale in time and space.

Bacteria can sense light, distinguish morning from evening, and use chemotaxis to tell nutrients from toxins. A corn plant can navigate a maze to find the fastest path to ammonium nitrate fertilizer in a corner. Plants react to the sound of caterpillars chewing by sending toxins or bad-tasting chemicals to the affected leaf, detect running water through a pipe and grow toward it, and possess around twenty senses compared with five or six in humans. Venus fly traps under anesthetic gas such as xenon do not clamp down when an insect crosses their threshold. Anesthetics remain poorly understood even in humans, and the speaker avoids calling the resulting state a loss of consciousness, describing it instead as a loss of sentience.

Simple rules build immense complexity. Nerve cells grow as far as possible, connect with as many other nerve cells as possible, and distinguish self from other. Dendrites and axons form elegant architectures through self-avoidance, branching away when too close to their own branches. Tree roots use similar rules, producing tiled systems where no tree or neuron gets too much space. Related plants may share soil and grow together, while unrelated plants of the same species compete. Plants shaded by other plants grow fast to get above them, but plants shaded by themselves do not compete in the same way. The speaker calls self and other a key rule while questioning how it leads to consciousness.

Consciousness can occur without a self. Meditation, psychedelics, and the moments after waking are offered as examples. A period of roughly five hundred milliseconds after waking precedes the self reconstituting, and in a hotel room it can stretch to around seven hundred fifty milliseconds. Plant medicine communities and people who spend time in jungles may hold real understanding of cross-species communication, though the speaker does not claim personal experience. Most drugs were originally bioprospected from jungle plants and other plants. Plants can sense humans and be poisonous, delicious, nourishing, or wonderful. The speaker’s mother, a rational gardener, believes talking to plants affects the relationship without believing plants understand language.

A psilocybin experience produced the feeling that garden plants were conscious, aware, benevolent, and returning his gaze. William James is cited for the idea that mystical insights are hard to verify but can be judged by usefulness or treated as hypotheses. This pragmatic turn led to studying plant intelligence and sentience. Domesticated plants manipulate human desires at the species level: corn dominates landscapes because it figured out what humans wanted through trial and error, and cannabis spread globally after producing THC. Coffee and tea chemicals are likely defense chemicals that alter consciousness rather than simply kill, because killing a host outright would select for resistance. A cat named Frank forgot where the catnip was, which the speaker frames as a plant strategy. Many psychoactive plant chemicals diminish appetite, another apparent strategy.

Dogs descend from wolves that benefited from patience and scavenging, leading to domestication and an expansion of breeds; only about fifty thousand wolves remain in the country, contrasted with far more dogs, now mostly family members rather than workers. Humans are said to be unique in self-awareness and the ability to imagine a future they are not in, while dogs may time travel only minutes or perhaps half an hour. Much brain activity is unconscious, monitoring the body and adjusting interoceptive signals without awareness. Social complexity is offered as a persuasive evolutionary explanation for why awareness rose above automatic response.

Michael Levin, a biologist at TUS, creates organoids and xenobots and studies behavior not dictated by genes. Xenobots made from tadpole skin cells clump into a new organism lasting about a week or two, repurpose cilia for locomotion, and can be conditioned and navigated through mazes. The word instinct is heard less often in biology now. Cesar Millan described growing up in a poor rural environment with frequent death, high stakes, and low resources, producing heightened instincts about safety and a strong ability to read people and animals.

Justin Sonnenberg’s microbiome work is cited for the claim that microbiota create critical chemicals for brain health and influence whether people feel sick, energetic, or outgoing. Microbial exchange occurs through handshakes, kissing, and exchanging bills or credit cards. Humans carry more bacterial genes than human genes and depend on them. Bacteria make metabolites including glutamate, GABA, serotonin, and short-chain fatty acids that fuel the brain and calm mood. The relationship is a two-way street: microbes influence us, while humans have outsourced production of useful metabolites to them. A nature documentary example describes male lions fighting, then one helping fight off hyenas attacking the other, illustrating a dynamic redefinition of us. The ventromedial hypothalamus is a shared structure in mice, humans, and lions.

Antonio Damasio and Mark Solms are cited for a theory that consciousness begins with feeling in the brain stem, not thought in the cortex. Homeostatic feelings such as hunger, warmth, cold, and itch register in the upper brain stem, with the cortex helping afterward by visualizing actions like finding food. William James described a spike in heart rate occurring first, then the brain labeling it fear. Some children are born without a cortex, and decorticated animals reportedly show expressions and behaviors suggesting conscious experience despite an inability to report emotion. Lisa Feldman Barrett is cited for the idea that cultures with many words for types of sadness allow more nuanced emotional labeling. Language labels for emotion are top-down, culturally created, and can shape how bodily sensations are interpreted. Children in meltdowns may not know whether they are hungry or tired until a parent helps them interpret the signals.

Body-to-brain traffic via the vagus nerve is stated as roughly eighty percent, while descending projections are about fifteen to twenty percent. Stress hormones and inflammation change mood and make people feel threatened. In one study, people given powdered ginger were less judgmental about morally repellent written scenarios, including incest and eating one’s dog. Ginger calms the stomach, and the result is used to argue that moral disgust is processed partly through digestive organs, making the mind-body split increasingly untenable.

Ego is described as a defensive structure; the self is a defense. In a high-dose psilocybin experience, the speaker saw himself explode into blue post-it notes that coalesced into blue paint, observed with total equanimity and no subject-object distinction, and merged with a Bach unaccompanied cello suite being played by the guide, becoming the music rather than listening to it. The legacy is more perspective on the ego, recognizing when it is being too critical, aggressive, or self-interested. Dacher Keltner’s awe experiment found participants drew themselves about a third smaller after an awe experience such as river rafting. Society celebrates the self while some of the happiest experiences involve escaping it. Sense of self is necessary to complete long projects but is also described as a trap.

The brain constructs an abstraction of reality from limited sensory inputs, while filter theories associated with Henri Bergson and Aldous Huxley hold that consciousness exists outside the brain as a field, with the brain and senses reducing it to what survival requires. Huxley described a reducing valve admitting only a measly trickle. The speaker does not dismiss panpsychism or a consciousness field, citing the lack of traction for emergent brain complexity. Christof Koch, a physicalist and former head of the Allen Brain Institute, had an ayahuasca experience and became convinced consciousness exists outside brains; the speaker respects this view more than before but is not personally convinced. The brain-as-computer metaphor breaks down, since silicon computers are unlikely to be conscious and a simulated feeling is not the same as a real feeling. Norbert Wiener warned that the price of metaphor is eternal vigilance.

Neuron experiments defied the expectation that a specific firing sequence is necessary for a behavior: replaying captured neurons in the same sequence produced the same behavior, but backward or all-at-once replay also produced it. The same neurons participate in multiple memories, which may be efficient and redundant, but the brain’s encoding of experience remains poorly understood. Gardening began at age four or five when the speaker planted watermelon seeds, forgot them, and later found a watermelon that had dropped and splattered; by age eight there was a garden and strawberries sold in Dixie cups. Gardening forces active decisions and recognition that plants have interests. About eight percent of the American landscape has been protected, and the speaker criticizes attempts to open protected lands in Utah, noting hunters and fishermen are angered because promised protections were threatened. Americans tend to think of nature as either virgin or abused, a strong binary, and need to learn how to behave on the remaining ninety-two percent of the landscape.

The industrial beef system is described as pathological: corn makes animals sick, requiring pharmaceuticals, and the chain floats on a sea of oil. A butcher on College Avenue in Oakland told the speaker he was the sixth person that week to ask for grass-fed beef after an eight-thousand-word piece following one cow from insemination to slaughter, later a chapter in Omnivore’s Dilemma. Progress on psychedelics has been faster than on food because there was less opposition; Rick Perry, a self-described knuckle-dragging Republican into heart medicine, works across the aisle for veteran access to psychedelics for PTSD and substance abuse. The food movement was once coded as left-liberal and elitist, criticism that is less common now as right-leaning figures support similar goals, including agreement on pesticides and removing ultraprocessed food from schools. Policy keeps bad food cheap while subsidizing corn and high fructose corn syrup, and the speaker argues healthy food must become cheaper relative to unhealthy food.

The current administration’s emphasis on healthy eating is described as mostly rhetorical: it has not regulated the food system and has cut farm-to-school and small and regenerative agriculture support. The only food-related change cited is voluntary removal of some cereal dyes, which the speaker considers minor. RFK Jr. is credited with surfacing a constituency of mothers focused on clean food and food as medicine. Cooperation between the food movement and MAHA activists stripped pesticide-industry lawsuit exemptions from an appropriations bill twice. Psychedelic policy is advancing through fast-tracked executive action: MDMA and psilocybin are described as close to FDA approval, with ibogaine already fast-tracked. Approval would be a societal earthquake, prompting questions about who they are for and requiring public education about risks. Cannabis is a cautionary example, since wider use has revealed addiction and psychosis risks, and psychedelics carry real risks for people predisposed to psychosis or with heart issues.

text:
A much longer explanation by Grok if you care to read: Trump appears in the Epstein-related court records, flight logs, emails, and later DOJ/FBI document dumps for a handful of documented, overlapping reasons—not because he was charged or placed on any verified “client list.”

**Social circle and documented contact (1990s–early 2000s)**  
Trump and Epstein moved in the same Palm Beach and New York social world for years. They were photographed together, and Trump publicly called Epstein a “terrific guy” in a 2002 interview. Flight logs and a 2020 prosecutor email show Trump listed as a passenger on Epstein’s jet at least eight times between 1993 and 1996. Some of those flights included his then-wife Marla Maples and children Eric and Tiffany; others included Ghislaine Maxwell. One 1993 flight lists only Epstein and Trump; another lists Epstein, Trump, and a redacted 20-year-old. Being on the plane is not itself evidence of a crime. Trump later said he was never on the plane; the logs contradict that specific claim.

**Mar-a-Lago and Virginia Giuffre**  
Giuffre (then Virginia Roberts) was working as a spa attendant at Mar-a-Lago around 2000 when Maxwell recruited her. Trump has said he banned Epstein from the club because Epstein was taking staff, including Giuffre. Giuffre herself described meeting Trump once at the club, said he was friendly and offered to help her find babysitting work, and consistently stated she never saw him at Epstein’s homes, never accused him of abuse, and did not believe he knew about Epstein’s crimes. That is her sworn and published account.

**Epstein’s own emails**  
In messages released from Epstein’s estate, he wrote that Trump “knew about the girls as he asked Ghislaine to stop” and that Giuffre “spent hours at my house with him” and that Trump was “the dog that hasn’t barked.” Those are Epstein’s words, written years later. The “knew about the girls / asked Ghislaine to stop” line is consistent with Trump’s stated reason for cutting Epstein off (recruiting Mar-a-Lago staff). It is not independent proof of knowledge of sex trafficking.

**Later FBI tips and interview notes**  
Larger 2025–2026 DOJ releases contain thousands of Trump mentions. A large share are news clippings, forwarded articles, and duplicate files. A smaller set consists of unverified public tips to the FBI (some submitted around the 2020 election) and interview notes, including uncorroborated assault claims. The Justice Department has described many of those claims as unfounded and sensationalist. No federal charges were brought against Trump in connection with Epstein.

**Palm Beach police contact**  
In a 2019 FBI interview, former Palm Beach police chief Michael Reiter recalled that Trump called him around 2006 after the local Epstein investigation became public, saying he was glad authorities were “stopping him” because “everyone has known he’s been doing this,” and that Trump was among the first people to contact police. That account, if accurate, undercuts a claim of total ignorance but is not a confession of participation.

**Bottom line**  
Trump is in the files because he was a known social associate, flew on the plane, owned the club where one prominent victim was recruited, was discussed by Epstein in emails, and generated news coverage and later unsolicited tips. High raw mention counts are inflated by clippings and repeats. Presence in the documents is not the same as proven criminal involvement; no court has found him liable in the Epstein cases.

text:
how to run AI slideshows profitably on TikTok:

a reel gets one shot.

a slideshow gets re-served to people who scrolled past it, so one upload gets several distribution windows.

they also pull the highest save rates on the platform, and DM shares weigh even more.

pick the format by the signal you want:

1/ hear me out, comment debate
2/ non-negotiables, saves
3/ green flags, sends
4/ ranked list, full swipes
5/ before and after, saves and comments

slides run on GPT Image 2.5 Flare, which OpenAI built for high volume social content.

every slide loads the same 4 references:

- character
- aesthetic baseline
- scene
- slide template

that's what stops the drift that makes automated slideshows obvious.

any slide with a face gets 6 to 8 variants, judged on realism, detail, and whether it reads as a real person in 2 seconds cold.

at 30 slideshows a day that's around 240 slides, generated in parallel batches.

9:16 at 1080x1920, text upper or center, since the eye enters from the top on every swipe.

bold, high contrast, bigger than feels right.

slide 1 is the hook, specific enough that the right viewer feels called out.

slide 2 is also a hook, because TikTok can serve the slideshow starting there.

"if you scrolled past, here's why this matters for your situation..."

a slide 2 that only works as a continuation loses every one of those re-served impressions.

slides 3 through 8 carry 1 idea each, every line pulling to the next swipe.

the last slide captures:

- 1 obvious keyword
- 1 question about their situation
- 1 specific promised thing

"comment SKINCARE and tell me your biggest struggle this year, i'll send the exact routine."

the keyword captures the lead and the question produces a real comment, both off 1 action.

and the free thing has to be genuinely good, since a thin PDF teaches people your keywords aren't worth typing.

then trending audio matched to the tone, which takes 10 to 15 minutes per batch.

distribution runs 10 accounts at 3 a day, staggered 30 to 90 minutes apart.

each on an isolated cloud phone, dedicated US proxy locked to a state, matched Google and Play Store region, non-VOIP number.

every new account runs the 4 week warmup, engagement only first, then 1 a day, then 2, then full.

accounts that post at volume on day 1 get suppressed in ways that don't recover.

the first 18 hours tell you almost everything.

strong saves and DM shares in the first 6 usually mean it keeps distributing for days.

new accounts get a geo check within hours, and anything under 80% US gets sorted before the account posts again.

keyword comments go into a 3 stage DM sequence:

1/ deliver what you promised, no pitch
2/ ask one question about their situation
3/ route the qualified ones to the offer

anything that clears the bar gets 5 variations the same day, keeping the format and CTA, changing the details.

1 winner turns into 6 to 12 pieces, and a strong week turns into a strong month.

text:
I found @MarcNovicoff's article about universal child care disappointingly one-dimensional. The entire premise rests on the idea that "universal child care" is defined by Dems as licensed centers, then he hand-waves away in a single paragraph the fact that two major Dem proposals have come out in just the past few months that directly contradict that. (Setting aside that center-only is factually incorrect -- current law and all child care proposals on the table include some form of support for family child care homes and family/friends caregivers -- using a Nancy Pelosi quote from 2012 to help make one's point suggests maybe one is reaching?)

There's also no engagement with the empirical evidence we now have of the popularity of current quasi-universal systems like those in New Mexico and Vermont. Similarly, no engagement with the fact that we offer all sorts of universal services that are proportionally used more by the affluent-- well-off people use the library much more than poor people, e.g. -- and that we have universal services that are offered across the board including to those who could easily pay (public schools). 

Novicoff would prefer just giving cash to families, ignoring the fact that any policy analyst will tell you it's all well and good if you want to do that as one part of a larger strategy, but unless the cash you're handing out is $15,000-20,000 or more per child (I argued for something along those lines as a thought experiment in my first book, but one has to name the level of per-person cash it would take!), you're not going to have any licensed programs left, and therefore no true choices for families.

There's a thoughtful article to be written about the nuanced politics and policy surrounding universal child care. I wish this would have been that, but alas.

text:
John Schnatter sold the car he loved to keep his father's bar from closing.

He grew up in Jeffersonville, Indiana, where his father was a judge who also co-owned a tavern called Mick's Lounge.

At 16 he was washing dishes and cooking pizzas at a local sub shop, and he spent $1,600 of what he earned on a gold 1971 Camaro Z28, then rebuilt the engine and brakes himself.

He has said the car got him through high school and college.

By 1983 he had a business degree and the family tavern was close to going under, so he sold the Camaro for $2,800 and put the money against his father's debts.

What was left went into $1,600 worth of used restaurant equipment.

Then he knocked out the broom closet at the back of the bar, put an oven inside it, and started selling pizzas to the people already drinking there.

The pizza did $600 its first week, then $1,500, then $3,000, and inside 14 months the business went from bankrupt to clearing over $100,000 a year.

Papa John's went public in 1993 with 232 stores, when Schnatter was 31.

In 2009 he offered a $250,000 reward for anyone who could find the Camaro, somebody did, and he paid it.

text:
Mainstream media is starting to fall in love with General Matter.

There is just one rather important detail:

We still don’t know how the company actually plans to enrich all that uranium.

Reuters was writing about General Matter before the company had really emerged from stealth. Bloomberg followed. Now Politico is profiling the startup and its plan to bring the “SpaceX playbook” to uranium enrichment.

It is an incredible story.

General Matter was only founded in 2024.

Since then, it has secured a 100-acre site at the former Paducah enrichment complex, received a $900M milestone-based DOE task order to build HALEU capacity and landed EXIM letters of interest supporting up to $4.2B of potential financing for Japanese and South Korean buyers of its enriched uranium.

Politico now reports that General Matter offered DOE an eventual 355 metric tons of HALEU capacity per year.

For comparison, Centrus initially proposed 12 metric tons per year under its own $900M award.

So you can understand why the story sells.

Former SpaceX engineer.
Peter Thiel backing.
Billions in potential government support.
America rebuilding its nuclear fuel supply chain.
A huge enrichment plant in Kentucky.

There is only one strange part.

General Matter still hasn’t publicly disclosed what enrichment technology it intends to use.

Centrifuges? Lasers? Something else?

The company describes its technology as proprietary. And that leaves investors in the unusual position of watching billions of dollars in potential government-backed support pile up around a company before the public can properly evaluate the technology at the center of the whole story.

Maybe General Matter really can do what it says.

But mainstream coverage doesn’t make the technical questions disappear.

That is exactly why I wrote:

“General Matter Looks Like America’s New Enricher. Look Again.”

I went through the DOE award, the licensing trail, the huge financing headlines and, most importantly, what we actually know about the technology General Matter intends to use.

Because before getting excited about 355 tonnes of future HALEU production, I’d first like to understand the machine that is supposed to produce it.

text:
Bernie.

"Join me in California to demand that billionaires finally pay their fair share and help elect strong progressives to Congress."

Oh, I will be joining you, Senator. Right here. In the replies. Pull up a chair. Bring a snack. This is going to take a while, and honestly, you earned every word of it.

Let me start with the thing I noticed first, before I even read the posters. Three likes. THREE. One repost. And right underneath it, X helpfully shows your post from yesterday, "THEY WANT IT ALL," sitting there with almost nine thousand likes and four hundred thousand views. So the angry slogan went viral, and the actual invitation to show up somewhere got three likes. Bernie, even your own fans read "Bakersfield, Sunday night" and went, "Yeah... I'm good." That's not a movement. That's a group chat where everybody leaves you on read.

Now let's look at those posters, because somebody on your staff clearly had a lot of fun with them.

"FIGHTING OLIGARCHY." In big bubbly rainbow letters. Each syllable in its own little colored circle. Fi. Gh. Ti. Ng. Bernie, that's not a political poster. That's the cover of a kids' cereal box. That's a birthday party invitation for a seven-year-old. I half expected a coupon for a free Happy Meal at the bottom. You're telling America the billionaires are an existential threat to the republic, and your graphic designer went with the same font as a bounce-house rental company.

And there's a DJ set. From Cuco. Nothing says "the working class is rising up against the oligarchy" like a DJ set on a Sunday night in a high school auditorium. The billionaires must be shaking in their yachts. "Sir, they're bringing a DJ." "Good heavens. Sell everything."

"Where We Go From Here." Bernie, I've been watching you ask that question for ten years. I'll answer it for you, since nobody else will. Where do the billionaires go from here? Nevada. Texas. Florida. Tennessee. Realtors up around Lake Tahoe have been talking for months about wealthy Californians buying just across the state line, where there's no state income tax and no wealth tax. Where do the JOBS go from here? Same moving truck. Where do YOU go from here? The next auditorium, with the next poster, telling the next crowd the billionaires were even more arrogant this time. It's not a movement. It's a subscription service.

Harvey Auditorium at Bakersfield High School, doors open at 4. Senator, I teach high school. I know what a high school auditorium on a Sunday night smells like. It smells like floor wax and a band concert nobody wanted to attend. You're 85 years old, flying in on donor money, to speak in the same room where the sophomores do the spring musical. Bless you. I mean that.

And then the second poster. "BALLOT OVER BILLIONAIRES." Monday, October 5. The Novo in downtown L.A. And standing right there next to you, in the nice suit, smiling like he just found a twenty in his jacket... Ro Khanna.

Oh, Bernie. Bernie, Bernie, Bernie. You put RO KHANNA on a poster that says "Ballot over Billionaires"?

Ro Khanna is one of the richest people in the entire United States Congress. His own household financial disclosures report assets somewhere in the range of 69 million to more than 167 million dollars, and some analyses of those same filings put it even higher. A huge chunk of it comes from his wife's family business. And those disclosures show a whole mountain of stock trades.

So let me get this straight. The poster that's supposed to rally working people against wealthy elites features one of the wealthiest men in Congress, standing next to a guy with three houses, in a rented concert venue in downtown Los Angeles. The only thing missing from that picture is a yacht in the background and a caption that says "Solidarity."

That's like holding an anti-sugar rally sponsored by Krispy Kreme. That's like a vegan protest catered by Texas Roadhouse. You didn't put a working-class hero on that poster, Bernie. You put the guy the poster is supposed to be ABOUT, and you just hoped nobody would check his disclosures.

I check. That's kind of my whole job.

Now, is Ro a billionaire? No. He's "only" worth somewhere between tens of millions and a couple hundred million. But here's the point, Senator. Prop 40 sets the line at a billion because that conveniently draws the line right above everybody on your stage. That's the whole trick. The people writing the tax always, ALWAYS draw the line one inch above their own heads. Every single time. When the income tax started in 1913, it was one percent and only hit the richest Americans. They promised it would never reach the working man. Now it's taken out of nearly every paycheck in the country before the worker ever sees it. The line always moves down. It never, ever moves up. And the people who drew it are always standing safely on the other side of it, smiling on a poster.

And the woman on that second poster, Jane Kim, is running for California Insurance Commissioner. That's wonderful. I've got a question for her, and I mean this sincerely. Can you explain to the families in California why State Farm stopped writing new homeowner policies there? Why so many insurers pulled back from the state? Because I promise you, a family in Paradise or Altadena who can't get fire insurance is a lot more worried about THAT than about Sergey Brin's stock portfolio.

And Randy Villegas, school board member, running for Congress. Randy, I'm a teacher, so let me say this one gently. When the tax base packs up and leaves a state, you know which budget gets cut first? The one YOU sit on. Schools. Every single time. Ask Illinois. Ask New Jersey. Ask Detroit. When people who pay the bills leave, the kids are the ones who feel it.

Now let's get to the actual words in your post, because they're even worse than the fonts.

"FAIR SHARE"

Bernie, you keep saying "fair share" like it's a unit of measurement. Like it's in the metric system. It's not. It's a mood. It's a feeling. It's a bumper sticker with a Senate pension.

So let me give you the actual measurement, since you never do.

The bottom half of American taxpayers pay about 3 percent of all federal income taxes. Three percent. The top 10 percent pay somewhere around three quarters of the entire bill. And the top 1 percent, the people you've spent an entire career turning into cartoon villains, pay roughly 40 percent of ALL federal income taxes by themselves.

So when the crowd in Bakersfield starts chanting "make them pay their fair share," what a lot of that room is actually chanting is "raise taxes on the people who already pay almost everything, so I can keep paying almost nothing." That's not a moral awakening, Bernie. That's a free lunch with a DJ set.

How much is fair? Fifty percent? Sixty? Ninety? You never say. You never, ever say. You could eat a bowl of alphabet soup and spell out a better economic plan than "a rally said so."

"BILLIONAIRES FINALLY PAY"

Prop 40 is a one-time 5 percent tax on the total net worth of Californians worth over a billion dollars. Not their income. Their NET WORTH. The paper value of their stock. Stuff they never sold and never got a dime from.

Bernie, unrealized is not a loophole. It's a word with a definition. It means it hasn't happened yet. Nobody pays income tax on a number that isn't income yet. That's how it's worked for over a hundred years. For you. For me. For the kid in the third row who actually does the reading. Taxing somebody's unsold stock is like me sending you a bill for sales tax on a house I'm only thinking about buying. You're pretty much like a rock, Senator, only dumber, because at least a rock doesn't send out fundraising emails.

And here's the part nobody at the Novo is going to hear. To pay a 5 percent tax on your stock, you have to SELL your stock. Billions of dollars of it, all at once. Who else owns that stock? Every teacher's pension in California. CalPERS. CalSTRS. Every nurse and firefighter with a 401(k). When somebody is forced to dump a mountain of shares, the price drops, and the retired teacher in Fresno watches her pension take the hit. You're going to "help" working families by shrinking their retirement accounts. Please stop helping. We can't afford it.

And because it's a ONE-TIME tax, you get one bucket of water. One. And your own post from last week said you wanted it to keep 3 million people's health care going. Health care is a monthly bill, Bernie. You don't pay a monthly bill with a one-time windfall. That's like selling your truck to pay the rent and calling it a retirement plan. Next year the bucket's dry and you're back in Bakersfield with a new poster and a new DJ.

Wait. A temporary pile of money for health care, with a cliff at the end, that working families fall right off of... where have I seen that before? Oh, right. The temporary COVID Obamacare subsidies. The ones you voted for in the American Rescue Plan and extended in the Inflation Reduction Act. The ones DEMOCRATS wrote the expiration date on. Not one Republican voted for either bill. So when premiums jumped this year and your whole party ran screaming to the cameras, that was YOUR cliff. And now you want to build another one in California. Bernie, you'd trip over a cordless phone.

"THE BILLIONAIRE CLASS WIELDS ENORMOUS POWER"

And we already know how this movie ends, because the whole world has already watched it.

France had a wealth tax. Wealthy people and their money left in such numbers that President Macron scrapped most of it in 2018. Sweden got rid of theirs back in 2007. Germany stopped collecting theirs back in the '90s. Norway still has one, and in recent years wealthy Norwegians have been packing up and moving to Switzerland in record numbers. The projected revenue evaporates. The companies move. The jobs follow the moving truck. Every time.

And moving from California to Nevada is a whole lot easier than moving from France to Switzerland. It's a four-hour drive. You don't even need a passport. Tesla's headquarters already left for Texas. SpaceX left. X left. Oracle left years ago. Texas already took California's spot as the state with the most Fortune 500 headquarters. That wasn't a wealth tax. That was just the regular California tax bill. And you want to pile a wealth tax on top.

The Hoover Institution went through Prop 40 person by person and found that roughly 30 percent of the wealth it's aimed at was already out of reach because of people and assets that already moved. California's own nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office warned the state could lose ongoing income tax revenue every single year from the people who leave. So you get one smaller bucket now, and a permanent leak in the roof. That's the plan. That's the whole plan. You're not fighting oligarchy, Bernie. You're running a lab that's already failed six times and asking for a seventh try.

In my classroom, when a student runs the same experiment six times, gets the same disaster six times, and asks to run it a seventh time exactly the same way, I've only got two options. Either the kid isn't the brightest bulb on the porch, or the disaster is the result he's actually after.

Here's something else. Your OWN SIDE is trying to kill Prop 40. Gavin Newsom, your party's governor, the same guy who never met a tax he didn't love, OPPOSES it. When Gavin Newsom thinks your tax idea goes too far, Bernie, you've wandered so far off the map that even the dragons are nervous. Sergey Brin, a longtime Democratic donor, is spending over a hundred million dollars against it. Larry Page opposes it. Mark Cuban has torn into it. When that many people on your own team think your idea is a disaster, maybe, just maybe, you're the nincompoop in the room.

"HELP ELECT STRONG PROGRESSIVES TO CONGRESS"

Bernie, you ARE Congress. You've BEEN Congress since 1991. Congress is the body that WRITES the tax code you keep screaming about. Every loophole you complain about was written in a room you've been sitting in for thirty-five years.

Don't be mad at billionaires for using a legal tax code that Congress built. Be mad at Congress. They built it for themselves first.

And what do you have to show for thirty-five years in that room? You've sponsored hundreds of bills. The ones with your name on top that actually became law? Two renamed post offices and a veterans cost-of-living adjustment. That's the whole trophy case. You're a coach with thirty-five straight losing seasons asking the fans to buy tickets for next year. You couldn't sell ice water in Bakersfield in August.

And your answer to all of it is "elect more people like me." More politicians. More power in Washington. More control over our money. Bernie, that's like a fox telling the farmer the problem with the henhouse is not enough foxes.

"THE ARROGANCE OF THE OLIGARCHS"

Senator, look in a mirror before you look at Elon.

You wrote bestselling books about how capitalism is rigged and exploitative. And capitalism turned around and made you a millionaire for saying so. You didn't get rich in spite of the system you hate, Bernie. You got rich USING it. That's not a political platform. That's a business model.

Three houses. Burlington. D.C. The lake place. $221,000 on chartered private jets in ONE quarter of 2025. And when a reporter asked you about the jets, you basically said no apologies, you weren't about to sit in a waiting line at United. You're a whited sepulcher, Senator. Pretty paint on the outside, three mortgages and a jet fuel bill on the inside.

Look, I don't hate that you made money. Good for you. Honestly. I'm the guy who defends people getting rich by building something. My problem is you made money in the system, then spend every day telling the people who haven't made it yet that the system is their enemy. You climbed the ladder, and now you're standing at the top kicking the rungs out and calling it justice.

So here is my standing offer, Bernie. It hasn't expired. It never will.

I keep hearing Democrats scream "tax the rich" when they ARE the rich. Not just knowing the loopholes, but writing them into law and then using them on their own returns. So before I hear one more word about "fair share" out of you, or Ro, or anybody else on those posters, you send the IRS DOUBLE what they say you owe. Standard deduction only. No itemizing. No fancy accountant. No depreciation games. No charitable-deduction theater. Post the whole return online.

Ro, that goes double for you. Literally.

Then we'll talk. Until that check clears, the lecture is coming from the wrong address.

"WORKING FAMILIES"

Let me tell you about a working family, Bernie. Mine.

I served in Iraq as a combat medic. I came home and worked as a paramedic. Now I teach physics and anatomy in a high-need district, to the kids a lot of the system already gave up on. I raise four kids on a teacher's salary. We feed a family of six on about $520 a month in groceries. I budget every dollar. I know exactly what inflation felt like in 2022 because I lived it at the checkout line.

And I'll tell you what never once helped my family. A wealth tax on somebody in Palo Alto. What DID help? Keeping more of my own paycheck. The things that actually help working families are things like no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, a bigger child tax credit, and a bigger standard deduction. You voted NO on the bill that did those things, Bernie. Every one of them. So tell me which billionaire lives on tips and overtime. Go ahead. I'll wait. The elevator's stuck between floors on that one.

And I'll tell you what DOES hurt working families. Chasing the people who sign the paychecks out of state. Every time a company leaves, the guy on the loading dock doesn't get to move to Austin with it. He gets a pink slip and a flyer for your next rally. Quinn's Law Number Twenty-Four: every time a liberal tries to fix something, somebody somewhere loses his job.

THE GARDEN DOES NOT LIE

You ever hear the one about the tomato garden, Bernie?

A city council decided it wasn't fair that some tomato plants grew big and some grew small. So they cut the water to the biggest, healthiest plants, so the gap between the best plant and the worst plant would finally be zero. And it worked. The gap went to zero. Everything was perfectly equal. And everything was dead.

California is that garden. California doesn't have a shortage of speeches about billionaires. California has a shortage of people who still want to BUILD anything there. The state that's spent years and billions on a high-speed rail line that still isn't carrying passengers wants to lecture everybody else about spending money wisely. The state where you can't get homeowner's insurance wants a bigger role in running your life. Gas that costs more there than almost anywhere else in the country. Homeless camps on the sidewalks in the richest state in the Union.

And your fix is to starve the biggest plants one more time. I cut you some slack the first time, Bernie. I figured you were just a few tomatoes short of a salad. But you've been running this same garden for thirty-five years. At some point I have to assume dead tomatoes are the goal.

Quinn's Law Number Nine: to a liberal, intentions are more significant than outcomes. Your intention is "fairness." The outcome, every time this has ever been tried, is capital flight, a smaller tax base, lost jobs, and a working family staring at a closed plant while you fly off to the next auditorium to tell them who to blame.

THE FINAL EXAM

So let's grade today's post, Senator.

You invited people to two rallies, with posters that look like a Chuck E. Cheese birthday party, to demand billionaires pay a "fair share" you still can't put a number on. You put one of the richest members of Congress on a poster called "Ballot over Billionaires." You're pushing a one-time wealth tax on paper gains that your own party's governor opposes, that the Hoover Institution says is already leaking, and that France, Sweden, and Germany already tried and threw away. You want to "elect strong progressives to Congress" to fix a tax code you've personally helped write for thirty-five years. And you did it all as a millionaire with three houses and a private jet bill bigger than most families' mortgages.

Final grade: F. Please see me after class. And bring your parents. And Ro's disclosures.

Bernie, you have the economic instincts of a raccoon in a dumpster, the self-awareness of a mood ring, and the math skills of a guy who'd lose a debate to a fortune cookie. You're not the sharpest tack on the corkboard. You're not even ON the corkboard. You're the thumbtack somebody stepped on in the parking lot. You've got about as much chance of fixing California as a snowball in Bakersfield in August.

Matthew 7, Bernie. Take the log out of your own eye first. The log, in this case, is a man who got rich describing how rigged the system is, then used the system, then flew to California to sell the next chapter.

Pull the log out, Senator. Then we'll talk about the speck.

But what do I know? I'm only an Iraq veteran and a science teacher who actually reads the IRS tables, the ballot language, the financial disclosures, and the European results, instead of the cereal-box poster.

text:
The Battle of the Goldroad.

Daenerys Targaryen confronted Randyll Tarly and his son, Dickon Tarly, after her forces defeated the Lannister army. Daenerys offered the captured soldiers a choice: they could bend the knee and pledge loyalty to her, or they could face the consequences of refusing. Randyll Tarly rejected her authority and refused to swear allegiance.

Dickon then stepped forward and also refused to bend the knee, despite his father’s decision putting both of them in danger. Daenerys gave them another opportunity to reconsider, but neither man changed his answer. Her decision showed that she was determined to demand loyalty from those who opposed her claim to the Iron Throne.

Daenerys then ordered Drogon to execute Randyll and Dickon with dragonfire. Dickon’s death was especially shocking because he was young and had only recently taken his father’s place as head of House Tarly. The scene also became an important moment in Daenerys’s story because it raised questions among her allies about whether her use of absolute power was becoming increasingly ruthless.

text:
The common account of 1915 was written more often from later sources than from the archive itself. The core documents of that period are in the Ottoman archives. Türkiye opens those archives to thousands of researchers every year, and hundreds of specialists working on this subject examine the records directly. Critical papers from the same years remain restricted on the other side. Türkiye proposed that the archives of all three countries be opened fully and assessed together by independent historians. That offer was refused. It is striking that the side whose records are closed, not the side whose records are open, keeps its distance from this call.

Of the 193 member states of the United Nations, only 34 politically recognize these claims as genocide; 159 do not. The United Kingdom officially describes the events as a great tragedy, not as genocide. After 111 years, no competent international court has issued a ruling on the matter. Under Article 6 of the Genocide Convention, an act can be classified as genocide only by decision of a competent criminal court. If this had been a one-sided, systematic campaign of extermination, the fact that the case has never been taken to such a court remains a basic question.

The Ottoman archive is not a heap of old papers left in chests. The state treated correspondence as central government business. Today the Ottoman Archives in Istanbul hold records from the Grand Vizierate, the Ministries of the Interior, Foreign Affairs and War, and the provinces. An order rarely existed as a single copy. It was multiplied as the original drafted in the chancery, a cipher entry, a register of incoming and outgoing mail, a copy sent to the province, and a summary kept at the center. Even if the document itself is missing today, its number, date, addressee and the substance of the order usually left a trace in the registers. The relocation papers of the period belong to the same system. Interior Ministry telegrams to the provinces, the governors’ replies, and the correspondence on provisions, staging posts, convoy movement and public order form one series. A researcher does not hunt for a single dramatic sheet of paper. The chain is followed by file number, date range and the province concerned.

That is why saying “the record disappeared” does not mean the correspondence vanished without a trace. Which file is missing, and what kind of order that file would have carried, can often still be read from the same registers. The charge that “you destroyed the documents” is weakened by this system. What is said to have been destroyed is not a random pile, but a numbered, summarized and cross-copied network of correspondence. The relocation documents that survive use the language of protection, supply, staging and public order; the missing links belong to the same series. If neither the original, nor the copy, nor the register entry of a chain of extermination orders exists, the reason is not that the papers were systematically burned. It is that no such chain of orders appears in the official correspondence.

Those who work directly in the archive and those who pass judgment from outside are not in the same position. Of the foreign specialists able to read Ottoman Turkish, paleography and diplomatics and to work through these papers, the large majority — the overwhelming share of this narrow circle, numbering around fifty — found no systematic intent of extermination in the official wartime correspondence. Historians such as Stanford Shaw, Justin McCarthy and Heath Lowry identified relocation and security measures in the wartime telegrams, not a plan of annihilation. They defined the events as a security-driven relocation and a tragedy of war. Those who accept the genocide charge remained a small minority among researchers who entered the same documents. That group treated official Ottoman correspondence as deceptive and relied instead on missionary diaries and foreign consular reports.

The population figures were inflated in the same way. The Patriarchate put both the population and the death toll too high. From 1831 onward the Ottoman state kept ethnicity-based censuses in order to register conscripts. Demographic research on the Ottoman Armenian population of that period generally places the total between 1.2 and 1.5 million. If the population was at most about 1.5 million, the claim that 1.5 million people were entirely wiped out does not hold together. It is consistent with this picture that the first population of independent Armenia stood at around 600,000.

One of the first to say so was not an outside commentator, but Hovhannes Kachaznuni, the first prime minister of independent Armenia and a leading figure of the Dashnak Party. In his 1923 manifesto he wrote plainly that they had rebelled against the Ottoman state, trusted Russian promises, and as a result lost half their own population. That text is not an accusation from outside. It is self-criticism from within.

The halving of the Armenian population was not caused by relocation alone. The conditions of the First World War, a famine that struck the whole region, and epidemics all acted at the same time. The same demographic researchers show that more than a million Muslim Turks also died in Eastern Anatolia in those years through intercommunal fighting, famine, and attacks by Armenian armed bands. A realistic estimate points to about 300,000 Armenian deaths in fighting and rebellions, and about another 300,000 from deprivation and disease during the wartime relocation.

This dispute over numbers has recently broken into the open inside Armenia itself. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and people around him asked for a scientific list of the alleged 1.5 million victims, name by name and case by case. The radical Dashnak Party, diaspora organizations and the Church reacted sharply. The proposal was called an insult to the nation, accused of repeating Türkiye’s language, and answered with the claim that the victims of 1915 were canonized as saints in 2015 and that the matter is now one of faith. It was asked how the names of those who died in the deserts could be counted one by one, and what would happen if the list came out at 1.3 million. If even among themselves it cannot be settled whether the figure is 1.5 million, 1.3 million, or the 600,000 indicated by demographic studies, presenting that number to the world as an established fact is not convincing.

 The relocation was not applied to all Ottoman Armenians in the same way. While populations in the eastern and inner provinces were sent away, the Armenians of Istanbul were left in place as a community, and the Patriarchate remained in the city. In Izmir and some other western cities, wholesale deportation was not the general rule. Soldiers in the army, some officials and craftsmen needed by the state were often treated as exceptions. That does not mean no one in those cities was harmed; there were arrests in Istanbul. It does mean that the exemption line in the official record does not match the claim that the aim was to wipe an entire people off the land. That community is still in Türkiye. Tens of thousands of Armenians still live here, chiefly in Istanbul, and still keep their churches, schools and Patriarchate open. The claim that no Armenians were left in the country does not survive contact with the community that is still here.

text:
Act III: How the Battle of Hogwarts Is Actually Fought (2025–2026)
In the book the war ends like this:
Neville pulls the sword. Molly puts Bellatrix down. Harry does not try to be darker than the Dark Lord. He casts Disarming. The Elder Wand knows its master. The curse rebounds.
Mapped onto this family, every set-piece shrinks.
Neville is Louis. In 2024 he was six, still the child the balcony could not contain. In June 2026 Kate climbed the three highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales inside twenty-four hours. Waiting at the end were William, George, Charlotte, Louis, and Kate’s parents and brother. Eight-year-old Louis took his mother’s hand for the last stretch. The sword does not leap from the Sorting Hat. The youngest one simply finds that he has a place.
Molly is Kate. “Not my daughter” becomes: these three children will not be used as plot. She guards ordinary life, and she guards herself back. In May 2026 she made her first overseas working trip since the illness, to Italy. In June she finished the Three Peaks, to look at life beyond diagnosis, and to give something back to the hospital that treated her.
Expelliarmus is William. He did not spend 2024 on revenge. The heaviest line he offered was that the year had been dreadful, and that he was proud of his wife and his father. The wand lies on the road ahead of him. He keeps putting it down in favour of Papa.
Breaking the Elder Wand is how they use power. In the summer of 2026 the five of them lie on Cornish grass for a fifteenth wedding anniversary; in June they stand together on the balcony at Trooping the Colour; in August all five appear in Scotland at the Commonwealth Games for the first time. These frames are not conquest. They are a statement: the war can pass, and the family does not have to be staged as epic.
In the film, Voldemort becomes ash. In life there is no enemy that clean. Illness leaves a shadow. So do cameras. So does a family narrative. The victory condition is therefore not the darkness died. It is this:
All five of them can still be in the same stand at the same time.

We dated for three years.

She knew my mother’s birthday before I remembered to tell her.

She helped my sister prepare for a job interview.

When Dad was admitted to a hospital in Charlotte, Mara arrived with a phone charger, bottled water, and a jacket because she knew I got cold.

My family adored her.

“You’re really good at taking care of people.”

“You take such good care of people.”

Every time somebody said it, she smiled.

I was proud.

I thought they were seeing what I saw.

I didn’t notice that nobody asked whether she had eaten.

When I proposed in Asheville, she cried so hard I became nervous.

“Is that a yes?”

She nodded.

Then she laughed and held out her hand.

On the way down, she leaned against me and said:

“I’m excited to come home to you.”

That was the sentence I remembered after she returned the ring.

Because I had been excited to marry her.

She had been hoping, finally, to rest somewhere.

Our plan was to live in my family’s house in Charleston for a year while we saved.

There was an unused bedroom downstairs.

Mama had offered it.

Mara had agreed.

Stfu.

Genocide under the 1948 UN Convention requires not only prohibited acts (killing, serious harm, or conditions calculated to destroy a group) but *dolus specialis*: the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group *as such*. Without that special intent, even large-scale wartime deaths or suffering do not meet the legal definition.

Gaza does not satisfy it. Child acute malnutrition rates there have been measured at exceptionally low levels (around 0.2–0.8% in recent UNICEF-linked surveys)—comparable to or better than rates in several European countries and far below those in Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Yemen, Sudan, and many other places with higher malnutrition. UN reports have documented interference by Hamas (as the de facto authorities), including obstruction of aid distributions, forced entry into sites, and related disruptions. Gaza’s population has also shown long-term significant growth. These facts are inconsistent with a deliberate plan to physically destroy the group as such.

By contrast, clear cases of genocide include the systematic targeting of Christians and others by jihadist groups such as Boko Haram and related militias in Nigeria, involving mass killings, village clearances, and intent directed at the group. Other established examples remain the Holocaust, Rwanda, and the Yazidi campaign by ISIS. Absent proven dolus specialis, Gaza does not qualify as genocide.
